Recent advancements in natural language processing (NLP) have enabled impressive capabilities in summarization, where the goal is to condense large volumes of text into concise, informative representations. However, most traditional summarization systems generate static and one-size-fits-all summaries, assuming a universal understanding or interest in the content among all readers. This approach overlooks the fact that users interact with texts differently, driven by personal interests, prior knowledge, and specific needs. A summary that is informative for one user may be irrelevant or incomplete for another, making the problem of adapting summaries to individual preferences a critical and under-explored challenge. To address this shortcoming, we propose the concept of Interactive Personalized Summarization (IPS), a novel paradigm that shifts focus from monolithic, generic summaries to an approach where summarization is shaped iteratively through user interaction. IPS opens the door to dynamic interactions, where users indicate their preferences in real-time (e.g., through clicks), and the summarization system incorporated these signals to tailor the output accordingly. This enables the generation of summaries that not only condense source documents effectively, but also align with the unique context and intent of each user. In this work, we present an optimization framework designed for IPS, combining two core capabilities: interaction modeling and personalized summary generation. Specifically, the framework dynamically adjusts summary content based on user feedback, ensuring that the output evolves alongside the user’s exploration of the document content. To evaluate our approach, we conducted comprehensive experiments across four diverse datasets comprising 5,197 documents. We compared our IPS framework with five competing summarization algorithms in both automatic and human evaluations. Although the system achieves results comparable to the best performer in terms of ROUGE metrics—a widely used measure of summary quality—our findings reveal a substantial advantage in user satisfaction, as measured by human evaluators. Notably, the lower ROUGE consistency among the summaries generated by the user-preferred models underscores the fundamental idea of personalization: summaries that are better aligned with individual interests can differ significantly in structure and content from one another, even when expressing the same source information. This work contributes to the broader vision of personalized NLP systems by formalizing the interactive summarization problem and demonstrating a principled approach to building systems that are as adaptive as they are functional. By enabling a more engaging and relevant summary experience, the framework not only improves user experience but also redefines the role of the user in the summarization pipeline.

Legal systems play a critical role in maintaining justice and order in society. One of the essential components of this system is the accurate determination of appropriate charges for a given case. This is particularly important in the development of legal assistant systems where users often provide factual descriptions of events, and the system is expected to generate a relevant legal response. The   charge prediction task  , which involves determining the most appropriate charges based on a given set of facts, has gained increasing attention in the field of legal technology and artificial intelligence. This task supports legal professionals by providing quick and informed decisions, reducing the risk of human error, and improving the efficiency of the justice system. However, accurately predicting charges is a complex and nuanced process. Laws and regulations are often intricate and context-dependent, making it challenging for automated systems to determine the most relevant legal provisions. In practice, relevant law articles serve as the foundation for charge decisions, and their inclusion is not only necessary for legal compliance but also for improving the accuracy of predictive models. Existing approaches to charge prediction have primarily focused on statistical or machine learning models based on factual descriptions of cases, without explicitly leveraging the legal basis underpinning the charges. In this paper, we argue that relevant law articles play a pivotal role in the charge prediction task. We propose an   attention-based neural network method   that integrates the charge prediction task with the   relevant article extraction task   in a unified framework. This method ensures that while the system predicts the most appropriate charge for a given case, it simultaneously captures and utilizes the most relevant law articles to support the prediction. By doing so, the model is not only improving its predictive accuracy but also providing   interpretable results   rooted in legal principles. Our experimental results demonstrate that incorporating relevant law articles significantly enhances the performance of charge prediction models. Furthermore, the proposed   attention-based unified model   proves to be effective in handling the   variability in the expression styles   of fact descriptions, which is a common challenge in legal data. The provision of legal basis does more than fulfill procedural requirements; it enhances the model's ability to discern subtle distinctions between similar charges based on nuanced factual scenarios. Ultimately, this work contributes to the advancement of   artificial intelligence-based legal decision-support systems   by integrating legal knowledge as an essential component of the learning process.

Sentence semantic equivalence identification (SSEI) is a fundamental task in natural language processing that aims to determine whether two sentences convey the same meaning or not. Its applications range from information retrieval to question answering, making it an essential area of research in both academic and industrial settings. While significant progress has been made in English SSEI, research in other languages, particularly Chinese, lags behind due to the lack of high-quality, domain-specific datasets. This is especially true in specialized domains such as the banking sector, where language use can be complex, jargon-heavy, and often differs from general-purpose text. In this context, the development of domain-specific Chinese datasets for SSEI is crucial to advance language understanding and cross-domain linguistic research. To address this gap, we introduce the Bank Question (BQ) corpus, a large-scale Chinese corpus specifically designed for sentence semantic equivalence identification in the banking domain. The BQ corpus is composed of 120,000 question pairs extracted from one year of online customer service logs of a bank. The scale and domain specificity of the dataset make it a valuable resource for both theoretical and applied research in Chinese lexical semantics and semantic matching. By drawing from real-world customer interactions, the corpus captures the nuances, variations, and linguistic patterns characteristic of the banking context, which are often absent in datasets constructed using crowdsourcing or web mining from general domains. A major challenge in preparing such a large-scale, manually annotated corpus is the efficiency of annotation. Given the sheer number of question logs and the high degree of variations in phrasing, a purely manual annotation process would be both time-consuming and resource-intensive. To tackle this, we propose a clustering-based annotation method that leverages the Word Mover's Distance (WMD) and Affinity Propagation (AP) algorithm. This approach groups semantically similar questions into clusters before the annotation process, effectively reducing the workload on annotators and ensuring consistent intent categorization. This methodology not only streamlines the annotation process but also ensures the quality and reliability of the final dataset. To further validate the usefulness of the BQ corpus, we present benchmark evaluation results using state-of-the-art SSEI models, demonstrating its practical relevance and performance characteristics. We hope that the BQ corpus will serve as a vital resource for the NLP community, enabling advances in both Chinese-focused and cross-lingual semantic matching research.

Recent advancements in natural language processing (NLP) have demonstrated the effectiveness of pre-trained word embeddings and language models in a wide range of tasks, from text classification to machine translation. These models are trained on vast amounts of unlabeled text and are capable of capturing semantic and syntactic properties of words, making them powerful tools in many downstream applications. However, dependency parsing, which aims to explicitly identify the grammatical structure of sentences by establishing relationships between words, often demands more than just semantic or sequential understanding. In particular, conventional pre-trained models may not directly capture the local and long-range connections between words essential for accurate parsing. This paper addresses the gap by focusing on a novel approach to improve dependency parsing through the implicit modeling of word connections derived directly from unlabeled data. Dependency parsing is one of the core tasks in syntactic analysis and forms a cornerstone of more complex NLP systems, such as information extraction and semantic role labeling. Traditional parsers rely heavily on annotated corpora and hand-crafted features, limiting their scalability and adaptability. Although neural models in recent years have reduced the reliance on manual feature engineering, the performance of these models is still heavily contingent on the availability of labeled data, which is often scarce or expensive to obtain for many languages and domains. In contrast to this, unlabeled data, which is inherently abundant, remains underutilized for capturing syntactic phenomena like word dependencies. In this work, we explore how implicit word connections can be learned from unlabeled text using a word ordering model augmented with a self-attention mechanism. The self-attention architecture allows the model to dynamically weigh the importance of different words in a sentence, effectively discovering implicit syntactic relations without explicit supervision. These learned connections are then incorporated as features into a state-of-the-art dependency parsing model. Our experimental results demonstrate that this approach significantly boosts performance, with substantial improvements in both unlabeled and labeled attachment scores. We further explore the synergy between these learned implicit connections and pre-trained language models. By integrating our proposed unigram transformation method with the outputs of a pre-trained language model, our system generates state-of-the-art accuracy metrics on the English Penn Treebank dataset. These results highlight the potential of combining unsupervised syntactic learning with deep contextual representations to enhance parsing models beyond what is achievable by individual components alone.

The identification and analysis of multiword expressions (MWEs) has long been a significant challenge in natural language processing (NLP), particularly in the context of syntactic parsing and semantic interpretation. MWEs, such as phrasal verbs, idioms, or fixed expressions, often exhibit lexical cohesion and unique syntactic or semantic behavior that deviates from standard compositional analysis. This issue is especially relevant in dependency parsing, where the standard approach focuses on sentence-wide grammatical structure without accounting for the internal syntactic relations within MWEs. To address this, contemporary research has increasingly aimed to integrate MWE analysis into the parsing process. This paper contributes to these efforts by investigating strategies for jointly predicting syntactic dependencies and the internal structure of contiguous MWEs. Specifically, we focus on a method that explicitly models the syntactic regularity of MWEs, allowing for their structural representation alongside the broader sentence syntactic structure. We test our approach using the dependency version of the French Treebank (Abeillé and Barrier, 2004) as instantiated in the SPMRL 2013–2015 Shared Tasks, which provide annotated syntactic and MWE information for this purpose. Our work is motivated by the idea that to fully understand and utilize MWEs, we need to move beyond simply identifying them and toward describing their internal grammatical structure. By doing so, we can capture not only the lexical and syntactic properties of MWEs but also their semantic compositionality—ranging from idiomatic expressions with fixed meaning to semi-compositional MWEs whose meanings are predictable from their components. This has important implications for downstream tasks such as machine translation, semantic role labeling, and information extraction, where being able to model the structure of MWEs provides a crucial boost in parsing accuracy and interpretation fidelity. Our system employs an alternative representation of syntactically regular MWEs that integrates their internal dependencies with those of the overarching sentence structure. Experimental results show that our approach achieves performance comparable to existing parsing systems on the dataset, while providing richer output by capturing both the external syntactic dependencies and the internal structure of MWEs. This dual focus makes our approach particularly valuable for tasks and models requiring fine-grained syntactic and semantic modeling of MWEs. Furthermore, our findings highlight the potential of integrating MWE structure into syntactic parsing frameworks, opening the door for novel architectures that better align linguistic theory with practical NLP applications. In the following sections, we will elaborate on the background and existing approaches to MWE analysis and dependency parsing, present our methodology for modeling syntactically regular MWEs, describe the experimental setup and results, and discuss the implications of our findings for future research.

Recent advancements in natural language processing have led to the widespread adoption of neural network-based language models, commonly referred to as Continuous-Space Language Models (CSLMs). These models, which leverage deep learning architectures to model language in a distributed vector space, have demonstrated significant improvements in capturing the syntactic and semantic nuances of natural languages. In the context of statistical machine translation (SMT), CSLMs have primarily been employed as rerankers, where they refine a set of top n-best candidate translations generated from a primary SMT system. This usage has yielded promising results, as CSLMs effectively exploit long-range dependencies and context in a way that traditional models often fail to achieve. Despite these successes, CSLMs remain underutilized during the first-pass decoding phase of SMT systems due to the computational inefficiencies inherent in integrating them into the decoding process. Unlike traditional n-gram back-off language models, which are computationally lightweight and can be seamlessly integrated with dynamic programming-based decoders such as beam search, CSLMs require complex neural operations that are time-consuming and memory-intensive during real-time translation. As a result, the full potential of CSLMs in driving the generation of initial translations has remained largely untapped. To address this limitation, we propose a novel approach for converting trained CSLMs into back-off n-gram language models (BNLMs). Our method enables the effective approximation of CSLM behavior using a traditional n-gram structure, making it feasible to incorporate the richness of neural language models directly into the decoding stage of SMT systems. The conversion process is designed to maintain the predictive capabilities and linguistic generalization of the original CSLMs while ensuring compatibility with standard SMT toolchains. Our experiments demonstrate that the converted BNLMs not only outperform the original n-gram models but also achieve performance comparable to the use of CSLMs as rerankers. This finding suggests that the information encapsulated in CSLMs can be effectively distilled into a more tractable form without a significant loss of modeling quality. By bridging the gap between the expressiveness of neural language models and the computational efficiency required for decoding, our approach opens new avenues for integrating advanced language modeling techniques into the early stages of translation pipelines. This could ultimately lead to more efficient and higher-quality statistical machine translation systems. In the following sections, we elaborate on related work, describe the proposed conversion framework in detail, present our experimental setup and results, and discuss implications for future research.

Recent advancements in natural language processing (NLP) have enabled significant progress in understanding temporal information in text, an essential component for tasks like event sequencing and temporal reasoning. Among the core challenges in this domain is  Temporal Relation Identification  (TRI), which involves determining the temporal relationships between events and time expressions in text. These temporal relations can be broadly classified into three types: event-time (ET), where an event is temporally related to a time expression; event-event (EE), involving the relationship between two event mentions; and document reference time (DT), where an event is related to the time the document refers to, often the document creation time. While previous approaches often focus on modeling these relations independently—typically through pairwise learning formulations—they often fail to consider the rich and complex logical interdependencies that exist among these relation types. In this paper, we argue that the relationships between events, time expressions, and the document reference time are not isolated but are subject to a set of logical constraints. For example, if an event $ e_1 $ occurs before another event $ e_2 $ (an EE relation), and $ e_2 $ is determined to have occurred after a certain time point $ t $ (an ET relation), it logically follows that $ e_1 $ must also be before $ t $. These inferences are not considered in pairwise approaches, leading to suboptimal performance and the potential for logical inconsistencies in the predicted temporal relations. To address this limitation, we introduce a novel approach for jointly identifying temporal relations of all three types—ET, EE, and DT—by formulating the task within the framework of  Markov Logic Network  (MLN). MLN allows the integration of logical rules with probabilistic graphical models, making it well-suited for capturing the complex, structured dependencies among different types of temporal relations. Our model not only learns the relations but also leverages domain knowledge expressed as logical constraints to guide inference and enhance coherence in predictions. Through extensive experiments on the widely used TempEval dataset, we demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach. Our experiments show improvements of approximately 2% in overall accuracy compared to event-pairwise baselines, and we achieve state-of-the-art performance among existing machine learning-based systems. These results underscore the value of integrating logical constraints and joint modeling in temporal relation identification, and highlight the potential of Markov Logic for structured prediction tasks in NLP.

Answering factoid questions—such as "Who created the character Harry Potter?"—is a foundational task in natural language processing that enables systems to understand and retrieve factual information from semi-structured knowledge sources like knowledge bases. While recent years have seen significant progress in artificial intelligence and machine learning, the challenge of mapping natural language questions to precise facts in large-scale knowledge bases remains formidable. This is largely due to the diverse and often ambiguous ways in which humans express questions that point to a single factual piece of information. For instance, the question "Who was the founder of Harry Potter" may be expressed as "Who invented the character Harry Potter" or even "Who wrote the books about Harry Potter?" The cornerstone of factoid question answering is the existence of large-scale knowledge bases (KBs), which are structured repositories of factual triples (subject-predicate-object). These KBs provide the factual ground truth necessary for answering open-domain questions. However, the difficulty lies in bridging the gap between the free, often noisy structure of human language and the rigid schema of these knowledge graphs. Furthermore, as these knowledge bases scale to millions or billions of facts, retrieval over them demands efficient and precise modeling. In this work, we propose a neural framework tailored for factoid question answering over large-scale KBs. Our method, CFO (Conditional Focused), is designed to address key challenges such as ambiguity in question phrasing and the vastness of the knowledge base. The CFO method builds on the premise that answering factoid questions hinges on two main components: identifying the most relevant KB entities (subject mentions) from the question, and accurately retrieving the correct predicate-object pair given the identified subject. It therefore combines entity-focused reasoning with conditional inference over the KB. Powered by deep recurrent neural networks and neural embeddings, our approach leverages end-to-end learning to understand complex linguistic structures while maintaining the efficiency required to scale to real-world question-answering systems. Our experiments demonstrate that CFO not only outperforms the current state-of-the-art methods by 11.8% absolute accuracy on a large dataset of 108k open-domain factoid questions but also achieves robust generalization across diverse question formulations. This performance improvement makes our approach particularly promising for deploying question-answering systems in real-world applications that require scalability and high accuracy. Our contributions include the design of an effective conditional focusing mechanism, a unified probabilistic inference framework, and the demonstration of how deep learning can be effectively applied to factoid question answering at scale.

The task of explicit discourse relation recognition (EDRR) is pivotal in understanding coherence in textual structure, particularly in identifying how clauses or sentences are related to one another within a discourse. In English and other widely studied languages, much research has focused on discourse connectives—markers that signal the relationship between discourse units. However, the interpretation of discourse connectives in Chinese presents a more complex landscape due to the language's structural and morphological characteristics. Chinese discourse connectives exhibit a variety of forms and uses that are often not directly translatable into English, and their function is influenced by factors such as the type of connective (word-pair or single-word), the direction of linking (forward or backward), their syntactic position, and their levels of ambiguity. These characteristics make the recognition of discourse relations a challenging task, especially when relying purely on linguistic rules or rule-based systems. This paper investigates the specific features of Chinese discourse connectives and how they affect the identification of explicit discourse relations. We propose that a deeper understanding of connective behavior, including their variability in form and function, is essential for improving EDRR performance. To this end, we present a semisupervised learning approach that leverages both a small labeled dataset and a much larger unlabeled corpus. The method learns the probability distributions of discourse functions associated with each connective, enabling it to generalize effectively from limited labeled data. By analyzing the statistical patterns of connective usage, our approach uncovers interesting linguistic phenomena. For example, we observe that synonyms often share similar distributional patterns, certain connectives can serve multiple discourse functions, and in many cases, the presence of coupled elements provides strong clues for resolving the underlying discourse relations. Our semisupervised method is evaluated on a Chinese discourse dataset and demonstrates promising results in capturing the complex and context-sensitive behavior of Chinese connectives. The insights derived not only enhance the performance of discourse relation recognition models but also contribute to broader research on discourse markers and their roles in cross-linguistic analysis. This work bridges the gap between linguistic theory and computational modeling by demonstrating how statistical patterns in unlabeled data can reveal subtle yet meaningful discourse relations. By focusing on the interpretive aspects of Chinese connectives, we hope to advance the state-of-the-art in NLP systems for discourse analysis and contribute to a more nuanced understanding of how meaning is constructed across sentences in Chinese discourse.

The Transformer (Vaswani et al., 2017) has revolutionized the field of machine translation through its self-attention mechanism and parallelization capabilities, enabling large-scale training and setting a new standard for translation quality across a variety of language pairs. Despite these remarkable advances, the Transformer architecture, like its predecessors, primarily operates on sentence-level input, often neglecting higher-level discourse and document-level contextual information that is crucial for accurate translation in real-world settings. Document-level phenomena such as anaphora, coherence, and referential consistency are often problematic when translated using models trained solely on sentence-level parallel corpora, as the models lack the ability to maintain context across multiple sentences or paragraphs. This shortcoming has led to increasing interest in extending Transformer-based models to incorporate document-level context, with numerous approaches proposed to integrate contextual information from surrounding sentences or entire documents. However, these methods often face two major challenges: (1) most document-level translation corpora are extremely limited in size and availability compared to monolingual and sentence-level data, and (2) the integration of document-level signals into the Transformer architecture is non-trivial due to constraints in memory and computational efficiency. In this work, we address these challenges by proposing a novel approach to enhance the Transformer translation model with document-level context. Our contribution lies in the design of a document-level context encoder that captures and propagates contextual information across sentences, enriching the representations in both the encoder and decoder of the Transformer. Importantly, we develop a two-step training method that leverages the abundance of sentence-level parallel data and the scarcity of document-level data in a principled way: pre-training the model on sentence-level corpora to establish a strong foundational performance, followed by fine-tuning with document-level data to adapt the model to context-aware translation. This method ensures maximal utilization of available resources while avoiding the problem of data scarcity in document-level training. We evaluate our approach on two widely used translation benchmarks: the NIST Chinese-English datasets and the IWSLT French-English datasets. Our experiments demonstrate that the introduction of document-level context through our extended model results in significant improvements in translation quality compared to the standard Transformer baseline. These results highlight the importance of integrating contextual information into neural machine translation systems and establish a promising direction for improving the performance of Transformer-based models in document-level translation tasks.

Recent advancements in natural language processing (NLP) have enabled parsing technologies to move beyond sentence-level analysis and begin modeling discourse structure — the way sentences and beyond are connected in a coherent whole. Discourse parsing, by identifying the relationships between discourse segments, plays a pivotal role in tasks like question answering, text summarization, and machine translation. However, despite the remarkable progress of probabilistic discourse parsers, their output remains far from optimal in terms of capturing complex hierarchical and semantic dependencies across discourse units. To this end, post-processing methods such as reranking have emerged as a promising strategy to refine the output of initial parsers. Reranking involves reevaluating the output of a prior parser using a more powerful, potentially discriminative model. The goal is to select the parse that best represents the underlying discourse structure by leveraging richer features and global contextual information. Tree kernels, a class of feature-based methods, have been shown to be particularly effective for capturing complex structural dependencies in trees and are well-suited for reranking tasks. Inspired by this potential, in this paper, we propose a discriminative reranking approach to refine discourse parse outputs using tree kernel methods. Unlike traditional reranking approaches that rely on manual feature engineering or local contextual heuristics, we introduce a framework that capitalizes on the global hierarchical properties of discourse trees. The key innovation of our work lies in the design of novel computational structures tailored for discourse trees, which are combined with standard tree kernel formulations to create new discourse-specific tree kernels. These kernels encode structural and semantic patterns across discourse relations, enabling the reranker to make more informed decisions in selecting superior discourse parses. We evaluate our reranking model extensively on standard discourse parsing benchmarks. Our results demonstrate that the proposed approach significantly improves the state-of-the-art sentence-level parsing accuracy from 79.77% to 82.15%, representing a relative error reduction of 11.8%. Moreover, this improvement at the sentence level translates to a notable boost in document-level parsing accuracy, increasing from 55.8% to 57.3%. These results underscore the effectiveness of the proposed reranking framework and highlight the utility of discriminative models incorporating tree kernels in discourse parsing tasks. As such, this work contributes to both theoretical and applied discourse analysis by advancing a new methodology that enables more accurate and robust capture of discourse structures. This paper builds on and extends the work described in the go-to introduction on this subject, aligning with its core findings and objectives.

Temporal relation extraction (TRE) is a crucial task in natural language processing, especially for constructing timelines and event-based summaries. The goal is to determine the temporal order or coincidence between events mentioned in a text. In previous studies, most systems focus on sentence-level information or consider only the coherence of different temporal relation types within the same sentence or adjacent sentences. While these approaches have made significant progress, they often neglect the relationships that span nonadjacent sentences. These so-called  discourse-level  temporal relations are critical for understanding the broader timeline of events in a document, as they can affect the overall temporal structure when event mentions appear in distant parts of the text. Previous work primarily assumes that temporal relations can be effectively inferred based on local contextual cues, such as temporal connectives like "after" or "before," or based on syntactic structure. However, this assumption is limited in capturing event semantics and broader discourse features. Additionally, local models often fail to maintain global consistency across the entire document, leading to fragmented and potentially contradictory temporal relations. In this paper, we propose a novel discourse-level global inference model to address these limitations in the context of Chinese temporal relation extraction. Our key contribution is the modeling of event mentions at the document level, incorporating long-range dependencies that reflect temporal relations across nonadjacent sentences. This is particularly important in Chinese, where temporal markers and discourse relations may be more implicit or rely on shared contextual knowledge. To enhance our approach, we further incorporate various types of  discourse-level constraints  derived from the semantics of events and the structure of the document. For example, if an event is described in one part of the document as a prerequisite or consequence of another event mentioned later, our model integrates such semantic expectations into the inference process. To validate the effectiveness of our proposed model, we conduct experiments on a Chinese temporal relation annotated corpus. Our results demonstrate the superiority of our discourse-level global inference model over two strong baselines that are based on sentence-level or local contextual modeling. Specifically, we show improvements in both precision and recall, indicating that our approach generates more accurate and consistent temporal relations at the document level. These findings suggest that focusing on global inference and discourse-level features is a promising direction for improving the performance of temporal relation extraction systems, especially for languages like Chinese with complex and sometimes implicit temporal expressions.

Recent advancements in natural language processing have equipped researchers with powerful tools to automatically extract relevant information from vast textual resources. Among these tasks, relation extraction stands out as a crucial step in understanding the semantic structure between entities in text. Traditional relation extraction systems often rely on annotated corpora, which are labor-intensive and domain-dependent. To address these limitations, distantly supervised relation extraction (DSRE) has been widely adopted. This approach leverages existing knowledge graphs, such as Freebase or Wikidata, to automatically label training data, thereby enabling large-scale relation extraction without manual annotation. However, while distant supervision has proven effective at scaling relation extraction, it introduces a critical challenge: the wrong labeling problem. Since only one relation is assumed to hold between the entity mentions in a sentence, and this is determined by matching entity pairs with knowledge graph triples, many sentences are incorrectly labeled, leading to noisy training data. Although numerous methods have been proposed to tackle label noise in DSRE by incorporating deep contextual representations, uncertainty modeling, and instance-level filtering, most existing approaches treat relations as isolated entities, ignoring the rich semantic structure that can be captured through hierarchical relationships among them. In real-world knowledge graphs, relations often form complex taxonomies, where some relations are specializations of broader ones (e.g.,  person born in city  as a specialization of  person related to location ). Exploiting these hierarchical relationships can provide valuable supervisory signals to improve extraction, especially for rare or long-tail relations that often lack sufficient training examples. In this paper, we explore the integration of relational hierarchies into the modeling process for distantly supervised relation extraction. We introduce a novel hierarchical attention mechanism that explicitly encodes relation hierarchies and operates in a coarse-to-fine manner. Our method allows the model to progressively focus on more specific relation types based on the hierarchical structure, enabling the model to better leverage the semantic context present in the relation taxonomy. This hierarchical filtering becomes particularly beneficial for extracting tail-end relations, which are often overlooked in flat modeling approaches. Extensive experiments on a large-scale benchmark dataset demonstrate that our hierarchical attention-based approach significantly outperforms state-of-the-art baselines. We further provide an analysis of the performance gains across different levels of the relation hierarchy, highlighting the usefulness of our method in capturing semantic relationships. Our work advances the field of relation extraction by demonstrating that modeling relation hierarchies can yield substantial improvements, especially when confronting the challenges of noisy distant supervision.

Multi-label classification is a fundamental task in natural language processing (NLP), where an input text can be associated with multiple labels simultaneously. In real-world scenarios, especially in domains like medicine, computer vision, and knowledge base construction, datasets often exhibit highly imbalanced label distributions. That is, while some labels appear frequently, others may be under-represented (few-shot) or even absent (zero-shot) in the training data. Most of the traditional multi-label learning frameworks are evaluated under the assumption of a large, balanced label space, leaving open questions about their effectiveness under practical imbalances and the absence of labels during training. This paper addresses the under-explored problem of few-shot and zero-shot multi-label classification, particularly when the labels are associated with a known hierarchical or semantic structure. Although recent work has explored general few-shot and zero-shot learning in NLP, the multi-label setting, especially for text classification, has received limited attention. Structured label spaces—wherein labels are organized in a taxonomy or semantic graph—offer a rich inductive bias that can be leveraged to improve performance on labels with sparse or no training examples. Our goal is to develop methods that utilize this structure to enhance prediction accuracy in both the few-shot and zero-shot regimes. A critical challenge in few- and zero-shot learning is the generalization of the model to unseen data, without requiring retraining. We adapt and extend state-of-the-art multi-label learning techniques to account for the label structure and demonstrate how incorporating domain knowledge can significantly improve prediction for infrequent or unseen labels. We conduct a comprehensive and fine-grained evaluation on two large-scale medical text classification datasets—MIMIC II and MIMIC III—both of which exhibit a wide variation in label frequency and rich hierarchical structure. Our experimental results show that our proposed methods achieve substantial improvements over prior approaches: for few-shot labels, we observe R@10 accuracy gains of 6.2% and 4.8% on MIMIC II and MIMIC III, respectively. More importantly, for zero-shot labels, we achieve significant improvements of 17.3% and 19% in R@10 on the respective datasets. We discuss the implications of these findings for scalability of learning systems to dynamically expanding label spaces and demonstrate the practical relevance of our approach in domains like medical text understanding, where new labels are frequently introduced without annotated training data. This work contributes both a deeper understanding of model behavior on structurally complex, imbalanced multi-label tasks and a scalable framework for label prediction in high-stakes applications.

Recent advancements in natural language processing (NLP) have enabled impressive improvements in a wide range of tasks, including syntactic parsing, semantic role labeling, and question answering. However, despite these gains, Word Sense Disambiguation (WSD) remains a persistent challenge, particularly in the context of all-words WSD, where the goal is to disambiguate the meaning of every content word in a text. This task has not seen a commensurate improvement, with systems still struggling to generalize adequately, especially for low-frequency word senses. In fact, contemporary WSD systems often exhibit a significant drop in accuracy when confronted with test instances belonging to senses that were either rare or even absent in the training data. This shortcoming is largely attributable to the disparities in sense distributions between training and test corpora—a problem exacerbated by the inherent variability of word usage across domains and contexts. Most prior work on addressing this issue has focused on either expanding the volume of training data through unsupervised or semi-supervised acquisition techniques or creating task-specific supervision in the form of sense inventories and annotated corpora, often tailored to the predominant sense. While such efforts are important, they tend to neglect the influence of meta properties of the data—such as the volume of data available for each sense, the provenance of the training samples (i.e., their origin and composition), and the balance between competing senses—on the final performance of WSD systems. These factors are critical in determining the system's ability to generalize to out-of-distribution examples and capture the nuances of polysemous words, which form the backbone of semantic richness in language. This paper investigates the role of these meta properties in WSD system performance and proposes a data-centric strategy to address the imbalance in sense distribution between training and evaluation sets. Working within the framework of a state-of-the-art WSD system, we conduct a series of experiments on the widely used SemEval-2013 English all-words dataset. Our findings reveal that both volume and provenance of training data are crucial for performance. More importantly, we demonstrate that actively balancing the sense distribution of training data—despite the intuitive advantage of including more data—can significantly boost performance by 21 points over unbalanced baselines, and even surpass the state-of-the-art by 14 points, using only simple features. These results advocate for rethinking current data acquisition strategies by incorporating explicit considerations of sense distribution and meta properties.

The dynamic nature of social media platforms has transformed them into vast ecosystems for opinion formation, expression, and propagation. Companies and researchers alike leverage these platforms to understand public sentiment towards products, events, and social issues. In such environments, a person's opinion is not formed in isolation; it is often shaped by a mixture of the content they encounter and the influence exerted by their social contacts. Traditional approaches to modeling opinion formation predominantly treat opinions as discrete or continuous values that evolve through predefined influence functions, typically based on social network interactions. However, these models often fail to capture the richer context provided by the semantic content of the opinions themselves, which plays a crucial role in shaping individual beliefs. Recent advancements in natural language processing (NLP) and deep learning have shown significant promise in analyzing and understanding text-based opinions. Yet, integrating content semantics into opinion influence modeling remains underexplored. Existing models either ignore the textual content altogether or treat it as an auxiliary signal for sentiment analysis, without explicitly modeling how content details influence an individual's changing views over time. The gap between the social interaction-based opinions and the content-driven insights limits the accuracy and interpretability of opinion prediction tasks. In this paper, we propose a Content-based Social Influence Model (CSIM) that explicitly considers both the semantic information embedded in user-generated content and the social relationships among users. Our model captures two complementary influence components: one derived from the content itself—what users are saying, and how it relates to prior opinions—and the other derived from social connections—how strong and prevalent a certain opinion is among a user’s peers. By combining these two components, the proposed model is able to uncover the implicit mechanisms that drive opinion evolution. The ability to incorporate meaningful semantic signals is a key advantage of our approach. Unlike traditional models that treat opinions as abstract sentiment scores, CSIM operates on rich textual features to reflect the true language-based opinions of users. This allows for a more nuanced and accurate prediction of future opinions. Furthermore, the model is trained on real-world social media data, where opinions are naturally expressed in free text, making it directly applicable to real-life use cases. We evaluate our proposed model on Twitter datasets, demonstrating that it significantly outperforms existing opinion formation models in terms of predictive accuracy.

The task of documenting understudied languages, particularly in the context of field linguistics, is both challenging and essential for linguistic diversity and heritage preservation. Central to this endeavor is the accurate annotation of syntactic structures, such as dependencies between words in a sentence. Dependency parsing has emerged as a valuable tool in linguistic analysis, allowing linguists to visualize and understand the grammatical relationships within a language. Field linguists, however, often work with minimal data and limited computational tools tailored to their specific needs. This paper addresses the challenge of building and using a dependency parser that is suitable for the low-resource, high-flexibility context of language documentation in the field. Our central contribution is to explore the feasibility of  incrementally learning a dependency parser —a parser trained on very small amounts of data and updated as more annotated examples become available. The parser is designed to integrate into the WordsEye Linguistics Tools (WELT), a suite of tools developed to support linguists during the process of eliciting and analyzing language data from native speaker informants (Ulinski et al., 2014a, 2014b). One of the key functionalities of WELT involves the documentation of spatial and motion event descriptions, typically elicited through pictures and video clips. To support the training and evaluation of our parser, we have created a new parallel corpus comprising descriptions of such events in English, Spanish, German, and Egyptian Arabic. These descriptions, collected from native speakers, provide a rich dataset for exploring syntactic structure across typologically diverse languages. The parser must be robust to linguistic variation and capable of functioning in an environment where annotation is often a collaborative and interactive process between the linguist and the parser. We evaluate the performance of two widely used dependency parsers—MSTParser (McDonald et al., 2006) and MaltParser (Nivre et al., 2006)—in this low-data scenario. Notably, we find that MaltParser performs more reliably when trained on limited data, making it a suitable candidate for integration into WELT. Through user experiments, we also show that even with minimal training (as few as one sentence), the parser can drastically reduce the time field linguists spend on manual syntactic annotation. This finding underscores the potential of incrementally trained parsers as an effective aid in language documentation, where efficiency and adaptability are critical. More broadly, our work contributes to the growing field of  linguistically aware NLP systems , emphasizing the design of tools that support human-in-the-loop linguistic analysis rather than attempting to fully automate it.

Name-aware Machine Translation is a crucial yet underspecified area in natural language processing, especially for handling multilingual content where proper nouns such as personal names, locations, organizations, and other named entities (NEs) play a central role in conveying meaning. Despite the impressive progress of neural machine translation (NMT) systems, the translation of named entities remains a challenging task, often resulting in distortions, omissions, or inaccurate translations that can degrade fluency and informativeness in translated text. These errors are particularly problematic in contexts such as news, legal, or biomedical documents, where the precise translation of names and identifiers is essential for preserving the factual accuracy and readability of the content. The conventional approach to name translation is often post-processing-driven and relies on separate modules for identification and translation of named entities, which are later integrated into the overall translation process. However, this modular approach leads to information loss and a lack of coordination between the detection of names and their translation, often resulting in errors when incorporated into the final output. To address these limitations, this paper introduces a   Name-aware Machine Translation (Name-MT)   framework that tightly integrates named entity processing into the architecture and training procedure of the MT model. Our proposed approach innovatively combines three key components: (1) the joint annotation and alignment of names in parallel corpora, which ensures that the model is exposed to consistent and accurate bilingual name information during training; (2) the extraction of name-aware translation grammar and rules, which help guide the model in learning to preserve and translate names more accurately; and (3) the incorporation of a name phrase table and a name-driven decoding strategy, which further refine the generation of names during translation. In addition to model development, we propose a   Weighted Translation Metric (WTM)   that evaluates the translation quality by assigning importance weights to words based on their contribution to the overall document's informativeness. This is especially useful for evaluating named entities and other key terms that are critical for the coherence and relevance of translated text. Experimental results on a Chinese-English translation task show that our Name-MT approach significantly outperforms strong NMT baselines in both overall translation quality and name translation accuracy, demonstrating the effectiveness of jointly integrating name processing into the translation pipeline. Our work provides a compelling step toward more informed and context-aware translation models suitable for real-world, domain-sensitive applications where proper name translation is crucial.

The ability to communicate is a defining feature of human language, enabling cooperation, coordination, and social understanding. Communication, however, presents a uniquely challenging problem in terms of its cognitive and computational underpinnings. In his seminal formulation, Paul Grice proposed that successful communication relies on the Cooperative Principle—  the implicit assumption that speakers make conversational contributions that are relevant, of high quality, and appropriately informative  —together with the associated maxims. These normative constraints, which have since become a cornerstone of pragmatic theory, suggest that effective communication is not just about encoding and decoding messages, but also about rational behavior shaped by mutual expectations. This paper asks whether these Gricean maxims arise naturally from rational principles in multi-agent systems, rather than being imposed arbitrarily by linguistic conventions. We argue that the Cooperative Principle and its associated maxims—  Relevance, Quality, Quantity, and, implicitly, Manner—can be derived from an underlying framework of rational decision-making   when agents engage in collaborative tasks and must reason about each other's beliefs and actions. Our approach moves beyond normative pragmatics into computational modeling by showing that Gricean constraints emerge from the combination of rational, utility-maximizing behavior and the inherent structure of cooperative problem-solving in decentralized environments. We employ the   Decentralized Partially Observable Markov Decision Process (Dec-POMDP)   as a formal model for multi-agent decision-making. This model captures the complexities of collaborative reasoning, where agents must act in a shared, uncertain environment and have only partial access to the state of the world. Importantly, in this framework, improvements in task performance depend not only on an agent's own actions but also on its ability to predict the actions and beliefs of others. This interagent reasoning is central to the emergence of Gricean communication. To make this computational model cognitively plausible, we incorporate   heuristics inspired by human reasoning strategies  , which enable agents to approximate the joint beliefs and utilities of a group while avoiding the computational intractability of precise inference. Our experiments in a cooperative task involving communication demonstrate that agents using these heuristics progressively develop behavior that aligns with the Gricean maxims. As a result, their collaborative performance improves significantly compared to agents whose communication is unregulated by such principles. This work bridges the gap between descriptive pragmatics and decision theory, offering a new perspective on the origins of cooperative communication. It suggests that Gricean norms are not merely linguistic conventions, but   emergent properties of rational agents in a shared interactive environment  .

The task of mapping natural language sentences to their corresponding logical meanings is a fundamental challenge in computational semantics and natural language processing (NLP). This problem, often referred to as semantic parsing, involves inducing a mapping from syntactically structured sentences to formal representations of their meaning, such as lambda expressions or first-order logic. Solving this task effectively is crucial for a wide range of applications, including question answering, information extraction, and dialogue systems. However, a significant challenge lies in generalizing parsing methods across languages and meaning representations, especially when training data is limited or noisy. Traditional approaches to semantic parsing have often been tailored to specific languages or meaning representations, relying on linguistically motivated prior assumptions that are difficult to adapt across domains. While static rules or manually crafted grammars can achieve good results in well-described settings, they suffer from limited scalability and adaptability. Learning-based approaches, on the other hand, automate the induction of parsing rules but may struggle with generalization, especially when faced with out-of-domain inputs or varying semantic structures. This paper presents a novel approach to the problem of semantic parsing by inducing a   probabilistic Combinatory Categorial Grammar (CCG)   from sentence-logical form pairs. CCG is a lexicalized grammar formalism that unifies syntax and semantics by associating semantic representations directly with linguistic categories. Our approach uses   higher-order unification   to define a rich and flexible hypothesis space of grammars, consisting of all possible grammars that are consistent with the training data. This hypothesis space enables the method to capture complex semantic composition patterns while remaining generalizable across meaning representations and languages. To efficiently search this hypothesis space and estimate the parameters of the grammar, we develop an   online learning algorithm   based on a   log-linear parsing model  . The algorithm incrementally refines the grammar and parameter estimates as it processes each training example, balancing the need for expressivity with computational efficiency. To evaluate the effectiveness of our method, we conduct experiments on benchmark datasets covering four languages and two distinct meaning representations, demonstrating that the induced grammars achieve high accuracy and robustness. This work offers a significant advancement in statistical semantic parsing by providing a general, efficient, and accurate method that can be applied across languages and meaning representations. The use of higher-order unification in the learning process is particularly novel and enables the model to scale to complex semantic structures beyond those captured by traditional first-order unification approaches.

Coreference resolution is a fundamental task in natural language processing (NLP) that aims to identify expressions within a text that refer to the same real-world entity. Despite its importance for applications such as machine translation, question answering, and text summarization, coreference resolution remains a challenging problem, especially in the unsupervised setting where annotated training data is not available. While traditional supervised approaches yield high performance by leveraging extensive labeled datasets, they are not applicable in domains where such data is scarce or nonexistent. This has motivated ongoing research into building robust unsupervised systems that can capture complex syntactic and semantic relationships between mentions. Most unsupervised coreference resolution methods rely on clustering algorithms or graph-based approaches to group mentions based on features such as syntactic parallelism, semantic similarity, and token co-occurrence. However, these approaches often lack the capacity to effectively model the nuanced interactions between mention entity pairs and consequently suffer from suboptimal performance. To address this limitation, this paper introduces a novel approach that focuses on identifying and utilizing the most informative relations between mention entities, thereby enabling more precise coreference decisions even in the absence of labeled training data. At the heart of our method is a precision-oriented inference framework that scores candidate entity clusters using a novel informativeness score. This score quantifies the relevance of a relation between two mentions to the decision of whether they corefer. By focusing on the most informative relations—those that are statistically significant and semantically discriminative—we enhance the discriminative power of our model and reduce the noise arising from ambiguous or irrelevant features. To learn the informativeness score in an unsupervised manner, we leverage the expectation maximization (EM) algorithm. Through a few iterations, our algorithm robustly estimates the informativeness of relations and refines the coreference clusters accordingly. This iterative process ensures that the most informative features are prioritized, improving the overall precision of the unsupervised coreference resolution system. Extensive experiments on widely used benchmark datasets demonstrate that our proposed method outperforms existing unsupervised approaches across the board. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first unsupervised coreference resolution framework that explicitly identifies and leverages the most informative mention pair relations. We hope that our method not only advances the field of unsupervised coreference resolution but also inspires further research into feature-focused learning in NLP tasks beyond labeled data constraints.
