Recent advancements in natural language processing (NLP) have enabled significant improvements in information extraction tasks. Event extraction, in particular, has attracted considerable attention due to its crucial role in understanding events from text. While a large body of research has focused on English event extraction, relatively little effort has been directed towards Chinese event extraction. This is partly due to the unique morphological, syntactic, and semantic characteristics of the Chinese language, which pose distinct challenges for traditional NLP pipelines. Additionally, Chinese event extraction benefits from a diverse set of linguistic features, ranging from lexical and syntactic features to discourse-level dependencies. However, most prior approaches, such as the model proposed by Li et al. (2012), adopt a pipeline architecture that suffers from error propagation and fails to fully utilize the rich linguistic patterns inherent in Chinese. In this paper, we aim to address these limitations by exploring two key innovations in the context of Chinese event extraction. First, we propose a joint modeling framework that integrates multiple subtasks—such as trigger identification, argument role classification, and event type classification—into a unified architectural paradigm, thereby mitigating the cascading error problem inherent in pipeline systems. Joint modeling not only encourages consistency among interdependent subtasks but also allows for the systematic exploitation of their mutual interactions and dependencies. Second, we investigate the incorporation of a wide spectrum of linguistic features tailored for Chinese. These features span character-level information (e.g., radical, Pinyin, and stroke count), word-level features (e.g., part-of-speech tags and syntactic dependencies), sentence-level features (e.g., co-reference and semantic roles), and discourse-level elements (e.g., temporal relations and rhetorical structures). By leveraging rich linguistic knowledge, our model can better capture the contextual and structural nuances essential for accurate event identification in Chinese texts. To evaluate the effectiveness of our approach, we conduct extensive experiments using the widely recognized ACE 2005 dataset. The experimental results demonstrate that our joint-modeling framework, combined with the integration of rich linguistic features, significantly outperforms the existing pipeline-based method proposed by Li et al. (2012). These findings highlight the importance of joint modeling and linguistic feature incorporation in improving the performance of event extraction tasks in the Chinese language domain. This work contributes to the growing effort to bridge the gap between English-focused NLP systems and their counterparts for the Chinese language by proposing a more robust and linguistically informed event extraction framework.

Recent advancements in machine learning have emphasized the importance of reducing annotation effort while maintaining model accuracy. A promising avenue in this domain is active learning, where the learning algorithm selectively queries the most informative data points to improve performance efficiently. Traditional active learning systems focus on querying labels for instance-level annotations, typically selecting those data points that provide the highest information gain for the model. However, these methods do not fully exploit the potential of prior knowledge about input features, which can guide learning more effectively when appropriately integrated into the annotation process. This paper introduces a novel active learning approach that shifts the focus from querying labels for instances to querying labels for features themselves. The method is inspired by generalized expectation (GE) techniques, where constraints on input features are used to train models with only partial information. Building upon these ideas, our framework treats feature-level annotation as a valuable resource that can be directly solicited from human annotators, allowing for a more structured and efficient learning process. By encoding prior knowledge and leveraging it during learning, the model can better understand the underlying task structure and inductive biases with minimal supervision. We evaluate our method on two sequence labeling tasks using both simulated and real user experiments. Our results demonstrate that labeling features—rather than full instances—can be more effective than both passive learning with features and traditional instance-based active learning. This is particularly important in scenarios where annotators may find it easier or more intuitive to provide feedback on specific aspects (features) of an instance rather than making global judgments. Additionally, we explore the design of novel annotation interfaces that enable the collection of multi-feature labels in an intelligent, task-aware manner. Our preliminary findings suggest that such interfaces not only enhance annotation efficiency but also contribute to better model performance. This work contributes to a growing body of research exploring how to make annotation processes more scalable and accurate by better aligning human and machine strengths. Our proposed method of feature-based active learning opens new directions for interactive learning systems that can leverage fine-grained human input to train more effective models with less overall effort. The implications of this approach extend beyond sequence labeling, suggesting broader applicability across tasks where domain knowledge on feature behavior is accessible or where annotation at the feature level is more natural and efficient.

Grammar errors in written text can significantly impact the readability and acceptability of a document, especially in multilingual or educational environments. The task of grammatical error correction (GEC) aims to automatically detect and correct these errors, enhancing the quality of user-generated text. While traditional statistical approaches based on phrase-based machine translation (SMT) have achieved strong results in GEC, more recent research has shifted towards neural models. However, despite their promise, neural GEC systems have not consistently matched the performance of their SMT-based counterparts. This discrepancy can be attributed in part to the inherent low-resource nature of GEC, where annotated training data is sparse and task-specific noise is abundant. In this paper, we propose a novel perspective by framing the neural GEC task as a low-resource machine translation (MT) problem. By drawing parallels between the two domains, we explore the applicability of techniques developed for low-resource MT to the GEC task. These techniques are often tailored to improve performance when training data is limited and noisy, making them a natural fit for GEC’s challenging setting. We introduce a set of model-independent methods inspired by the low-resource MT literature that can be readily integrated into most neural GEC systems. These approaches include adding source-side noise during training to improve robustness, applying domain-adaptation techniques to accommodate diverse writing styles, formulating a task-specific training objective that better aligns with grammatical correction goals, leveraging transfer learning with monolingual data to augment limited labeled data, and employing model ensembling to combine the strengths of multiple independently trained models and language models. Furthermore, this work contributes to the broader GEC community by establishing practical guidelines for achieving reproducible and reliable results with neural systems—especially in data-scarce settings. The proposed techniques combine to significantly boost the performance of neural GEC models. Experimental results demonstrate that our approach outperforms the previous best neural GEC systems by more than 10% in M2 score on the CoNLL-2014 benchmark, and over 5.9% on the JFLEG test set. Notably, the performance is also competitive with prior non-neural systems, surpassing them by more than 2% on CoNLL-2014 and 4% on JFLEG. These results confirm the effectiveness of our low-resource MT-inspired strategies for neural GEC and open the door to more robust and scalable GEC systems in the future..large stadiums. While SMT-based approaches have historically dominated the field, the recent shift toward neural models has introduced new architectural and training possibilities.

Recent advancements in natural language processing (NLP) have enabled significant improvements in understanding unstructured text data, particularly in the extraction of structured information such as entities and their relationships. Entity and relation extraction (ERE) has long been a core task in information extraction, with applications ranging from question answering and semantic web to knowledge graph construction. Traditionally, ERE has been approached as two separate tasks: entity extraction and relation extraction. However, these two tasks are inherently interdependent, as accurate entity identification is a prerequisite for determining relations, and conversely, understanding relations can assist in disambiguating entity mentions and their classifications. Recognizing this co-dependency, recent research has focused on joint modeling approaches that extract entities and relations simultaneously, aiming to improve overall performance by leveraging task interactions. Despite progress, existing joint models often face limitations in capturing complex interactions between entity and relation components, partly due to the use of localized or heuristic training objectives. These models may optimize per-task losses independently or sequentially, which can lead to suboptimal joint inference results. The challenge lies in designing a shared representation and training mechanism that can effectively coordinate the outputs of the entity and relation tasks, taking into account the global structure of the problem rather than isolated decisions. In this paper, we introduce a novel and lightweight joint learning framework for ERE based on   minimum risk training   (MRT), a strategy known for its ability to optimize global objectives in structured prediction tasks. MRT aims to minimize the expected loss over all possible model predictions, making it particularly suitable for joint tasks where decisions interact in complex and non-linear ways. Our approach defines a global loss function that explicitly models the joint distribution of entities and relations, allowing the model to learn from the full spectrum of possible interactions between the two subtasks. Furthermore, we propose a simple yet powerful neural network architecture that facilitates efficient implementation of the MRT framework without the need for complex architectures or domain-specific feature engineering. Through extensive experiments on widely used ERE benchmarks, including the ACE05 and NYT datasets, we demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach. Our method achieves state-of-the-art performance, highlighting the benefits of a globally coherent training strategy that fully integrates entity and relation inference. The experimental results not only confirm the superiority of our model but also provide insights into the advantages of joint MRT in capturing long-range dependencies and avoiding error propagation common in sequential models.

The ability to infer the meaning of a new word from a small number of utterances is a hallmark of human language acquisition. In stark contrast, traditional distributional semantic models (DSMs), such as Word2Vec or GloVe, depend on large corpora with extensive word occurrences to generate reliable word representations. This discrepancy between human cognitive flexibility and computational models presents a fundamental challenge in the field of natural language processing (NLP): how can machines efficiently adapt to new words with minimal exposure, mimicking this human-like capability? In this paper, we address this challenge by introducing   Mem2Vec  , a memory-based word embedding learning approach that leverages a pre-trained semantic space to perform robust few-shot word representation learning. Our inspiration is rooted in cognitive theories that emphasize the role of semantic similarity and memory in human language comprehension. Specifically, when encountering a novel word, humans draw upon their existing mental lexicon and use syntactic and contextual cues to form an educated guess about its meaning. Mem2Vec operationalizes this cognitive process through a memory-augmented neural architecture that integrates long-term semantic knowledge to guide the interpretation of new or underrepresented words. Unlike traditional DSMs that treat each word independently, Mem2Vec operates in a context-aware way by utilizing a memory module to store and retrieve semantic information from the pre-trained embedding space. This memory acts as a proxy for prior knowledge, providing guidance when constructing vector representations for new words. The core insight is that the surrounding words in a local context can be interpreted more reliably due to their existing high-quality embeddings. By anchoring the meaning of a novel word in this established semantic network, Mem2Vec can generate high-quality representations even with minimal co-occurrence data. We demonstrate the effectiveness of Mem2Vec through a series of experiments on challenging few-shot word similarity tasks, where it consistently outperforms competitive baselines. Importantly, the embeddings generated by our model also transfer effectively to downstream NLP tasks such as named entity recognition and sentiment classification, achieving significant improvements over previous methods. This work contributes to the growing literature on few-shot learning in NLP and offers a new perspective on how long-term memory mechanisms can enhance model adaptability. By restricting the need for large-scale data to learn new words, our approach brings us closer to bridging the gap between human-like language learning and machine learning efficiency. Furthermore, it opens new avenues for developing models that can dynamically expand their vocabularies in novel domains or low-resource settings.

Parsing discontinuous constituents is a central challenge in syntactic analysis, particularly in languages where constituents do not occur as continuous spans in the sentence. Traditional transition-based parsers often struggle with this because standard operations do not allow for arbitrary displacement of elements, and consequently, parsing discontinuous structures requires the introduction of special transition operations, like swaps or insertions. These extend the transition system and complicate both the transition model and the oracle strategy. In the context of discontinuous constituency parsing, a critical limitation of current models is their dependence on modeling only local components of the parsing configuration. Transition-based systems based on the structured perceptron or similar models capture the state using a small set of features, which are extracted mostly from the top of the stack and the current buffer token. While this local modeling is efficient, it introduces a bottleneck: information about the configuration is limited to a short memory window, and decisions are based on only the most accessible parts of the structure. This is particularly problematic for discontinuous structures, where relevant information may need to traverse deep into the stack in order to make the correct parsing decision. In this paper, we address this issue by proposing a neural transition-based parser that computes a global, recursive representation of the parsing configuration. Our model replaces the traditional structured perceptron with a neural network that learns hierarchical representations of the core components of the configuration: individual words, existing trees, and the structure of the stack itself. This global representation allows even the most remote parts of the parsing state to influence decisions, thus overcoming the memory limitations inherent in previous approaches. Moreover, we conduct a thorough analysis of how the global representation is constructed, which components are most informative, and how the model integrates different types of information. We also investigate the impact of different swap oracle implementations on parsing performance, a key consideration in discontinuous parsing due to the ambiguity about how transpositions should be recovered from annotated data. To our knowledge, this is the first neural architecture designed specifically for discontinuous constituency parsing. We evaluate our model on four benchmark datasets and show that it outperforms all previously published models on three of them, achieving second place on the remaining one by a small margin. These results demonstrate the efficacy of using neural global representations in modeling discontinuous syntax, and suggest that such models can provide a more expressive alternative to traditional feature-based systems in this domain.

The task of identifying text polarity—determining whether a word or phrase expresses a positive or negative sentiment—is a fundamental problem in Natural Language Processing (NLP). Its applications span across various domains, including text classification, content filtering, product review analysis, survey response analysis, and the study of online discussions. The ability to accurately identify the sentiment of words and phrases is key to understanding human opinions and emotions within textual data. Traditionally, approaches for sentiment analysis have relied on either rule-based systems that use human-crafted lexicons or machine learning models that are trained on annotated datasets. While these methods have seen considerable success, they often come with limitations: either they lack the flexibility to generalize across domains (in the case of rule-based systems) or they require substantial labeled training data that may not be available for all use cases (in the case of supervised learning models). In this paper, we propose a novel approach to the task of text polarity identification by leveraging the principles of Markov random walks on a large-scale word relatedness graph. The core idea is to model the relationships between words in a semantic network and perform label propagation through a graph-based random walk process that captures the notion of sentiment diffusion. This method operates in both semi-supervised and unsupervised settings. In the semi-supervised setting, a set of labeled words is used to initialize the walk and then the polarity labels are propagated through the graph. In the unsupervised version, only a small set of seed words representing the two extreme ends of the polarity spectrum (i.e., highly positive and highly negative) are required to initialize the process. The resulting method is efficient, interpretable, and effective at capturing the subtle nuances of word sentiment through graph-based relatedness. Our experimental evaluation is conducted on a manually labeled set of positive and negative words, a standard benchmark for evaluating polarity identification methods. We demonstrate that the proposed method significantly outperforms existing state-of-the-art techniques in the semi-supervised setting and provides competitive performance in the unsupervised setting. Additionally, the method's computational efficiency and minimal reliance on large corpora position it as a promising advancement in the field of sentiment analysis. Through this work, we aim to contribute a scalable, accurate, and flexible framework for text polarity identification. Websites like Yellow Pages London can benefit from such advancements by offering more accurate location-based services.

The task of modeling how the meaning of a sentence arises from the meanings of its constituent parts—what is known in linguistics as  compositionality —is one of the central challenges in natural language processing (NLP). Compositionality implies that the meaning of complex expressions can be derived from the combination of simpler semantic components through a well-defined set of rules. While traditional symbolic approaches to semantics have relied on syntactic structures to define how meanings compose, a recent wave of interest has emerged in learning semantic representations directly from data, using high-dimensional vector spaces. In particular, vector space models (VSMs) have demonstrated impressive successes in capturing the distributional properties of individual words, but modeling how these properties combine into the meaning of phrases and sentences remains an open challenge. Early work on distributed semantic models primarily focused on word-level representations, with methods like Word2Vec and GloVe capturing rich statistical information about how words co-occur. However, assembling these representations into compositional sentence embeddings while preserving grammatical structure has proven difficult. Many approaches propose simple operations such as averaging, concatenation, or addition, which do not account for the hierarchical and structured nature of language. As a result, the semantic composition is often overlooked, leading to distributions that struggle to distinguish between structurally dissimilar but semantically similar sentences. In this paper, we explore a promising direction in modeling compositional semantics that explicitly incorporates the syntactic structure of a sentence, and demonstrate that syntactic parsing can be instrumental in guiding the learning of semantic representations. We draw on the generative and compositional properties of Combinatory Categorial Grammar (CCG), a linguistic formalism that provides a transparent interface between syntax and semantics. Using the combinatory operators of CCG as architectural primitives, we introduce  Combinatory Categorial Autoencoders  (CCAs), a novel type of neural language model that performs non-linear semantic composition guided by syntactic derivations. The motivation for this approach stems from the observation that syntax not only reflects the surface structure of language but also encodes deeper semantic relationships. By integrating CCG combinators into a neural model, we enable the model to learn compositional transformations that are informed by grammatical rules while being flexible enough to adapt to the semantic landscape of the data. This leads to a more principled integration of syntax and semantics, enabling the induction of sentence representations that are both linguistically interpretable and functionally effective. Empirically, we demonstrate that CCAs can learn high-quality semantic embeddings of sentences that outperform or match strong baselines on a range of semantic similarity and sentence-level classification tasks.

Semantic parsing from denotations is a crucial yet challenging problem in natural language understanding, where the goal is to automatically learn a semantic representation of text from partial supervision—denotations (e.g., factual answers or database entries)—without explicitly provided logical forms. This task has broad applications in question answering, program synthesis, and automated reasoning. However, two fundamental challenges hinder the training of effective models:   (1)   the lack of candidate semantic parses during training—a problem commonly referred to as the semantic gap—due to the absence of fully annotated logical forms; and   (2)   the choice of an optimal learning algorithm for model update, which affects generalization performance and training efficiency. Traditional approaches mostly rely on heuristic methods, such as greedy decoding, to generate semantic parse candidates from denotations, which are often inaccurate and limited in coverage. Moreover, these methods do not provide strong or reliable supervision signals for the model, especially in cases where multiple parses could lead to the same denotation. As a result, learning from denotations remains an underspecified and underconstrained problem, requiring strong, data-driven solutions for effective model training. In this paper, we present two key contributions that address these core challenges in a principled and generalizable manner. First, to improve the quality of supervision, we introduce   policy shaping  , a novel approach that biases the search procedure toward candidate semantic parses that are more likely to be valid and semantically consistent with the input text. By incorporating prior knowledge and syntactic patterns, policy shaping enables the model to explore the search space more effectively and find better candidate parses for training. This in turn provides more informative supervision signals, leading to improved learning performance. Second, we derive a   generalized update equation   that unifies and generalizes three distinct families of learning algorithms—including fully supervised, partially supervised, and reinforcement learning-based methods—into a single flexible framework. This formulation allows for a modular and systematic exploration of different learning strategies during training, and it facilitates the rapid adaptation of new algorithms within a common theoretical foundation. The generalized update equation also enables efficient hyperparameter tuning and offers better convergence properties in complex model settings. We evaluate our framework on a recent sequential question answering dataset, which is particularly challenging due to its compositional semantic structure and large space of possible logical forms. Our experiments show that the proposed method achieves a   new state-of-the-art   performance, outperforming previous approaches by   5.0% absolute improvements   in exact match accuracy.

Sentence simplification is a fundamental task in natural language processing (NLP) that aims to transform complex sentences into simpler, more accessible versions while preserving the essential meaning. This task is particularly important for improving readability in educational settings, aiding language learners, and enabling better accessibility for people with cognitive or developmental disorders such as dyslexia or autism. Traditionally, sentence simplification has been approached with various techniques, ranging from rule-based systems to statistical models, and more recently, from deep learning architectures inspired by machine translation. These conventional methods have largely focused on implicitly learning simplification patterns from parallel corpora of complex and simplified sentence pairs. While such data-driven approaches have led to significant progress, they often suffer from a lack of explicit knowledge about the real-world simplification rules that guide human simplification behaviors, such as paraphrasing, substitution of complex words, and syntactic restructuring. Recent advances in Transformer-based models, with their powerful multi-head attention mechanisms and ability to capture rich contextual representations, have opened new possibilities for more sophisticated simplification systems. However, in most cases, these Transformer-based models still rely solely on the patterns learned from the training data, without explicitly incorporating domain-specific simplification knowledge. In this paper, we propose a novel approach that integrates a Transformer-based framework with an external human-curated paraphrase knowledge base—Simple PPDB (A Paraphrase Database for Simplification)—to explicitly incorporate a wide range of simplification rules into the model's decision-making process. This integration allows the model to not only learn from the data but also to leverage existing linguistic expertise in the form of simplification paraphrases. Our proposed method demonstrates two key advantages: first, the combined model significantly outperforms several state-of-the-art sentence simplification baselines across standard evaluation metrics. Second, an analysis of the rule utilization reveals that the integration of Simple PPDB helps the model prefer the most accurate and appropriate simplification rules during inference. This approach not only improves the performance of sentence simplification models but also enhances their interpretability by offering insights into the types of rules being applied. Our experiments are conducted on widely used datasets for sentence simplification, and the code as well as model configurations are made publicly available to facilitate reproducibility and further research in this area. The integration of external knowledge sources with modern machine learning models represents a promising direction for building more robust and interpretable sentence simplification systems.

Recent advancements in deep learning have significantly improved the performance of sequence tagging tasks, such as Named Entity Recognition (NER), Part-of-Speech tagging, and beyond. Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) networks, in particular, have become a dominant architecture due to their ability to model long-term dependencies in sequences. As the research community increasingly relies on these models to drive insights and develop new methodologies, it is critical to ensure that comparisons between systems are rigorous and meaningful. However, this paper highlights a subtle yet significant pitfall in current practices of model evaluation: the reliance on a single performance score to gauge and compare the effectiveness of non-deterministic deep learning models. The initialization of neural networks, including LSTM-based models, typically involves the use of random seed values for the random number generator. While it is widely understood that randomness can influence training stability and convergence, the impact on final performance metrics is often overlooked. In our work, we demonstrate that for sequence tagging tasks, the choice of seed value can lead to statistically significant differences in model performance (p < 10^−4^), even within the same training and evaluation setup. For example, we observe variations of over one percentage point in the F₁ score for two recently proposed NER systems, depending solely on the seed used for training. These differences are large enough to alter the perceived ranking of a model from “state-of-the-art” to “mediocre” or vice versa, thereby undermining the reliability of performance evaluations. Given this finding, we argue against the current standard of reporting single-point performance estimates for non-deterministic models. Instead, we advocate for a more comprehensive approach: the evaluation and comparison of score distributions obtained through multiple model executions. By analyzing a large-scale set of experiments involving 50,000 LSTM networks applied to five different sequence tagging tasks, we not only show the variability in performance due to randomness but also present a set of network architectures that are both highly effective and more resilient to hyperparameter settings. This stability is crucial for reproducibility and fair comparison across different models and research groups. In the following sections, we provide empirical evidence supporting our claims, detail our experimental methodology, and discuss the implications for future deep learning research in NLP. Our full experimental results are available in the accompanying technical report (Reimers and Gurevych, 2017), and our codebase is publicly accessible to promote transparency and further research in this direction.

Semi-supervised learning has emerged as a powerful paradigm for bridging the gap between fully supervised approaches and unsupervised techniques in natural language processing (NLP). While traditional unsupervised methods rely entirely on large quantities of unlabeled data to learn general language features, they often fall short in capturing domain-specific nuances. On the other hand, fully supervised models require extensive annotated data, which may be scarce or expensive to obtain in many real-world applications. A promising middle ground is semi-supervised representation learning, which combines both labeled and unlabeled data to extract robust and discriminative features. This is particularly critical when dealing with open-domain NLP tasks, where the lack of domain-specific annotated data limits the application of supervised learning techniques. Domain adaptation, the ability of a model trained on one domain (source) to generalize to another (target), remains a significant challenge in NLP. Datasets from different domains often exhibit substantial distributional shifts in vocabulary, syntax, and semantics, which can hinder the performance of standard models. To mitigate this, recent research has focused on learning domain-invariant representations that can minimize the divergence between the source and target distributions. However, these methods often over-rely on deep neural networks and ignore the potential impacts of task-specific structure. In this paper, we introduce a dynamic dependency network model that supports semi-supervised representation learning by leveraging both task-specific labeled data from the source domain and unlabeled data from both the source and target domains. Our approach is designed to adaptively model domain dependencies and dynamically adjust the learning process based on the input context. By integrating principles from structured prediction and statistical dependency modeling, our proposed method not only enhances feature generalization but also improves model performance on open-domain tasks. We evaluate our model on two classic NLP tasks: part-of-speech tagging and syntactic chunking. The experiments are conducted using the Wall Street Journal dataset for the source domain and MEDLINE and Brown corpus for the target domains. Our results demonstrate that the semi-supervised learning approach outperforms existing unsupervised methods, showing the effectiveness of incorporating dynamic task structures with domain-invariant learning. This work contributes a novel framework for domain adaptation in NLP, demonstrating the potential of semi-supervised learning to produce robust and transferable linguistic representations. The findings also highlight the importance of exploiting both labeled and unlabeled data when annotated target domain data is unavailable.

Semantic parsing is a core problem in natural language processing (NLP), aiming to convert natural language utterances into formal, machine-executable representations of meaning. Its applications range from answering database queries and interacting with knowledge bases to supporting intelligent virtual assistants and conversational agents. Despite significant progress, semantic parsing remains a challenging task due to the ambiguity and complexity of natural language, as well as the need for precise and structured formal representations that reflect the semantics of the input. Traditionally, semantic parsing systems have relied on symbolic rules, handcrafted grammars, and pipeline architectures that separate syntactic parsing from semantic interpretation. While these methods are interpretable and efficient in domain-specific settings, they often lack robustness and scalability when applied to flexible, open-ended language inputs. Recently, there have been two promising directions in semantic parsing: (1) the representation of meaning using semantic graphs, which provide expressive, structured, and knowledge-base-compatible outputs, and (2) the use of neural networks to better model the complex patterns in language and generate semantic representations directly from text in an end-to-end manner. However, existing approaches tend to focus on one of these directions, limiting the benefits that integrating both could offer. In this paper, we propose a neural semantic parsing framework —  Sequence-to-Action , which unifies and advances both aforementioned directions in a single, end-to-end model. Our approach treats semantic parsing as a graph generation task: given a natural language sentence, the model outputs a sequence of actions that collectively construct a semantic graph as the meaning representation. These actions modify a partially built graph by adding, removing, or updating nodes and edges in a bottom-up manner. By modeling the process of building the graph through action sequences, our method is able to incorporate the structural and relational richness of semantic graphs while benefiting from the end-to-end training and prediction power of neural networks. We employ a recursive neural network (RNN) to process input sentences and infer the appropriate action sequences that generate the target semantic graphs. Our model combines both linguistic and semantic information, using the sentence as input and generating graph actions as output. The proposed approach does not rely on intermediate syntactic parses, thereby avoiding error propagation from prior NLP components. Additionally, by being tightly integrated with knowledge bases through semantic graphs, our method facilitates the application of semantic parsing in real-world settings such as question answering over databases and semantic search.

Community-based Question Answering (cQA) services, such as Stack Overflow, Quora, and Reddit, have become essential platforms for knowledge sharing and problem-solving across various domains. In these environments, users post their questions, and others contribute answers, often leading to rich and diverse discussions. A critical first step in effectively leveraging these platforms for information retrieval is the accurate  detection  of questions within the often unstructured and noisy content generated by online users. Question detection (QD) plays a pivotal role in question retrieval (QR), which aims to find previously asked and answered questions relevant to a given query. However, the task of QD in the context of cQA is markedly more challenging than in formal written language due to the informal, conversational, and variable nature of the text. Unlike traditional question detection in well-formed corpora, where syntactic cues like the presence of a question mark and semantic features such as 5W1H (Who, What, When, Where, Why, How) words are relatively reliable indicators, in online content these signals are often absent or misleading. This paper addresses the challenge of effectively identifying question sentences in cQA platforms by exploring the subtle, yet salient, patterns that distinguish questions in informal online contexts. We focus on developing a robust and automated QD model that leverages both  lexical  and  syntactic  features to accurately identify question sentences. Our approach is designed with a particular emphasis on the idiosyncratic nature of community-based discourse, where the language tends to be highly variable and context-dependent. By capturing these salient characteristics, our model not only offers improved accuracy in question detection but also contributes to the downstream task of question retrieval by filtering out irrelevant content and focusing on the central question components. The empirical evaluation of our approach shows a significant boost in performance over traditional methods, both in terms of QD accuracy and the effectiveness of question retrieval in cQA. Our results underscore the importance of tailoring language models to the unique characteristics of online text, thereby setting the stage for more intelligent and scalable cQA systems. Chinese, as a language with a unique writing system, presents distinct challenges and opportunities in natural language processing (NLP). Unlike alphabetic languages such as English, Chinese characters often carry inherent semantic and morphological information, making their representation a subject of particular importance. While distributed word representations have proven highly effective in capturing semantic relationships in languages like English, Chinese characters and their components often encode meanings that are not easily captured by traditional word-level embeddings. This is primarily due to the complex compositionality of Chinese characters, which are built from radicals and other components that contribute to their meaning and pronunciation. Several works have explored character-level embeddings for Chinese, but few address the intrinsic compositional features of Chinese characters. Given that character components often act as semantic and phonetic indicators, leveraging them in embedding models could enhance the semantic richness of character representations. This paper is motivated by the observation that the structural properties of Chinese characters, and the roles played by their components, are valuable for capturing meaning and contextual usage. We, therefore, propose two innovative component-enhanced Chinese character embedding models and their bigram extensions, which explicitly integrate the hierarchical composition of characters during the training process. The key idea behind our approach is to represent a character not just as a standalone entity but as a combination of its component parts. By doing so, the proposed models capture composition-based semantic relationships that are essential for both task-specific learning and general language understanding. Our models are trained using large-scale unlabeled corpora, and the learned embeddings are evaluated on two fundamental NLP tasks: word similarity and text classification. The experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness and robustness of our models in capturing both syntactic and semantic patterns in Chinese character usage. The contributions of this work include: (1) a novel component-based representation strategy for Chinese character embeddings, (2) the development of two embedding models with their bigram variants that incorporate such compositional information, and (3) empirical validation on multiple benchmark tasks showing significant improvements over baseline and state-of-the-art methods. By harnessing the compositional richness of Chinese characters, our approach not only advances the field of Chinese NLP but also opens new avenues for representing morphologically complex languages with similar writing systems. This work highlights the importance of integrating linguistic knowledge into learning models to achieve more interpretable and effective embeddings. In the following sections, we first describe the proposed models in detail, followed by a comprehensive evaluation of their performance on various downstream tasks.

The recognition and parsing of multiword expressions (MWEs)—combinations of words that exhibit non-compositional semantic or syntactic behavior—are key challenges in natural language processing (NLP). Properly identifying these expressions can significantly enhance a variety of NLP tasks, including syntactic parsing, semantic role labeling, machine translation, and information retrieval. MWEs, such as phrasal verbs (e.g.,  give up ), compound nouns (e.g.,  apple pie ), and idioms (e.g.,  kick the bucket ), often do not conform to standard syntactic and semantic rules, making them difficult to process under traditional compositional models. Consequently, integrating MWE recognition into syntactic parsing is an area of active research, with the goal of improving overall parsing accuracy by explicitly modeling these expressions within the parsing process. A substantial body of work has demonstrated that, in controlled settings where MWEs are perfectly pre-identified prior to parsing, their inclusion can lead to significant improvements in parsing performance. Such improvements are typically reflected in better attachment scores and reduced parsing ambiguity, as the parser is provided with a more coherent representation of the sentence structure. However, real-world data presents a more complex scenario: MWE recognition is itself a challenging task and rarely perfect. Recognition errors can introduce noise into the parsing process, risking degradation in overall performance when incorrect MWE segmentations are fed into the parser. This paper evaluates and contrasts two empirically motivated strategies for the integration of MWE recognition and syntactic parsing in a real-world constituency parsing task. The first strategy involves pregrouping MWEs using an off-the-shelf recognizer before performing a standard parsing procedure. While this approach yields improvements in the recognition of MWEs and unlabeled attachment scores under certain conditions, we find that its benefits do not consistently translate into statistically significant improvements in overall F-score. This is largely due to the cascading effects of MWE recognition errors that negatively influence downstream parsing decisions. In the second approach, we explore the integration of MWE handling directly within the parsing framework. Specifically, MWEs are incorporated into the parser's grammar, and their preferences are further refined via a reranking step tailored specifically to MWE-related constructions. This end-to-end integration produces more stable improvements across all evaluation metrics, suggesting that a more direct and coordinated treatment of MWEs within the parser can yield better performance than post-hoc or pre-processing strategies. This paper contributes a detailed comparative evaluation of these two strategies, offering insights into the practical and empirical trade-offs involved in the integration of MWE recognition and parsing.

Recent advancements in natural language processing (NLP) have enabled significant improvements in the automatic correction of grammatical errors in written text. Grammatical error correction (GEC) is a challenging NLP task due to the diverse types of errors that learners may produce, ranging from local, surface-level issues such as spelling mistakes and inflectional errors to more complex, global-level problems involving incorrect word order and syntactic structures. Effective GEC systems must address both categories of errors simultaneously to enhance the fluency and correctness of non-native language output. Traditional rule-based or feature-based approaches to GEC have limitations in generalizing across the wide variability of grammatical mistakes, leading to the adoption of neural sequence-to-sequence (seq2seq) models, which have demonstrated promising results due to their ability to learn patterns from large-scale parallel data. Among the most successful neural architectures for GEC are those based on encoder-decoder frameworks with attention mechanisms. These models leverage self-attention to better capture contextual information and align source and target sentences. However, despite their effectiveness, such models often struggle to handle both local and global errors due to the restrictive nature of conventional attention mechanisms that aggregate information over the entire sequence without explicitly distinguishing between different types of edits. In this paper, we propose a novel   Nested Attention Neural Hybrid Model   for grammatical error correction that extends traditional seq2seq architectures by introducing a   nested attention mechanism   at both the word and character levels. This hierarchical attention design allows the model to selectively focus on larger syntactic patterns for global correction while simultaneously attending to small-scale lexical modifications essential for local error correction. Our approach is also hybrid in the sense that it integrates subword and character-level knowledge with surface-level word representations, enabling the model to address a broader range of error types more effectively. To evaluate the performance of our model, we conduct comprehensive experiments on the widely used   CoNLL-14 Shared Task dataset  , a standard benchmark for GEC. Our results demonstrate that the proposed model outperforms existing state-of-the-art neural models for GEC in terms of both accuracy and robustness. An in-depth error analysis further reveals that the nested attention architecture contributes significantly to the performance gain, especially in the correction of local errors that require fine-grained orthographic or inflectional adjustments. This work highlights the importance of designing attention mechanisms that are sensitive to the multi-granularity nature of error correction in written language.

The task of accurately pluralizing nouns is a foundational requirement in natural language generation and is essential for the development of linguistically aware software systems, particularly in user-facing contexts such as machine translation, dialogue systems, and content generation. While robust solutions exist for major world languages like English or Spanish, the same cannot be said for the languages of the Bantu family, which exhibit complex morpho-syntactic structures and rich noun class systems. Noun pluralization in Bantu languages is not a simple transformation governed by a small set of rules; rather, it is influenced by a confluence of morphological, syntactic, and semantic factors. This complexity is particularly pronounced in agglutinating Bantu languages, where noun classes serve as the primary grammatical marker for classification and agreement across a wide range of grammatical features, including number, gender, and animacy. The process of pluralization is intricately tied to the noun class system, with many languages employing distinct plural markers for different singular noun classes. However, mastering this task computationally requires not just a static understanding of noun class prefixes, but also the ability to model context sensitivity and variability, which can differ even among closely related dialects. Recent studies on isiZulu and Runyankore have suggested that effective pluralization strategies can be bootstrapped by incorporating both morphological and syntactic data, lending optimism to the possibility of cross-linguistic generalization across Bantu languages. Motivated by these initial findings, this work tests and expands on this hypothesis by investigating the pluralization task in seven Bantu languages spanning three distinct Guthrie language zones. Our analysis reveals that traditional linguistic descriptions, such as Meinhof's classification of noun classes, are insufficient for computational modeling due to ambiguities and non-determinism in prefix assignment. We address this by refactoring noun classes into a more precise system consisting of 53 classes from 29, and demonstrate that this enhanced representation supports the development of a highly accurate generic pluralizer that achieves over 93% coverage accuracy and over 94% precision on a random sample. These results are comparable to language-specific models for isiZulu and Runyankore, suggesting a promising path toward scalable and reusable solutions for NLP systems across the Bantu language family. For the duration of this paper, the emerging findings related to the Bantu language pluralization will be discussed in detail, providing further insights into the linguistic and computational challenges faced in this area.

Transliteration — the process of representing a text in one script using another — is a crucial yet challenging task in natural language processing. It plays a vital role in cross-lingual applications such as information retrieval, cross-lingual named entity recognition, and multilingual computational systems, particularly when dealing with languages with differing writing systems. Typically, transliteration is viewed as a phonetic translation problem, where the phonetic representation of a source word is mapped to its transcription in a target script. Such models focus primarily on leveraging pronunciation features, often encoded through phoneme or grapheme-to-phoneme conversion systems. However, in practice, the decision of how to represent a word in a foreign script is influenced not only by its pronunciation but also by its orthographic characteristics and existing lexical preferences, which introduces a complex interplay between spelling and phonetic similarity. Recent works have started exploring the value of multi-source transliteration strategies, incorporating information from multiple linguistic dimensions — often including source spelling, source pronunciation, and target spelling — in creating more robust and versatile transliteration systems. However, existing approaches often treat these representations in isolation or rely on post-processing stages to integrate multiple transliteration candidates into a final decision. This paper presents a novel framework that explicitly learns to jointly generate transliterations from multiple source representations, simultaneously leveraging orthographic, phonetic, and cross-lingual information from the input. By constructing a model that learns to integrate complementary cues during the decoding process, we enable a more nuanced and informed generation of transliterations. Beyond the use of internal linguistic features, we also examine the impact of external resources, such as reranking components and external lexicons, which are known to significantly improve transliteration quality in rule-based systems. Critically, we extend our model to incorporate knowledge from multiple languages, enabling it to make use of cross-lingual transliteration patterns and improving the robustness of the system when faced with out-of-vocabulary or rare names. Experimental results on a diverse set of evaluation datasets demonstrate that our proposed model achieves substantial improvements in transliteration accuracy compared to state-of-the-art approaches that focus on single-source or minimal joint modeling. These results highlight the importance of explicitly incorporating multiple complementary representations in the transliteration process and suggest that joint generation models can provide a more principled and effective methodology for transliteration tasks across languages. This work thus makes an important contribution to the field of machine transliteration, offering a more holistic and accurate framework for transliteration generation.

The disambiguation of quantifier scope is a fundamental challenge in natural language understanding. Quantifiers like "every" or "some" can scope over multiple elements in a sentence, leading to multiple logical interpretations, only one of which is typically intended by the speaker. For example, in the sentence "Every student read some books," the meaning might differ depending on whether "every student" scopes over "some books" or vice versa. This ambiguity has significant implications for logical inference, semantic parsing, and other tasks in natural language processing (NLP), making accurate scope resolution a critical objective in the field. Traditional approaches to quantifier scope disambiguation often rely on syntactic cues or surface patterns, but such methods frequently fall short in capturing the nuanced pragmatic knowledge that speakers use to resolve ambiguities. Pragmatic knowledge encompasses contextual, world, and speaker-based knowledge, and although it is acknowledged as essential in disambiguating meaning, it is traditionally harder to model than structural or lexico-syntactic features. This is due in part to the implicit, non-formalized, and context-dependent nature of pragmatic knowledge, which makes it difficult to encode in traditional NLP pipelines. Despite the difficulty of obtaining and formalizing pragmatic knowledge, research in recent years has demonstrated the immense value of such knowledge in language tasks ranging from machine translation to dialogue systems. The challenge, however, remains: how can one automatically extract and integrate pragmatic knowledge into models for quantifier scope disambiguation in a tractable and scalable manner? In this paper, we propose a novel approach to quantifier scope disambiguation that leverages automatically extracted pragmatic knowledge. We present an open information extraction (OIE) technique designed specifically for identifying pragmatic relations between quantified expressions and their possible scoping elements in context. These extracted relations are then incorporated into a probabilistic model using the Markov Logic Network (MLN) formalism, allowing the system to reason jointly over syntactic and pragmatic cues. By integrating both types of information, we demonstrate improved performance on quantifier scope disambiguation tasks compared to models that rely solely on syntactic indicators. This work represents a preliminary but promising step towards utilizing pragmatic knowledge in deep language understanding systems, and we believe it opens new directions for integrating extraction-based machine learning and formal models of meaning. Our results underscore the importance of pragmatic knowledge in NLP and suggest that the development of more sophisticated methods for its acquisition and use could lead to substantial gains in a wide range of language processing tasks.

Recent years have witnessed a growing interest in the processing of microblogging data, such as social media posts, due to their immense volume and potential for real-world applications in natural language understanding, sentiment analysis, and information extraction. However, the informal and error-prone nature of microblog texts presents unique challenges for traditional natural language processing (NLP) techniques. Tasks like word segmentation, part-of-speech (POS) tagging, and normalization of text—commonly treated in isolation—are particularly affected by this data's idiosyncratic characteristics, such as abbreviations, typo errors, and the blending of languages or contexts. Most prior work addressing these tasks on microblog data assumes the availability of annoted corpora, which is a limiting constraint given the relatively small and domain-specific size of such datasets. As a result, approaches often rely on task-specific features or domain knowledge, restricting their generalizability and scalability. Additionally, handling these subtasks in isolation often results in error propagation, as the output of one step serves as input for the next, and a mistake at the segmentation stage, for instance, may have a cascading effect on the POS tagging and normalization steps. In this paper, we propose a transition-based model that simultaneously performs word segmentation, part-of-speech tagging, and text normalization as a unified process, thus circumventing the limitations of existing task-specific pipelines. Our model is built on the observation that these three tasks share common representations and dependencies and benefits from the joint modeling of their interrelated decisions. Notably, the proposed model can leverage standard text corpora, which are more readily available and diverse in contrast to the scarce annotated microblog corpora, allowing it to generalize better across different types of inputs. To evaluate the effectiveness of our joint model, we create an annotated microblog corpus, carefully crafted to reflect the diversity and noise typical of such texts. Empirical results show that our model outperforms traditional sequential baselines that process each task in isolation. Specifically, we observe a 12.02% error reduction in segmentation accuracy compared to traditional methods. These results demonstrate the viability and effectiveness of a transition-based joint approach for microblog text processing, paving the way for future research on integrated models for unstructured text. Through this work, we aim to address the pressing need for more robust and generalizable NLP techniques tailored for the dynamic and complex landscape of microblogging content. By bringing together segmentation, tagging, and normalization into a unified pipeline, our model not only enhances performance but also provides a more flexible and scalable solution for emerging applications in natural language processing.

The task of Native Language Identification (NLI) has become a focal point in applied linguistics and natural language processing (NLP), aiming to infer an individual's first language (L1) from their second language (L2) use. This task is not only of academic interest but also has practical implications, including forensic linguistics, personalized language learning, and content filtering. At the heart of NLI lies the exploration of linguistic patterns that are characteristic of speakers with different native language backgrounds. Such patterns often emerge from subtle, but systematic differences in grammatical structures, syntactic constructions, and morphological preferences. However, the application of these linguistic features in machine learning (ML) models for NLI faces challenges such as data sparsity, high dimensionality, and the difficulty of isolating informative patterns from noise. Recent advances in ML have prioritized the development of robust, high-performance models, often at the expense of the interpretability and theoretical grounding of the features used. In contrast, variationist sociolinguistics provides a rich theoretical framework in which language variation is analyzed as a function of speaker, context, and linguistic variables. This approach emphasizes the systematicity of linguistic choices and the interaction between sociolinguistic variables and usage distributions. Taking inspiration from variationist linguistics, we propose a hierarchical clustering approach that groups linguistic features based on their behavior relative to the target class (e.g., native language). This method aims to create a more abstract and general representation of linguistic feature spaces, enabling both quantitative and qualitative insights into the use of language by speakers of different native backgrounds. Our method facilitates label-informed feature grouping, wherein features that exhibit similar patterns of use across native language categories are clustered together. By clustering features at a higher conceptual level, the method not only reduces the dimensionality of the input space and mitigates data sparsity, but also provides a scaffold for linguistic interpretation. We evaluate this approach in the context of NLI, focusing on verb subcategorization patterns as a case study. The results demonstrate significant performance gains while also offering new insights into how native language influences the choice and use of syntactic constructions in a second language. By bridging empirical ML methods with theoretical insights from linguistics, this approach contributes to both applied NLI research and the broader understanding of language variation and acquisition. More importantly, it opens the door to forming and testing hypotheses about the mechanisms by which native language influences emerge in L2 linguistic production.

Explaining the causes and effects of events, particularly in temporal settings, is a critical task that has wide applications in domains like business intelligence, social sciences, healthcare, and finance. In scenarios where both structured time series data and associated textual data are available, there is a growing need for methods that can jointly analyze them to uncover temporal dependencies and generate interpretable explanations. While traditional event detection systems focus on identifying occurrences of events over time, the next crucial challenge lies in understanding  why  or  how  these events are connected, involving both backward-looking (causal) and forward-looking (consequential) reasoning. This problem becomes even more complex when the data sources are heterogeneous, as is often the case when temporal data is combined with unstructured text sources such as news articles, social media, or reports. In this paper, we address this challenge by introducing a novel problem:   _detecting and explaining the causes of a time series event using textual data_  . Specifically, we define the task of explaining an event in a temporal context by identifying relevant causal and effect relationships from textual data and constructing a logical chain of causality that connects them over time. The core of our approach involves two components: (1) detecting causal impacts in time series data by analyzing their textual representations and (2) generating coherent explanations by linking textual features through logical inference. To detect causal signals in textual data, we exploit the statistical properties of time series and extend the concept of  Granger causality  to text-based features extracted via N-grams, topic modeling, and sentiment analysis. These features capture the linguistic evolution of events in text, and their temporal relationships can be used to assess statistical significance of causality between different time series. Moreover, in order to construct a meaningful chain of causality between such features, we rely on a commonsense knowledge base of causal relationships, such as those found in causal event databases. To bridge symbolic and neural representations, we introduce a   neural reasoning algorithm   trained on these causal tuples, which predicts the most plausible next step in a causal chain based on context. This hybrid approach allows us to combine statistical rigor with human-like reasoning. Our method is evaluated through a combination of quantitative analysis—including statistical significance tests and evaluation of explanation coherence—and human judgments to validate the interpretability of the generated explanations. The results demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach in delivering meaningful, actionable, and interpretable causal explanations derived from temporal event data and their textual counterparts.

The prediction of eye movements during reading is a vibrant area of research in cognitive science, computational linguistics, and human–computer interaction. Models of eye movement prediction often aim to simulate how readers process text, with applications ranging from readability assessment and educational tools to the design of more intuitive interfaces and improved reading aids for individuals with visual or cognitive impairments. Understanding and modeling individual variability in eye movement patterns, however, remains a significant challenge. Most approaches focus on modeling eye movements within a single reader, assuming a high degree of consistency in visual and cognitive processing patterns. Yet, as Nilsson and Nivre (2009) highlight, the inherent variability between readers can render cross-subject generalization difficult—despite a strong theoretical motivation to build robust, person-independent models. Nilsson and Nivre introduced a tree-based model to predict eye movements during reading, achieving good results within individual readers but reporting a sharp decline in performance when generalizing across them. They concluded that such generalization was, in practice, unattainable with the methods used at the time, underscoring the challenges posed by the substantial inter-subject variability in reading behavior. However, this view raises an important question: are tree-based models—while intuitively appealing for capturing the hierarchical structure of reading and the apparent non-linearities in fixations and saccades—the most effective or only viable approach? Moreover, can the challenge of reader variability be overcome with alternative modeling strategies that offer more inductive bias and robustness in learning? In this paper, we explore these questions by investigating an alternative approach to eye movement prediction in reading. We demonstrate that a linear Conditional Random Field (CRF) model, equipped with a carefully designed feature set, is not only sufficient to achieve results comparable to tree-based models but also remarkably robust when applied across different readers. Importantly, we find that training such models using the cumulative gaze data from multiple readers leads to minimal performance degradation when tested on new, unseen readers. This is a notable deviation from previous claims and opens up new possibilities for building generalizable, cross-subject eye trackers that require no per-reader calibration. Our findings suggest that the generalization problem is not as insurmountable as previously thought and that the choice of model architecture and the capacity to learn from diverse input data can allow models to "see beyond the blinkers" of individual variability, paving the way for truly robust, adaptable systems in the domain of reading behavior analysis.

Recent advancements in natural language processing (NLP) have enabled parsing technologies to understand and analyze complex syntactic structures in sentences. One particular area of focus has been on modeling the relationships between words and phrases, with dependency parsing being a core technique in this domain. Dependency parsing aims to extract syntactic information by representing the grammatical relations between words in a sentence as a directed graph. Traditionally, many parsing systems have treated certain expressions as pretokenized units—especially complex concatenations such as conjunctions and determiners, where phrases like  ADV+que  or  de+DET  appear as fixed multiword expressions (MWEs). While this approach simplifies parsing, it is not always linguistically accurate. These expressions can be ambiguous, and their treatment as atomic units may obscure important syntactic relationships, especially when morphological or phrasal structure plays a role in their interpretation. This paper addresses the challenge of jointly modeling dependency parsing and MWE tokenization. We propose an integrated model that enables the system to recognize MWEs dynamically in context and parse the sentence structure simultaneously. By treating complex function words as individual tokens and representing their internal lexical-morphological composition through morphological dependencies, we preserve both grammatical and morphological nuances that are often lost in pretokenization approaches. This allows the parser to better accommodate variability and ambiguity in expressions such as conjunctions and determiners, which can be critical for accurate syntactic analysis in languages with rich morphological systems like French. Our model is a graph-based dependency parser that incorporates second-order features and verbal subcategorization features derived from a syntactic lexicon. These features improve the model's ability to capture long-range dependencies and function word constraints, leading to more robust syntactic representations. To train and evaluate our system, we use a modified version of the French Treebank that has been enriched with morphological dependencies. This data augmentations enables our model to learn the hierarchical structure of MWEs and their interactions with the rest of the sentence. Experimental results on this augmented dataset show that our joint model achieves high performance in MWE identification and dependency parsing. Specifically, we report an 81.79% recall and 91.57% precision for recognizing  ADV+que  conjunctions, and 82.74% recall with 86.70% precision for  de+DET  determiners. These results go beyond previous work that relies on pretokenization or monolingual heuristics, showing that a statistically motivated joint model can significantly enhance the parser's ability to handle complex syntactic phenomena in context. This approach not only improves the accuracy of dependency parsing but also contributes to a better understanding of how MWEs function within larger syntactic frameworks, particularly in morphologically rich languages.

The task of verifying the truth of a given claim in the context of a vast amount of text has emerged as a central problem in natural language processing (NLP). This challenge is particularly pertinent in domains such as fact-checking, misinformation detection, and knowledge curation, where accurate claim verification is essential. The core problem can be formalized as een Textual Entailment: determining whether the content of a textual source supports (i.e., entails) a claim, refutes it, or is too inconclusive to draw a judgment. Despite its importance, effective claim verification is hindered by the dual and interdependent challenges of identifying relevant evidence within large text corpora and accurately evaluating the logical connection between the evidence and the claim. Most prior work on claim verification typically approaches these two challenges separately, adopting a pipeline architecture. In such systems, one module first identifies a set of candidate evidence from the text and feeds it to the next module responsible for determining the truth value of the claim. However, this separation limits the system’s ability to optimize for the combined objectives of both evidence selection and claim evaluation, potentially leading to suboptimal performance. Moreover, pipeline systems often struggle with determining the appropriate number of evidence items to consider—some claims may be supported by a single piece of evidence, while others may require multiple pieces from different sources to yield a confident judgment. In light of these limitations, we propose TWOWINGOS (Two-Wing Optimization Strategy), a novel framework that unifies evidence identification and claim verification into a single, jointly optimized model. TWOWINGOS treats the problem as two co-dependent optimization processes: first, identifying a subset of candidate evidence that is most relevant to the claim, and second, determining the truth value of the claim based on that evidence. By combining these tasks into a single model, TWOWINGOS facilitates flexible evidence set sizes and allows the learning signal from the claim verification task to inform the evidence selection process, and vice versa. This joint optimization leads to a more coherent and context-aware system, where the model can adaptively discern which pieces of evidence are most useful and how they contribute to the overall truth value of the claim. The architecture of TWOWINGOS is designed to handle the complexity of real-world text corpora, where claims may be supported by nuanced or implicit evidence and where the same piece of text may serve conflicting roles in different verification scenarios.

The task of identifying topical shifts within a document is crucial for a variety of natural language processing (NLP) tasks such as document summarization, information retrieval, and discourse parsing. Existing approaches largely rely on lexical information, particularly changes in vocabulary, to detect boundaries between contiguous discourse segments that represent distinct topics. While this lexically driven approach has achieved considerable success in generic domains, its performance is not always consistent across diverse text genres. In particular, for narratives and texts with complex information structures—such as literary prose or lecture transcripts—the lexical signal may be insufficient or ambiguous to capture the true nature of topical transitions. This issue prompts a need to explore additional linguistic cues that can complement or refine lexical signals in identifying topical shifts. In this paper, we focus on another potential source of information that has received limited attention in the topical segmentation literature: the structure and type of referring expressions. Our hypothesis is that the referential form used to reintroduce a discourse entity is closely tied to the accessibility of its antecedent and, consequently, the likely temporal or topical continuity between utterances. That is, when speakers or writers use short and ambiguous referring expressions (e.g., pronouns like “he” or “this”), it typically indicates that the antecedent is immediately accessible in the discourse context and the current utterance continues the previous topic. In contrast, elaborated referential forms (e.g., "the man wearing the hat with the long, curly hair") imply a distancing from the antecedent or a shift to a new topic. Thus, the nature of referring expressions can be used as a supplementary indicator of topical continuity or change. Building on this idea, we propose a lexical cohesion model that integrates referring expression types as a feature in topical segmentation. We evaluate our method on two distinct text genres: literary narratives and lecture notes, both of which present different patterns of verbal structure and information flow. We show that our enhanced model either slightly improves segmentation performance or maintains it at the same level while offering a more robust and interpretable signal, particularly for certain types of referring expressions. Our experiments suggest that while word repetition remains a key cue for topical shifts, integrating the coherence conferred by referential structure can improve performance in practice and deepens our understanding of how speaker choices in reference construction affect discourse interpretation.
