Through extensive experiments on benchmark datasets spanning different domains, we demonstrate that our model is highly competitive with — and in some cases outperforms — current state-of-the-art EL systems, while being entirely data-efficient and feature agnostic. Additionally, we show that our system is capable of effectively embedding and linking entities not present in the training data, offering significant advantages for extending EL to dynamic or evolving knowledge bases. Our results suggest that the joint modeling of diverse entity aspects is a promising direction for building more robust and adaptable entity linking systems.

Neural Machine Translation (NMT) has achieved remarkable success in recent years, primarily through the use of encoder-decoder architectures with attention mechanisms. These models are often trained at the sentence level and make translation decisions by attending to source words within a single sentence. While this has led to high-quality sentence-level translations, many languages and translation scenarios require a deeper understanding of coherent expression at the discourse level, such as pronoun resolution, verb tense consistency, and context-dependent word choice. Document-level translation, which considers a group of sentences or paragraphs as a single input, is crucial in maintaining fluency, consistency, and style across a larger span of text. Despite its importance, prior research on document-level NMT is still relatively limited compared to sentence-level work. A major challenge in document-level NMT is how to capture and utilize rich contextual information effectively. Most traditional NMT models are not inherently designed to attend to document-level structure and may struggle with assembling coherent outputs when document-level context is incorporated naively. To address this issue, we propose a novel approach that extends the standard sentence-based NMT architecture with hierarchical attention mechanisms. This model introduces a structured, dynamic context modeling layer over the source document and the target translation history, enabling the model to selectively focus on both local and global context when generating each target word. At its core, our model integrates document-level context into the standard NMT framework through a hierarchical attention mechanism that operates at two levels: one for the source document and the other for the target sentence sequence. These mechanisms work in tandem to condition the encoder and decoder on the preceding context, allowing the model to retain and utilize information from earlier parts of the document effectively. By doing so, the model can make informed decisions about ambiguous or context-sensitive words and phrases based on the broader document-level discourse, rather than relying solely on the immediate source sentence. We hypothesize that such hierarchical attention models can significantly improve document-level translation by capturing not only the direct dependencies between source and target language but also the indirect relationships that manifest over a sequence of sentences. Our experiments on well-known translation task benchmarks confirm that the proposed hierarchical attention mechanism consistently outperforms strong baselines and achieves new state-of-the-art performance on document-level NMT, with an absolute 0.45 BLEU score improvement over the best existing models.

Recent advancements in natural language processing (NLP) have spurred interest in opinion inference, particularly in the context of expressions concerning events that produce positive or negative effects on entities—so-called $+/-$effect events. Such events are fundamental to understanding and interpreting opinions within textual data, as the sentiment or stance toward these events can be crucial for downstream tasks such as sentiment analysis, event detection, and argument mining. While previous research has made progress in identifying and classifying such events at a syntactic or semantic level, a key challenge remains: the acquisition of a comprehensive and accurate lexicon of $+/-$effect events at the sense level, rather than merely at the word level. Word-level lexicons, though useful, often fail to capture the nuanced meanings associated with polysemous terms that may exhibit conflicting $+/-$effects depending on the context in which they appear. For example, the word "strike" may refer to a labor action (positive for employees, negative for employers) or an act of hitting (typically negative), depending on the underlying sense in which it is used. This inherent ambiguity necessitates the development of a sense-level lexicon to accurately represent the context-dependent nature of $+/-$effect events, thereby improving the precision and robustness of opinion inference models. This paper introduces   EffectWordNet  , a novel approach to constructing a sense-level $+/-$effect event lexicon. Unlike traditional methodologies that rely solely on either lexical resources like WordNet or machine learning classifiers using feature-based inputs, our approach combines graph-based and classifier-based methods to exploit complementary sources of information. Specifically, we incorporate the hierarchical and semantic relationships in WordNet with the predictive power of a classifier trained on gloss-based features. Our experimental results demonstrate that a hybrid model, integrating both types of approaches, outperforms baselines and provides a reliable method for identifying $+/-$effect senses beyond a given seed set. Importantly, our work not only contributes a robust methodology for automated sense-level lexicon construction but also provides a valuable tool to guide manual annotation efforts. By effectively processing and ranking ambiguous senses based on their likelihood of being $+/-$effect events, our model supports the efficient and accurate expansion of manually annotated datasets. This is particularly critical given the limitations of manual effort in scalability and coverage within large lexical resources. In the following sections, we elaborate on the methodology, describe the experimental setup, present results, and discuss the implications of our approach for various NLP tasks involving opinion and event analysis.

Sentence compression is a key technique in text simplification, aiming to shorten a sentence while retaining its essential meaning. Traditionally, this task is performed in a monolingual setting, where a single sentence is compressed by removing redundant or less informative content. This process is often used to improve readability, as well as to support tasks like summarization and question answering. However, the availability of parallel corpora—collections of sentences that are translations of each other—offers new opportunities for extending sentence compression into a bilingual setting. In such a context, the goal is not just to compress one sentence, but to create parallel compressions for a pair of sentences in different languages. This extended version of the task, which we term   Parallel Sentence Compression (PSC)  , has the potential to benefit various multilingual natural language processing (NLP) applications, such as example-based machine translation, parallel corpus filtering, and cross-lingual training of language models. The challenge in PSC lies in maintaining parallelism—ensuring that the compressed sentences still align in content and meaning across languages. This is particularly important, as even small discrepancies can degrade the usefulness of the corpus for downstream multilingual tasks. To address this challenge, this paper explores approaches that leverage bilingual information during the compression process. We investigate two strategies: one that explicitly aligns and jointly compresses sentence pairs, and another that compresses sentences independently while ensuring cross-lingual consistency through post-processing. These methods are evaluated on a parallel news corpus, where the goal is to measure their effectiveness in producing parallel compressions that maintain both linguistic quality and bilingual coherence. This work contributes to the broader field of multilingual NLP by introducing a new variant of the sentence compression task and by proposing methods to leverage bilingual data effectively during compression. Furthermore, the experiments conducted provide insights into the trade-offs between joint compression strategies and independent compression techniques, shedding light on how to balance monolingual fluency and cross-lingual alignment. The resulting compressions not only serve as more compact representations of parallel text but also open new possibilities for improving the efficiency and effectiveness of multilingual language technologies. Ultimately, this study underscores the value of integrating bilingual knowledge into text simplification tasks and lays the groundwork for future research in parallel text generation and cross-lingual representation learning. In the following sections, we formalize the problem of PSC, describe the methods considered, and present the results of our evaluation.

Chinese syntactic analysis is a foundational task in natural language processing, particularly for languages like Chinese that exhibit rich morphological and syntactic structures yet lack explicit word boundaries in raw text. Traditional approaches to Chinese syntactic analysis often adopt a cascading pipeline, performing word segmentation, part-of-speech (POS) tagging, and dependency parsing sequentially. While such methods are intuitively structured, they suffer from the   error propagation problem  , where early errors in segmentation or tagging can significantly impact downstream tasks like parsing. To overcome these limitations, joint modeling approaches have emerged, where multiple linguistic tasks are solved   simultaneously   using a single, unified model. Recent advances in   deep learning  , particularly in sequence labeling and transition-based parsing, offer promising avenues for developing such models. However, existing joint models for Chinese syntactic analysis still face several challenges, especially when integrating subword and contextual representation strategies into a multi-task framework in a   transition-based parsing   setting. In this paper, we propose a   neural joint model   that integrates Chinese word segmentation, POS tagging, and dependency parsing as a single, end-to-end task. Unlike previous frameworks, our approach directly addresses the issue of error propagation by learning shared latent representations across all tasks during training. A key innovation in our work is the   use of character-level string embeddings in addition to standard word embeddings  , enabling the model to recover meaningful subword representations – particularly important for out-of-vocabulary (OOV) words and unnamed entities that often degrade the performance of pipeline models. Furthermore, we explore the effectiveness of   bi-directional long short-term memory (bi-LSTM) networks   in reducing the need for hand-crafted feature engineering, allowing the model to learn complex, hierarchical contextual representations in an   unsupervised   manner. Empirical experiments on standard Chinese syntactic analysis datasets show that our joint model not only outperforms existing pipeline systems in   word segmentation and POS tagging  , but also achieves   superior parsing accuracy  , demonstrating the viability of end-to-end joint modeling for Chinese linguistic tasks. Our results indicate that incorporating character-based string features into the joint task significantly enhances performance, especially for morphologically complex or infrequent words, which are common in Chinese. We hope this work encourages further research into unified deep learning frameworks for multilingual syntactic analysis and error-resilient parsing architectures. This study marks a crucial step toward building robust, scalable, and linguistically aware joint syntactic models for Chinese and contributes new insights into transition-based dependency parsing with neural joint modeling.

The comparative study of historical contexts provides valuable insights into the evolution of social, cultural, and political dynamics across different epochs and regions. Histories of the nineteenth and twentieth centuries offer a compelling yet complex narrative, shaped by specific events, revolutions, and paradigm shifts. Similarly, histories of the nineteenth and twentieth centuries present unique yet interrelated themes, including industrialization, nationalism, and global conflicts. These themes provide a framework for analyzing how various societies have navigated the pressures of change, adaptation, and continuity. From a historical perspective, studying the differences and similarities between these two periods can illuminate how past experiences influence present understanding. The nineteenth century emerged as a transformative period marked by the spread of industrialization, the reconfiguration of national boundaries, and the expansion of European colonial empires across Africa and Asia. In contrast, the twentieth century saw the culmination of many of these nineteenth-century developments, as well as the rise of global conflict, ideological shifts, and widespread technological innovation. By examining the historiographical approaches and primary sources that frame these two centuries, scholars can better appreciate the nuances of historical narratives and how they are shaped by contemporary interpretive frameworks. This paper directly compares the historiography, concepts, and themes of two influential studies written in two different languages: one in English and the other in Arabic. These works, although rooted in different linguistic and cultural backgrounds, address the same central historical period and subject matter. Through this comparative analysis, we seek to uncover how language, cultural context, and scholarly methodology influence the interpretation and representation of history. In doing so, this study not only assesses the factual content of the two texts but also explores the implicit biases, perspectives, and epistemologies embedded within them. The overarching goal of this paper is to highlight the methodological value of cross-lingual and cross-cultural historical analysis, particularly in an increasingly globalized academic landscape. By critically engaging with these two works, we aim to contribute to a broader conversation about the nature of historical knowledge, the role of language in shaping scholarly discourse, and the potential for interdisciplinary collaboration in understanding the past. This approach not only enriches the understanding of a specific historical period but also encourages a deeper reflection on the epistemic diversity within the discipline of history. Ultimately, this paper invites readers to consider the implications of such comparative studies for the study of history as a global, multilingual, and multi-perspective academic discipline.

The automated extraction of structured medical information from clinical text has become a vital task in healthcare informatics, with applications in electronic health record (EHR) management, clinical decision support, and comparative effectiveness research. Clinical notes, which are unstructured and free-form text documents created during patient encounters, are often accompanied by coded diagnoses and procedures (such as ICD and CPT codes) that capture the essence of the clinical event. However, the mapping between the text and these codes is typically implicit and unannotated, making it difficult to trace how a particular diagnosis or treatment was derived from the clinical description. This lack of transparency not only poses challenges for auditing and quality assurance but also hinders efforts to understand and explain the reasoning behind medical decisions, which is crucial for both patient trust and regulatory compliance. In this paper, we address the problem of predicting medical codes directly from clinical text while simultaneously providing explanations for these predictions in the form of local text segments that are most responsible for each code assignment. Existing approaches for code prediction from clinical text frequently rely on black-box models that, while accurate, offer little insight into the reasoning behind each prediction. As a result, clinicians and researchers are often unable to validate or interpret the system’s output, undermining its utility in real-world settings. To bridge this gap between performance and interpretability, we propose an attentional convolutional neural network model that combines the strengths of convolution for hierarchical feature extraction with the power of attention mechanisms for highlighting explanatory text segments. The core idea of our approach is to encode the clinical text using convolutional operations that capture local and sequential patterns, then apply an attention mechanism to identify the most salient parts of the text contributing to each potential code. This enables our model to not only generate accurate code predictions but also to produce human-interpretable explanations in the form of key clinical findings, symptoms, or procedures mentioned in the text. Empirical results on a clinical document dataset demonstrate that our method achieves strong predictive performance, outperforming prior state-of-the-art methods in terms of precision@8 (0.71) and Micro-F1 (0.54), while also providing meaningful and validated interpretability. We further evaluate the interpretability of our attention-based explanations through qualitative review by medical experts, who confirm that the selected text segments are clinically relevant and representative of the underlying diagnosis or intervention.

The growing ubiquity of voice assistants has transformed how users interact with mobile devices, especially for tasks such as searching for local businesses. Voice search, in particular, has emerged as a dominant modality for directory assistance, enabling users to quickly and conveniently locate nearby services and establishments. Despite the convenience, one persistent challenge remains: the accuracy of speech recognition on business listing names, especially in the context of local directory searches, is often suboptimal. This is due in part to the vast number of businesses across a country, the diversity of naming conventions, and the dynamic nature of local business landscapes. Traditional speech recognition systems rely on large, static language models that either cover a broad domain or lack specificity, leading to imprecise results and user dissatisfaction, particularly when users are in areas with high business density or changing commercial ecosystems. In response to these limitations, there is a need for more contextually adaptive and geographically targeted language models that enhance the accuracy of speech recognition for voice-assisted business searches. This paper introduces geo-centric language models, a novel approach designed to tailor speech recognition specifically to local business environments, leveraging the geographic context of the user. Our method directly addresses the inefficiency and lack of precision associated with generic, nationwide language models by generating location-aware language models that dynamically adjust to the local business density. This enables more accurate recognition of business names by focusing on the most relevant vocabulary relative to the user's geographic location, reducing out-of-vocabulary errors and improving recognition performance. A core advantage of our approach lies in its ability to pre-compile these language models, thereby enabling fast recognition times while maintaining high accuracy. This preprocessing ensures that the system can deliver real-time search results without the computational overhead associated with on-the-fly model generation. Additionally, our method is universally applicable—language models can be generated for any location and user, ensuring broad usability while maintaining the specificity required to improve the local search experience. Through an empirical evaluation using real-world spoken queries from a business directory assistance service, we demonstrate the efficacy of our approach. Our experiments reveal a 16.8% absolute improvement in speech recognition accuracy compared with a nationwide language model, as well as a threefold reduction in recognition time. These performance gains highlight the potential of geo-centric language models to significantly enhance user experience in local business voice search tasks and open the door for more location-aware, context-sensitive language model applications in the field of spoken language processing.

Numbers like "131 million dollars" can often feel abstract and difficult to grasp. A dollar sign followed by six or seven zeros is technically informative, yet often lacks the contextual richness that would help readers truly understand the scale and implications of such figures. In journalism, economics, and technical communication, such numeric data is common, but humans struggle to translate them into relatable intuitions. For instance, what does 131 million dollars mean in everyday terms? How does it compare to familiar human or economic scales, such as the cost of a building, the number of people it could support for a month, or the duration of a large public event? To address this challenge, we propose a new computational task: generating  compositional descriptions  that put numbers in perspective. The core idea is to provide readers with vivid, concrete descriptions that serve as intuitive anchors for otherwise abstract magnitudes. For example, the phrase "$131 million is about the cost to employ everyone in Texas over a lunch period" offers a relatable frame of reference that makes the number more meaningful. Our goal is to automate the generation of such descriptions, enabling real-time or on-demand contextualization of numerical values in news articles, data visualizations, or educational content. We believe this capability is particularly valuable in today’s data-saturated world, where media consumers are regularly exposed to large and complex numbers without the necessary scaffolding to interpret them effectively. To achieve this, we introduce a dataset collected from news articles containing numeric mentions, each annotated with a set of rated perspectives. These perspectives are human-curated factual comparisons that help put the numbers in everyday context. Drawing on this dataset, we develop a two-stage system: first, constructing a   formula   that represents a plausible comparison using logical and numerical reasoning from a knowledge base; and second, generating a   natural language description   from the formula. We evaluate the first stage using formula construction metrics and the second using standard NLP evaluation measures like BLEU. Experimental results show that our compositional approach significantly outperforms a non-compositional baseline, achieving a 15.2% F1 improvement in formula construction and a 12.5 BLEU point advantage in description generation. Our contributions include a new NLP task, a novel methodology for compositional numeric reasoning, and an annotated dataset that supports future research in this area. This work not only enhances the readability of numerical information but also opens up new avenues for using semantic composition in natural language generation.

Recent years have witnessed a growing interest in multi-sense word embeddings as a promising way to capture the rich semantic diversity of real-world language. Traditional word embedding models often struggle to disambiguate between different meanings of polysemous words, leading to diluted representations that can limit downstream performance in natural language processing tasks. Various approaches have been proposed to address this problem, including discrete latent variable models that explicitly model sense variation. However, most of these approaches primarily rely on monolingual information and do not exploit the additional knowledge that can be gained from bilingual data. In this paper, we propose a novel framework for learning multi-sense word representations that integrates both monolingual and bilingual context in a unified probabilistic model. Our approach is based on a discrete autoencoder formulation in which an encoder component uses contextual information (both monolingual and parallel) to select a sense for the target word, and a decoder component reconstructs the surrounding context based on the chosen sense. By jointly optimizing the encoder and decoder components, the model learns continuous word representations conditioned on discrete senses, effectively modeling the different meanings of polysemous words. A key aspect of our model is the inclusion of bilingual information, which we exploit by training on parallel sentences across two languages. Even though the final representations and sense models only use monolingual data during inference, we find that exposure to bilingual data during training leads to improved performance across a range of evaluation tasks. This phenomenon suggests that bilingual context provides additional constraints and signal that help the model learn more discriminative and generalizable sense representations. Our experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed bilingual learning approach. We evaluate our model on sense induction and word similarity tasks and observe consistent improvements over strong baselines that rely solely on monolingual data. These findings underscore the value of integrating cross-lingual information in the context of multi-sense embeddings and open up new avenues for leveraging parallel corpora to improve semantic representation learning. This work contributes to the growing area of cross-lingual knowledge transfer for word representations. By showing that bilingual data can enhance the learning of high-quality multi-sense word embeddings, we aim to encourage further exploration of how alignment and translation signals can be utilized for more robust and interpretable language models. Our approach not only advances the technical capacity for learning contextualized word senses but also highlights the importance of multilingual resources in building stronger foundational models for natural language understanding.

Linguistic alignment is a pervasive phenomenon in human conversation, referring to the tendency of interlocutors to adopt similar linguistic forms when communicating with each other. This alignment can manifest in various ways, such as syntactic structures, lexical choices, and phonetic patterns. A growing body of research in computational linguistics, psychology, and sociolinguistics has explored the variables that influence the degree of alignment between speakers. One influential hypothesis in this domain is that social power affects linguistic alignment. The idea is that speakers with higher power are more likely to influence their counterparts, leading to a greater degree of alignment towards the language of the more dominant interlocutor. This has been supported by several studies showing that individuals in higher power positions tend to receive more alignment from their interaction partners. However, the interpretation of these findings has often been limited to high-level social and contextual factors, with less attention paid to the influence of low-level linguistic features that may confound the observed patterns. For example, utterance length, speech rate, or the complexity of a speaker's language input might naturally encourage greater alignment from interaction partners, independent of social power dynamics. This raises an important question: To what extent do low-level linguistic features account for the observed variation in alignment, and how does this insight inform our understanding of the role of social power in language production? In this paper, we re-examine the relationship between social power and linguistic alignment by rigorously controlling for a comprehensive set of low-level linguistic features. Using logistic regression models on two distinct conversation datasets, we demonstrate that the apparent effects of social power on alignment diminish or even reverse when these features are included in the analysis. These findings suggest that the influence of social power on linguistic alignment may not be as robust or as central as previously assumed. Instead, low-level factors may provide a more reliable and consistent explanatory framework for observed patterns in verbal alignment. This paper challenges the dominance of social power as a primary driver of linguistic alignment and emphasizes the need to consider a broader spectrum of factors—including cognitive, contextual, and linguistic—in the development of predictive models of language behavior. By addressing these confounding variables, future research can build a more accurate and nuanced picture of the mechanisms that govern human communication. We hope to contribute to a more evidence-based approach to studying the interplay between language use and social dynamics in dialogic interaction.

The accurate identification and recovery of unbounded dependencies—syntactic structures where elements are separated by arbitrary distance, such as long-range subject-verb or adjunction relations—is a critical challenge in natural language processing (NLP). These dependencies are essential for accurate semantic interpretation, particularly in downstream tasks like information extraction, question answering, and discourse analysis. Traditional approaches to modeling syntactic structure often struggle with capturing these long-distance relationships due to either their restrictive formalisms or the computational intractability of their mechanisms. In particular, conventional phrase structure grammars and dependency grammars frequently fail to account for the flexibility and structural generalization required when dealing with cross-sentential or quantifier domain dependencies. Categorial grammars, with their emphasis on function-argument composition and their algebraic nature, offer a promising alternative, especially for modeling rich syntactic constructions and their semantic interpretations via principled, grammar-driven mechanisms. However, the expressivity of these systems must be carefully balanced with learnability and efficiency, particularly when leveraging existing linguistic resources. This paper presents a novel approach to unbounded dependency recovery by introducing a categorial grammar framework that combines the formal elegance and lexical constraints of categorial grammar with the representational flexibility of head-driven constraint-based formalisms like Head-Driven Phrase Structure Grammar (HPSG). Our proposed grammar employs a compact and linguistically interpretable set of composition operations while generalizing over syntactic categories to reduce superfluous complexity and improve learnability. A key contribution of this work is the development of a reannotation system that maps large existing syntactic resources—such as the Penn Treebank, constructed within the Government and Binding theoretical framework—into this new categorial representation. This mapping not only preserves the essential hierarchical and dependency information from original annotations but also allows for the integration of head-driven syntactic constraints crucial for modeling unbounded dependencies. We evaluate the effectiveness of our grammar and reannotation pipeline on an established unbounded dependency recovery task, demonstrating that the new system significantly improves upon prior work while maintaining linguistic interpretability, computational tractability, and broad empirical coverage. Our approach demonstrates the feasibility and practicality of using minimalist yet powerful grammar formalisms for syntactic representation, paving the way for more robust and semantically grounded NLP models. In doing so, it contributes to the growing effort to bridge the gap between formal linguistic theory and practical NLP systems, particularly in the domain of long-range syntactic dependencies. Looking forward, this work opens new avenues for research into grammar-driven semantic parsing and the integration of theoretical linguistic insights into the training and evaluation of high-performance NLP models.

Recent advancements in natural language processing have led to an increased interest in Open Information Extraction (IE), a task aimed at extracting real-world facts from text without the need for predefined ontologies or domain-specific constraints. Open IE systems strive to derive subject-predicate-object triplets from unstructured text, enabling downstream applications in data mining, knowledge base construction, and question answering. While these systems aim to ingest and process vast textual corpora to identify meaningful relations efficiently, recent studies highlight a major challenge: the outputs from current state-of-the-art systems are often saturated with noise, containing a significant number of uninformative and semantically incoherent extractions. This not only reduces the utility of the extracted information but also presents a barrier to the seamless integration of Open IE technologies into real-world applications. The limitations of current systems suggest an urgent need for methodologies that enhance the precision and coherence of extracted relations. In this paper, we contribute to this effort by introducing two simple yet effective syntactic and lexical constraints, designed to refine the identification of binary relations expressed through verbs. These constraints, grounded in principles of linguistic structure, are applied to filter out non-relevant or poorly formed extractions while preserving the richness of the information available in natural text. We implement these constraints within the REVERB Open IE system, demonstrating a substantial improvement in extraction quality. Our results show that REVERB more than doubles the area under the precision-recall curve compared to previous extractors such as TEXTRUNNER and Word-Image-Based Open IE (WOE pos). Moreover, over 30% of the extractions from REVERB are achieved at a precision level of 0.8 or higher, a marked contrast with earlier systems, which produced virtually no extractions at such precision thresholds. This paper presents not only the technical contributions and empirical validation of our approach but also a critical analysis of the remaining limitations and common errors present in REVERB's output. Through this analysis, we identify areas for future research, such as the integration of deeper linguistic structures and contextual knowledge, which can further enhance the robustness and scalability of Open IE systems. Ultimately, this work positions Open IE as a more practical and reliable tool for transforming unstructured textual data into actionable knowledge. In doing so, it contributes to the growing effort to bridge the gap between human language and machine understanding. The remainder of the paper is organized as follows: Section 2 provides a survey of related work in Open IE, Section 3 introduces our proposed constraints, Section 4 presents our experimental setup and results, and Section 5 discusses the system's limitations and

Recent advancements in natural language processing (NLP) have underscored the importance of high-quality word representations, with neural word embeddings such as SkipGram and Global Vectors (GloVe) becoming foundational components in modern NLP pipelines. These embeddings learn dense, continuous vector representations of words based on co-occurrence statistics in large corpora, capturing rich semantic and syntactic relationships. However, many applications impose diverse dimensional requirements on embeddings, making it challenging to reuse pre-trained vectors across varying contexts without additional processing or ad hoc adjustments. This discrepancy between embedding dimensions and application needs can lead to either dimensionality mismatches or suboptimal use of pre-trained vectors through projection operations, which may degrade performance. In this paper, we address the issue of dimensionality flexibility in word embeddings by proposing a novel incremental learning strategy for neural word embedding methods. Our approach iteratively constructs embedding vectors one dimension at a time, enabling the generated vectors to exhibit a unique structural property: any right-truncated vector (i.e., a vector with the last $ k $ dimensions removed) corresponds precisely to the solution of the embedding in the lower-dimensional subspace. This property, which we refer to as  right-truncatability , ensures consistent and coherent representations across different embedding sizes. Crucially, this property opens new possibilities for embedding reuse in NLP workflows. A single embedding vector, once learned, is inherently capable of satisfying a range of dimensional constraints, eliminating the need for retraining or transforming the vector to fit specific application needs. This is particularly valuable in large-scale systems where multiple components may require different embedding dimensions, or in scenarios with resource constraints where reducing vector size can lead to memory and computational savings. Our method introduces a novel training mechanism that ensures the preservation of this right-truncatability property through a carefully structured learning process. We demonstrate its effectiveness through experiments on a variety of language modeling and downstream tasks, showing that our embeddings perform competitively with standard fixed-dimensional counterparts while providing the added flexibility of variable dimensionality. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first work that explicitly designs neural word embeddings with built-in dimensionality adaptability. Beyond technical innovation, the development of right-truncatable embeddings represents a step toward more modular and resource-conscious NLP architectures. In the remainder of this paper, we provide a formal characterization of our approach, analyze its implications for model design, and present experimental validation of the proposal.

The task of cross-lingual lexical substitution (CLS) aims to identify equivalent words or expressions across languages in a given context, and it plays a crucial role in various natural language processing applications such as machine translation, cross-lingual information retrieval, and multilingual lexicon induction. While substantial progress has been made in leveraging parallel corpora and cross-lingual embeddings for this task, the role of semantic attributes such as subjectivity has not been thoroughly explored. A subtle but critical aspect of semantic representation is a word's subjectivity—the degree to which a word evokes opinions, beliefs, or emotions rather than objective facts. Subjectivity is well known to influence human language interpretation, yet its impact on CLS remains underexplored. This paper investigates how word sense subjectivity affects the performance of cross-lingual lexical substitution. The core intuition is that subjectivity is an important feature for preserving the original sentiment of a word when transferring its meaning across languages. A suitable substitution should not only capture the literal meaning but also align in terms of contextually relevant emotional or attitudinal characteristics. By focusing on the English-Chinese language pair, we present experimental evidence that taking word sense subjectivity into account significantly enhances CLS performance. We introduce a methodology where both the source and target lexical candidates are annotated with respect to their associated senses’ subjectivity. We demonstrate that incorporating this information—even as a coarse proxy—is often as effective as performing detailed, fine-grained word sense disambiguation (WSD) when dealing with polysemous words that have both subjective and objective senses. Our results also highlight that subjective meanings are often more distinctive and carry higher contextual value, making them easier to match across languages. These findings contribute a new perspective to cross-lingual lexical tasks: that subjectivity is not merely a peripheral semantic attribute but a central factor in the reliable identification of cross-lingual equivalents. We argue that integrating subjectivity not only improves CLS performance but also provides a more nuanced understanding of cross-lingual semantic variation. This work opens new avenues for incorporating sentiment-aware features into multilingual language models and cross-lingual lexical knowledge extraction pipelines. Ultimately, it marks an important step toward more human-like language understanding in cross-linguistic settings. Our experiments with English-to-Chinese substitution further reinforce the utility of subjectivity as a robust and transferable source of lexical similarity information, with implications for go-to linguistic resources such as sentiment lexicons and emotion-aware embeddings in multilingual settings.

Recent advancements in statistical machine translation (SMT) have enabled impressive improvements in translation quality across a broad range of domains and language pairs. However, the performance of SMT systems is highly dependent on the availability of large, high-quality parallel corpora that are representative of the target domain. In practice, such in-domain corpora are often scarce or nonexistent, particularly for low-resource language pairs or niche application domains. This limitation poses a significant challenge for efficiently adapting general-domain models to specific target domains, where the goal is to maintain or even improve performance despite the domain mismatch. Domain adaptation in SMT has traditionally relied on either collecting in-domain data, which is often expensive and impractical, or incorporating in-domain features into the model, which may not always capture the relevant domain-specific nuances. In this work, we propose a novel and computationally efficient approach to domain adaptation based on the selection of pseudo in-domain data: sentences extracted from a large general-domain parallel corpus that are most relevant to the target domain. This selection is performed using cross-entropy based methods, which allow us to identify segments in the general-domain data that are linguistically and contextually similar to the in-domain target examples. Our approach is efficient in both time and space, as we consider only a subset—1%—of the general-domain data for training. These selected subcorpora form what we term "pseudo in-domain" subsets, which are then used to train compact and efficient domain-adapted SMT systems. Surprisingly, these systems outperform models trained on the full general-domain data, demonstrating that the quality and relevance of the training data are more important than quantity. Furthermore, we show that combining our pseudo in-domain models with a true in-domain model results in even greater improvements in translation quality, as evaluated using standard metrics such as BLEU. This work highlights the value of domain-sensitive data selection in the context of SMT and shows that leveraging only a small portion of the data can lead to significant gains. Our findings also suggest that the integration of in-domain and general-domain knowledge during decoding can further enhance model robustness and adaptability to domain shifts. These insights provide a practical and scalable solution for domain adaptation in scenarios where true in-domain data is limited, and they open new avenues for research into hybrid domain adaptation strategies.

Entity mentions play a critical role in various natural language processing (NLP) tasks, such as entity recognition, coreference resolution, and relation extraction. Traditional approaches often assume that entity mentions are non-overlapping and do not nest within each other. However, this assumption is often violated in real-world texts, where one mention can contain another mention recursively. For example, in the sentence “John, the   Vice President of the United States of America  , announced a new policy,” the entity mention “  Vice President of the United States of America  ” includes the nested mention “  United States of America  .” Modeling such nested mentions is essential for accurately capturing the complex structure of referring expressions in text. Existing methods for handling nested mentions typically fall into two categories: span-based models and constituency-based models. Span-based models identify all possible spans in a sentence and classify them as mentions, while constituency-based models treat mentions as hierarchical constituents. However, both approaches face significant challenges when it comes to efficiently and effectively modeling the recursive structure of nested mentions. The complexity increases exponentially with the sentence length and the number of nested layers due to the combinatorial nature of span generation or constituent combination. In this paper, we propose a neural transition-based model that addresses the limitations of current approaches by leveraging the idea of shift-reduce parsing in a bottom-up manner. Our key insight is to map sentences with nested mentions to a forest of constituents, where each constituent corresponds to a mention and the forest structure captures the nesting hierarchy. This model incrementally builds the forest structure through a sequence of predefined actions—represented in a continuous space via a Stack-LSTM—ensuring a compact and scalable algorithm whose maximal action sequence length is linear in the sentence length. To further enhance the model’s robustness, we integrate a character-based component into the system, enabling it to capture letter-level patterns such as prefixes, suffixes, and capitalization cues, which are particularly useful for detecting entity mentions with irregular or ambiguous boundaries. Our model not only offers favorable efficiency, but also demonstrates strong performance on the well-known ACE dataset, achieving state-of-the-art results in recognizing nested mentions. These results highlight the effectiveness of our proposed framework in modeling complex mention structures while maintaining computational tractability. This work opens up promising directions for improving the modeling of mention structures in real-world NLP applications, particularly in scenarios where recursive and nested expressions are common.

Recent advancements in machine translation have significantly benefited from the integration of deep learning techniques, especially in leveraging both supervised and unsupervised learning paradigms to extract meaningful features from raw data. Despite the traditional reliance on human-engineered features grounded in intuitive, linguistic, and domain-specific knowledge, the increasing complexity of modern data suggests the potential for automated feature learning to achieve more effective and robust representations. These representations are particularly valuable in statistical machine translation (SMT), where the transcription from one language to another hinges critically on accurate and interpretable features. This paper investigates a novel approach to feature learning in the context of SMT using deep auto-encoders (DAEs), a class of neural networks designed for unsupervised feature learning through the reconstruction of input data. Our primary contribution lies in the development of a semi-supervised learning pipeline within the DAE framework. Instead of relying solely on DAEs trained in an unsupervised fashion, we initialize the DAEs with pre-trained parameters from deep belief networks (DBNs) and incorporate a supervision signal through input phrase features, enabling semi-supervised fine-tuning. This hybrid approach effectively combines the advantages of unsupervised pre-training with the precision of labeled data, resulting in the extraction of more powerful and stable features. A critical innovation of our methodology is the design of deep architectures that utilize vertically stacked DAEs, facilitating the learning of increasingly abstract and high-dimensional feature representations. This hierarchical construction, often referred to as a “deep” auto-encoder, allows the model to capture non-linear variations in phrase features, thereby enhancing the feature space for translation tasks. The resulting features are more discriminative and compactly represent the underlying statistical properties of the translation process. To validate the effectiveness of the proposed framework, we conduct experiments on two widely adopted Chinese-English translation benchmarks: IWSLT and NIST. Our results demonstrate statistically significant improvements over both unsupervised DBN features and traditional baseline features. Specifically, we achieve BLEU score improvements of up to 1.34/2.45 for IWSLT and 0.82/1.52 for NIST, confirming the utility of the semi-supervised DAE features in capturing critical linguistic patterns for translation. This work opens new directions for feature learning in SMT, emphasizing the value of semi-supervised learning with deep architectures for scalable and effective translation models. By moving beyond intuition-based feature design, we advocate for data-driven mechanisms capable of automatically discovering complex features essential for modern language modeling tasks.

Recent years have witnessed a growing interest in the development of intelligent conversational agents, especially for open-domain dialogue systems where the goal is to generate natural and engaging responses to user inputs. In such systems, generating responses that are not only relevant and coherent but also diverse and natural has remained a key challenge. Traditional neural response generation models, such as those based on Seq2Seq architectures with attention mechanisms, have demonstrated proficiency in capturing context and producing grammatically correct responses. However, these models often suffer from the issue of generating "safe responses"—responses that are generic, reasonable, and acceptable but lack the specificity or novelty that characterizes human-generated dialogue. This tendency arises from the intrinsic properties of maximum likelihood estimation (MLE), the standard learning objective used in training such models. MLE encourages the model to produce responses that are likely to occur within the training data, often resulting in conservative, safety-biased outputs and a lack of diversity in generated text. To address this limitation and improve the quality of generated responses, adversarial learning has been explored as an alternative or complementary approach, with the Generative Adversarial Network (GAN) framework showing promise in various generative modeling tasks. In the context of neural response generation, a GAN consists of two core components: a generative model that learns to generate realistic responses, and a discriminative model that learns to distinguish between human-written and machine-generated responses. By jointly training these models in an adversarial way, the generator is encouraged to produce responses that are not only semantically accurate and contextually relevant but also diverse and challenging for the discriminator to classify. However, directly applying GAN to sequence generation is not straightforward due to the non-differentiability of the decoding process in the generator. This complicates the gradient computation through the sampling process, making it difficult to optimize the model in an end-to-end fashion. In this paper, we propose a novel GAN-based approach for neural response generation that introduces an  approximate embedding layer  to overcome the non-differentiable sampling process, thereby enabling smoother and more stable adversarial training. Our approach not only improves the diversity of the generated responses but also enhances their coherence and relevance, as demonstrated through extensive experiments on both Mandarin and English dialogue corpora. The results show that our method outperforms existing response generation models in terms of diversity metrics, while also achieving comparable or better performance in relevance.

Grammar induction techniques have grown to be a crucial component in natural language processing, especially in scenarios where annotated resources for a target language are limited or non-existent. Among these techniques, unsupervised and bilingual projection-based methods have been widely studied for their ability to induce syntactic structures without the need for manually annotated data. However, each approach has its limitations: unsupervised grammar induction tends to suffer from model instability and low coverage of rare grammatical phenomena, while bilingual projection-based methods often depend heavily on the quality of translation resources and may fail to generalize well when transferred to the target language. This paper introduces a novel strategy called   Bilingually-Guided Monolingual Dependency Grammar Induction  , which leverages the complementary strengths of both approaches to overcome these challenges. At its core, our method introduces a framework that integrates bilingual projection with unsupervised structure learning to induce dependency grammars for a target language using syntactically rich information from an annotated source language, typically English. This is achieved by projecting English dependency structures onto the target language through word alignments and then combining this projected information with distributional, monolingual syntactic cues. By doing so, the method avoids over-reliance on the bilingual translation system—thereby reducing noise from imperfect alignments—while still benefiting from the strong syntactic priors available in the source language. The key innovation of our approach lies in its harmonious integration of external bilingual guidance and internal monolingual structure exploitation. Rather than treating the projected dependency information as a rigid constraint, as is common in many projection-based systems, our method uses it probabilistically in combination with unsupervised learning strategies. This allows the model to effectively scale down the search space of potential grammatical structures and weigh different hypotheses according to both monolingual syntactic coherence and bilingual consistency. This is particularly advantageous for morphologically richer or structurally divergent languages where the alignment-induced syntactic projection can be highly noisy and fails to capture the idiosyncrasies of the target language independently. To evaluate the effectiveness of the proposed framework, we conducted experiments on five diverse languages, guiding the grammar induction process using English dependency information. Our results demonstrate that the bilingually-guided method significantly outperforms both previous unsupervised models and standard projection-based systems. Specifically, it achieves a 28.5% improvement over the unsupervised baseline and a 3.0% improvement over the best projection-only baseline on average. These results affirm the viability of our approach as a robust and scalable solution for monolingual grammar induction in low-resource scenarios.

The task of constructing effective arguments often hinges not just on the logical strength of claims, but also on the vividness and relatability of evidence used to support them. In this context, anecdotes—brief narratives that illustrate a point through a personal experience—play a crucial role. They not only serve as persuasive tools but also act as bridges that connect abstract ideas to everyday experiences. Traditionally, the use of anecdotes has been intuitive and subjective, with individuals relying on personal knowledge or curated collections to source these narratives. However, with the increasing availability of large-scale textual data, particularly argumentative writing, the potential arises for automating the process of recognizing and recommending anecdotes in a structured and scalable manner. This paper introduces a novel task:   Anecdote Recognition and Recommendation   (ARR). The goal of ARR is to extract and recommend anecdotes in a structured format, enabling their use as evidence in argumentation and as pointers for further reading. We model an anecdote as a tuple: < person, story, implication >, where  person  refers to the individual involved,  story  captures the narrative, and  implication  reveals the underlying meaning or thematic context of the anecdote. A key challenge is uncovering the implication, which often remains implicit and requires insight into the discourse structure of argumentative texts. Our approach is grounded in discourse role identification, a task from the field of discourse analysis that identifies the functional roles of different parts of a text, such as thesis, main ideas, or supporting examples. We leverage this understanding to locate anecdotal stories and their associated implications within structured argumentative essays. By mapping stories and their implications to discourse roles, we are able to isolate anecdotes and extract their rich semantic content. Once recognized, these anecdotes can then be used as part of a  recommender system  that identifies and suggests relevant anecdotes in response to user-defined topics. Our experiments show that the most effective linkage between user interests and anecdotal content is achieved through the implications of the anecdotes, which act as the semantic bridge between the anecdote and the topic. This work not only introduces a new task with clear pragmatic applications but also contributes to the broader goal of making argumentation-based writing more accessible, supported by the accurate and contextually suitable use of real-world examples. With the increasing need for reliable and interpretive tools in the realm of argumentation and discourse, the Anecdote Recognition and Recommendation system represents a significant step forward in harnessing unstructured text for structured reasoning.

Semi-supervised learning has emerged as a powerful paradigm for natural language processing (NLP) tasks, particularly in scenarios where labeled data is scarce and unlabeled text is abundant. In sequence labeling tasks, such as part-of-speech tagging, named entity recognition, or chunking, the ability to leverage unlabeled data can greatly enhance model performance and robustness. While traditional supervised approaches yield strong results when sufficient annotated data is available, their performance is often suboptimal in low-resource settings. Such limitations motivate the exploration of modeling techniques that can integrate both labeled and unlabeled data in a principled way. In this paper, we introduce  Variational Sequential Labelers , a family of multitask variational methods designed for semi-supervised sequence labeling. Our models combine the strengths of generative and discriminative learning by introducing a rich latent structure that captures contextual, label-specific, and word-specific information. At the core of the approach is a latent-variable generative model that defines the conditional probability of a word given its context, inspired by objectives traditionally used in pretraining word embeddings such as word prediction or masked language modeling. This allows our models to learn lexical and semantic representations from large quantities of unlabeled text, similar to contextualized embedding techniques like BERT. Crucially, we integrate a discriminative labeler into this generative framework, enabling the model to inject label-related information directly into the latent space. This dual objective—generating words from context while also learning to predict sequence labels—creates a form of multi-task learning that better captures the joint structure of lexical and label-level information. Our approach further explores various configurations of the latent variable structure, including a hierarchically structured variant that enables the model to disentangle different sources of variability in the data. Specifically, this formulation allows the model to separate out context about the sequence labels from word-specific properties, improving the interpretability and efficiency of the learned representations. We evaluate our models across eight diverse sequence labeling datasets and demonstrate consistent improvements over standard sequential baselines. More importantly, we show that the performance advantage increases substantially when unlabeled data is incorporated into training. These results highlight the efficacy of our approach in leveraging unlabeled text for sequence labeling, making it particularly valuable in resource-constrained scenarios. Overall, our work contributes a novel methodology for semi-supervised sequence labeling and opens the door to further exploration of structured latent variational models in sequential NLP tasks.

Morphological analysis is a foundational task in natural language processing (NLP), especially for languages with rich morphology, such as Japanese. It involves the decomposition of words into their morphological components (e.g., stems, affixes) and is essential for numerous downstream applications, including syntactic parsing, machine translation, and information retrieval. However, morphological analysis becomes significantly more complex for unsegmented languages, where word boundaries are not explicitly marked in the written form. In such languages, segmentation errors can propagate to subsequent modeling steps, leading to degraded performance in both linguistic and NLP tasks. Hence, finding robust methods that can jointly model word segmentation and morphological features is a critical challenge. Traditional approaches to morphological analysis in unsegmented languages typically rely on statistical sequence models such as Hidden Markov Models (HMMs) or Conditional Random Fields (CRFs), which are trained on annotated corpora of segmented words and their corresponding morphological features. While these methods have been effective, they generally treat segmentation and morphology in isolation or in a pipelined fashion, where segmentation is conducted first, followed by feature extraction. Such frameworks are vulnerable to segmentation errors—especially when trained on automatically segmented corpora that are prone to inaccuracies—and struggle to capture the contextual and semantic properties of word sequences. Recent advances in deep learning, particularly the use of Recurrent Neural Network Language Models (RNNLMs), have opened new avenues for addressing these challenges. RNNLMs are capable of capturing long-range dependencies and semantic cues in text, making them well-suited for modeling the fluid and context-sensitive nature of morphological phenomena. In this work, we propose a novel approach to morphological analysis that leverages RNNLMs to incorporate the semantic plausibility of word sequences directly into the modeling process. Unlike conventional language models that are trained on raw word sequences, the RNNLM we employ models generalized semantic representations, allowing us to indirectly account for segmentation ambiguities and morphological variations. To evaluate the efficacy of our approach, we conduct experiments on two Japanese corpora known for their linguistic richness and segmentation complexity. Our results demonstrate a significant improvement over baseline models, underscoring the value of semantic modeling via deep neural networks in morphological analysis for unsegmented languages. More broadly, our findings suggest that integrating higher-level semantic representations can enhance the robustness and accuracy of low-level linguistic processing tasks, offering a promising direction for future research in NLP. This work not only advances the state of the art in Japanese morphological analysis but also provides a generalizable framework applicable to other unsegmented or under-resourced languages.

Document segmentation is a critical task in natural language processing, enabling the organization of free text into coherent topical segments. Traditional approaches often yield flat, non-hierarchical segmentations, which fail to capture the complex, nested structure of many documents, especially articles, essays, and narratives with multiple topic shifts at different granularities. Hierarchical segmentation addresses this issue by identifying segments at multiple levels of detail, with top-level divisions capturing broad thematic shifts and lower-level nodes capturing subtle topical fluctuations. However, constructing such a hierarchy is challenging, particularly since the number and structure of segments are often unknown in advance and documents may vary significantly in style and content. In this paper, we introduce Hierarchical Affinity Propagation for Segmentation (HAPS), a novel method for hierarchical topical segmentation in free text. HAPS is inspired by the Affinity Propagation (AP) clustering algorithm, known for its ability to determine the number of clusters without prior specification. HAPS extends AP by incorporating document structure into the clustering process, generating a hierarchical segmentation where top-level segments represent major topic changes and lower-level nodes capture finer topical details. For each resulting segment in the hierarchy, HAPS identifies a "segment center"—typically, a sentence or paragraph that typifies the content of the segment. A key innovation of HAPS is its capacity to build a hierarchical segmentation without assuming the correct number of segments, a major advantage over most existing methodologies that require predefined parameters. This property makes HAPS particularly suitable for real-world applications where prior knowledge of the document's structure is limited. Additionally, the hierarchical output aligns more naturally with human reading and processing of documents, which typically involves shifts in attention from broader themes to more detailed content. To evaluate the effectiveness of HAPS, we conducted experiments on two types of corpora: a manually annotated dataset, where multiple human annotators created hierarchical segmentations, and a dataset of English Wikipedia articles, which present naturally occurring topical shifts. Our results demonstrate that HAPS outperforms existing methods that rely on iterative, one-level segmentation, particularly in capturing the hierarchical nature of topics within documents. By introducing a principled, parameter-free hierarchical segmentation model, HAPS advances the field of document structure analysis, offering a scalable solution for tasks such as summarization, information retrieval, and content organization. Our work not only enhances segmentation accuracy but also provides a robust framework for modeling complex topical hierarchies in textual data. The proposal of HAPS serves as a promising direction for future research on structured text processing and deep topic modeling in language technology.

Interpreting anaphoric shell nouns (ASNs), such as "this issue" or "this fact," is a crucial task in natural language understanding, often serving as a bridge between discourse segments by referring to specific entities or propositions introduced previously in the text. Despite their prevalence in written and spoken discourse, the interpretation of ASNs remains a significant challenge in computational linguistics due to both the ambiguity inherent in their referents and the scarcity of annotated data that captures such references. Anaphoric resolution involving shell nouns, in particular, adds another layer of complexity as it often requires not just identifying the referent but also interpreting the proposition or event that underlies the anaphoric expression. Traditional approaches to anaphora resolution typically rely on well-annotated corpora and are well-suited for resolving pronouns or definite noun phrases. However, when it comes to interpreting the meaning of ASNs, these methods often fall short due to the specific linguistic structure and the lack of direct syntactic connections to their antecedents. To address this challenge, we propose a novel approach that leverages the structure of cataphoric shell nouns (CSNs) to automatically interpret ASNs. While ASNs refer forward to their antecedents, CSNs, such as "the fact that X," explicitly embed their antecedent in their structure, making them naturally easier to interpret. By exploiting the information available in CSNs, we can sidestep the need for manually annotated training data for ASNs. Specifically, we propose a method that automatically extracts the antecedents of CSNs and uses them as training instances for models designed to interpret ASNs. This strategy not only reduces the dependency on scarce annotated resources but also introduces a new paradigm for exploiting inter- and intra-dataset structure in anaphora resolution. Empirically, we show that our method achieves substantial gains over the baseline, with precision rates ranging from 0.35 to 0.72 across different shell nouns, demonstrating the feasibility and effectiveness of using cataphora as a resource for interpreting anaphora. Our approach opens up new directions for the investigation of long-distance anaphora and contributes to the broader goal of building more robust models for natural language understanding. In the following sections of this paper, we elaborate on the linguistic properties of shell nouns, describe our proposed method in detail, and present the results of our experiments along with their implications for the field of computational linguistics. Combinatory Categorial Grammar (CCG) is a highly expressive and flexible grammar formalism that has proven effective in modeling syntactic structures and capturing long-range dependencies in natural language. Unlike context-free grammars, which are constrained by their hierarchical tree-like structures, CCG incorporates function application and composition combinators, allowing it to represent complex grammatical relationships more naturally. This makes CCG particularly suitable for parsing tasks that require precise syntactic analysis. However, the practical deployment of CCG in large-scale language processing tasks remains a significant challenge due to the difficulty of obtaining and maintaining extensive, manually annotated CCG treebanks. These resources are both expensive and labor-intensive to create, limiting the accessibility of CCG for a broader range of languages and applications. A promising alternative to manual annotation is the unsupervised induction of CCG grammars from plain text, where the grammar rules are learned automatically from unannotated corpora without relying on prior linguistic knowledge. This approach is especially valuable when linguistic resources are scarce or nonexistent for a given language. The work by Bisk and Hockenmaier (2012) provides a foundational model for unsupervised CCG induction, using a maximum entropy approach to associate lexical items with syntactic categories. While their work demonstrated early success in inducing CCG grammars, there is still room for improvement in both the accuracy and utility of the induced grammars. In this paper, we present two key improvements aimed at enhancing the unsupervised induction of CCG grammars. First, we incorporate boundary part-of-speech (POS) tags to better capture lexical and syntactic patterns in the input text. These boundary tags provide additional cues about the grammatical roles of words at sentence boundaries, which can significantly aid in disambiguating syntactic structures. Second, we introduce a nonparametric Bayesian inference framework based on the Pitman-Yor process to model the grammatical structure more robustly. This method allows for the learning of more compact and generalizable grammars, while also accounting for the underlying distributional regularities in the language data. We evaluate our improved approach on the English Penn Treebank dataset and demonstrate that the proposed techniques lead to performance gains over previous unsupervised CCG induction models. These results suggest that integrating lexical boundary information with Bayesian inference methods can contribute meaningfully to the development of more scalable and effective grammar induction systems. Our work points to a promising direction for advancing unsupervised grammar learning, with potential applications in syntactic parsing, language modeling, and cross-lingual grammar transfer.

Recent advancements in neural machine translation (NMT) have spurred claims of machine translation (MT) achieving human parity—the point at which MT systems produce translations indistinguishable from those produced by professional human translators. These claims, often based on sentence-level evaluations of well-curated datasets such as the WMT Chinese-English news translation task, suggest that current NMT systems can rival human performance on isolated sentences. While such findings are undoubtedly impressive, they raise a crucial but often overlooked question: Do these conclusions hold when evaluating translation quality at a more linguistically and cognitively natural unit—such as the full document level? Translation is, by its nature, a holistic task involving coherence, consistency, and fluency across a much broader scope than a single sentence can capture. Document-level evaluation offers a more comprehensive lens for assessing translation quality, capturing long-range dependencies, contextual consistency, and stylistic appropriateness. Yet, the majority of current evaluation protocols in the MT literature remain rooted in sentence-level, often segment- or token-based metrics like BLEU, or human evaluation settings that assess isolated sentences without regard to their broader discourse context. In this paper, we directly test the human parity claim by benchmarking MT systems against human translation using two distinct evaluation protocols: one that focuses on isolated sentences and another on full translation documents. We employ a pairwise ranking task in which human raters assess adequacy and fluency of translation outputs, contrasting their preferences in both sentence-level and document-level conditions. Our results show a consistent and statistically significant preference for human translation when raters evaluate entire documents, in stark contrast to the more mixed outcomes observed in sentence-level assessments. These findings suggest that MT systems may not yet match professional human translation when evaluated under conditions that more accurately reflect real-world use cases. Crucially, as MT systems improve and begin to outperform humans in local linguistic aspects such as grammar and lexical choice at the sentence level, global qualities—such as discourse coherence and document-level consistency—are becoming key discriminators of translation quality. Our work thus advocates for a fundamental shift in how MT quality is evaluated: toward more holistic, document-level assessment protocols. Doing so will not only provide a more accurate picture of system performance but also help guide the development of next-generation NMT systems that can truly rival human translators in both local and global linguistic quality.

Neural Machine Translation (NMT) has achieved remarkable success in recent years, especially for high-resource language pairs where large parallel corpora are available to train deep neural models. However, the performance of NMT systems significantly degrades when dealing with low-resource language pairs, particularly when the target language is rare and lacks sufficient annotated parallel data. This issue is becoming increasingly important as global multilingualism and international collaboration drive the demand for translation into and from a wide array of less commonly spoken or written languages. In such scenarios, modeling a low-resource language pair (X, Z) directly is often impractical due to the scarcity of training data. To address this challenge, we propose a novel   Triangular Architecture for Rare Language Translation (TA-NMT)  , leveraging the concept of tri-lingual modeling by introducing a third, rich-resource language Y. This intermediate language Y serves as a linguistic bridge, enabling the translation between the low-resource languages X and Z by sharing information through better-served bilingual pairs (X, Y) and (Y, Z). The key insight is that by forming a triangular relationship among the three languages, we can more effectively utilize the shared semantic and syntactic spaces, especially when one of the languages is rare or has limited resources. In our architecture, Z is treated as an   intermediate latent variable   that connects X and Y in a joint optimization framework. The translation models for the language Z are optimized in a unified bidirectional Expectation-Maximization (EM) algorithm, with the goal of maximizing the overall translation likelihood of the primary task (X, Y), even when direct data for (X, Z) is minimal or absent. This approach not only improves the modeling of the rare language Z but also enhances the cross-lingual knowledge transfer across the three languages, enabling more robust and generalizable translation systems. Our experiments are conducted on two benchmark datasets,   MultiUN   and   IWSLT2012  , covering a diverse range of language pairs, including several rare and low-resource targets. The results show that our triangular architecture significantly outperforms direct NMT approaches as well as existing methods that use back-translation. Moreover, incorporating back-translation into our framework further boosts performance, demonstrating that our architecture is not only effective in itself but also highly compatible with data augmentation techniques. This work contributes a novel approach to rare language translation by structurally rethinking how multilingual knowledge can be leveraged in deep learning models.

Entity linking (EL), a crucial task in natural language processing, aims to identify mentions of named entities in text and link them to their corresponding entries in a structured knowledge base (KB), such as Wikipedia or Freebase. EL is inherently a disambiguation problem, as a single surface entity—whether a person, organization, or location—can refer to multiple different entities in the KB, depending on the context. Traditional approaches to EL typically focus on context modeling through concatenation of contextual words around the mention or top-k search results from a KB, which may not capture richer semantic or positional dependencies adequately for disambiguation, especially in complex or ambiguous cases. Recent advances in language modeling and information retrieval techniques have opened new directions for handling such disambiguation by incorporating deeper contextual and knowledge-driven signals into the matching process.
