In line with the growing trend of integrating semantic representations with traditional syntactic processing, this paper presents a system that directly addresses the complexity of deep, multilingual sentence realization using richly annotated data and discriminative machine learning techniques.

Part-of-speech (POS) tagging remains a core task in natural language processing, forming a foundational building block for downstream tasks such as syntactic parsing and semantic role labeling. While recent advances in deep learning have yielded impressive performance on benchmark datasets, models often struggle with robustness when exposed to domain shifts—scenarios where the distribution of test data diverges from that of the training data. These shifts are particularly common in real-world applications, where data can include noisy transcription from speech, web text, or other informal text formats. The problem of robustness in machine learning under distribution shifts has gained considerable attention, particularly through the lenses of robust optimization and adversarial learning. However, relatively few efforts have explored these ideas specifically in the context of structured prediction tasks such as POS tagging. This paper proposes a novel approach to robust POS tagging within the framework of structured perceptron learning. Motivated by principles from robust generalization and adversarial learning, we introduce a method that explicitly accounts for potential distribution shifts during model training. The objective of our algorithm is to minimize the average loss not only over the source distribution, but also under adversarial corruptions modeled via random Zipfian distributions. Zipfian corruptions are chosen due to their ability to simulate domain shifts commonly observed in natural language data, such as changes in word frequency distributions. These shifts are particularly relevant in text data drawn from the web or other domains where power-law word distribution patterns dominate, and where rare or unseen words often appear. By restricting the scope of possible distribution shifts through the use of constrained corruptions, our method ensures the learned model remains effective under a broader range of input conditions. We test our approach on the English Web Treebank and the Danish Dependency Treebank, both of which represent real-world and varied linguistic domains. Empirically, we find that our method consistently outperforms standard POS tagging approaches, achieving an average error reduction of 4.4%. This improvement not only highlights the value of considering distributional robustness during training, but also suggests that domain-aware corruption strategies can play a pivotal role in building more reliable NLP systems. The next section further elaborates on the theoretical foundations and implementation of our proposed Zipfian corruption framework. We hope this contribution advances the discussion on robustness in structured prediction and encourages further exploration of distribution-aware learning in the field of POS tagging.

Recent advancements in computational linguistics and neuroscience have emphasized the potential of using semantic representations derived from large corpora to model and predict human conceptual processing. Mitchell et al. (2008) pioneered this field by demonstrating that corpus-based semantic models, extracted through statistical analysis of textual co-occurrence patterns, could predict neural activation patterns in fMRI data. However, despite its contributions, fMRI is a resource-intensive and logistically demanding modality that limits the scope of data collection and experimental design. To address these limitations, researchers have explored electroencephalography (EEG) as a complementary and more accessible neuroimaging tool for studying semantic processing. While fMRI excels in spatial resolution, EEG offers high temporal resolution, making it particularly suited for capturing the rapid neural dynamics involved in language and cognition. Previous studies have shown that EEG signals contain sufficient information to differentiate between broad conceptual categories, suggesting that the temporal dynamics of brain responses to semantic stimuli can be effectively modeled. These findings imply that semantic representations derived from text may not only predict distributed brain activity maps but also short-latency electrophysiological responses. This paper advances the line of research by investigating whether corpus-generated semantic models can also predict EEG activation patterns in response to conceptual stimuli. By leveraging the temporal richness and accessibility of EEG, this study aims to evaluate the extent to which semantic representations derived through different corpus-based modeling techniques can foresee neural activation patterns. We examine the performance of multiple semantic models in this prediction task to determine which models are most effective at capturing the nuances of conceptual processing as reflected in neurophysiological data. The central contribution of this work is to demonstrate that, despite the distinct methodological characteristics of EEG compared to fMRI, the representational power of corpus-based semantic models remains robust and informative. Our results not only validate the cross-modal generalizability of these models to a fundamentally different type of neural response but also provide insights into how different semantic modeling approaches align with real-time neural processes. This interdisciplinary exploration bridges computational semantics with cognitive neuroscience, opening promising possibilities for utilizing EEG in the evaluation and refinement of semantic models of human language and thought. Natural language processing systems often face significant challenges in dealing with the syntactic and semantic intricacies of language, particularly in the case of multiword expressions (MWEs). MWEs, such as fixed phrases, idioms, phrasal verbs, and conventional collocations, are ubiquitous in spoken and written language. These expressions often exhibit non-compositional or partially compositional meanings, making them notoriously hard to disambiguate using standard grammatical rules. Moreover, their syntactic structure can appear divergent from conventional phrase structures, leading to high syntactic ambiguity. Traditional parsing models, which are often compositional by design, struggle with MWEs due to the fact that these expressions behave as single semantic units regardless of their internal syntactic complexity. A Tree Adjoining Grammar (TAG)-based parsing approach has been developed to better model the hierarchical structure of language and handle long-distance dependencies, which are common in MWEs. However, even TAG systems often fail to effectively incorporate MWE patterns into their processing pipelines in a way that dynamically promotes these expressions over alternative, non-idiomatic analyses, particularly when faced with syntactic ambiguity. This is primarily due to the over-reliance on compositionality and the inability to utilize lexical and contextual knowledge about MWEs early in the parsing process. In this paper, we address this issue by introducing a heuristic-based strategy for enhancing TAG parsing with a strong bias towards MWE-oriented analyses. Our approach is grounded in the observation that, for certain types of MWEs—especially those with idiomatic readings—selecting the MWE analysis as the first available option in an ambiguous syntactic context often results in a correct parse. By favoring MWE-based structures early in the derivation, the parser can significantly reduce the size of the search space in syntactically ambiguous cases, without sacrificing accuracy. Crucially, our method avoids the typical downside of MWE assumptions: in cases where the MWE hypothesis is incorrect, the parser is still able to recover and pursue the correct, non-MWE derivation. This not only improves parsing efficiency but also enhances the overall robustness of the parsing model. Our experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach, showing substantial performance gains when MWEs are accurately identified and incorporated into the parsing process. More broadly, our work highlights the value of integrating lexical and phrasal knowledge into formal grammar-based parsing models, particularly in the context of syntactically complex expressions. This paper contributes a new method for MWE-aware parsing within the TAG formalism, with implications for further research in syntax-driven language understanding and parsing optimization.

Lexical taxonomies play a central role in the representation of semantic knowledge, acting as hierarchical frameworks that reflect generalization and abstraction in language. These taxonomies are often grounded in is-a (hypernymic) relationships, where one concept categorizes another—such as  dog  being a kind of  animal . Building accurate and comprehensive lexical taxonomies is a key goal of natural language processing research, as they underpin tasks ranging from information retrieval and question answering to semantic reasoning and knowledge integration. However, constructing large-scale, high-quality taxonomies remains a challenging endeavor, as it requires resolving lexical ambiguities and generalizing across a wide range of linguistic domains. Recent advances in distributional semantics have provided powerful tools for modeling lexical knowledge through the use of word embeddings. These representations capture semantic similarity and relationships by analyzing the co-occurrence patterns of words in large corpora. While unsupervised methods for hypernym discovery have made significant progress, they often lack the precision and contextual grounding required for constructing robust taxonomies at scale. On the other hand, purely supervised approaches, though potentially more accurate, typically require large annotated datasets that are costly and time-consuming to create. In this paper, we propose a supervised distributional framework for hypernym discovery that addresses these limitations. Our approach operates at the sense level, which is critical for disambiguating overlapping meanings and ensuring that the resulting taxonomies accurately reflect the intended semantic relationships. We leverage semantic regularities inherent in embedding spaces, where the vector representations of hyponyms and hypernyms exhibit consistent patterns. Additionally, we incorporate domain adaptation principles through the use of a domain clustering algorithm, enabling the model to adapt to the characteristics of different application domains. This adaptability is essential when developing taxonomies that span diverse and specialized areas of knowledge. To evaluate our framework, we consider a variety of configurations trained using a combination of annotated data from a manually curated knowledge base and hypernymic relations inferred from open information extraction (OIE) systems. The integration of these complementary sources of information significantly enhances the model's ability to discern hypernymic patterns, particularly in the presence of ambiguity and minimal examples. Our experiments, conducted across ten different domains, demonstrate that the proposed approach outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods in both automatic and human evaluation metrics. These results underscore the value of combining domain-aware adaptation with supervised learning for scalable, sense-level hypernym discovery. Our work contributes to the broader goal of automating the construction of disambiguated lexical taxonomies and supports the development of more accurate and context-sensitive semantic representations in natural language processing applications.

The ability to infer relationships between events is a cornerstone of human engagement with narrative, especially in domains such as film, literature, and everyday conversation. A particularly compelling aspect of this is the reasoning about  contingency —the likelihood that one event leads to another or that a particular condition must be met for another to occur. In narratives, such reasoning is instrumental in building expectations about what will follow, and thereby contributes significantly to the viewer's or reader's immersion and comprehension. In computational narratives and natural language processing (NLP), modeling these contingencies is vital for a host of applications, from improving dialogue understanding to enhancing story summarization and creative writing tools. Previous research has explored modeling event contingency from various perspectives. Some approaches frame the problem as inferring the  CONTINGENT  discourse relation, a task rooted in the rich field of discourse analysis. Others situate the problem in broader terms, such as in the domain of common-sense causal reasoning, often relying on large-scale knowledge bases or learning from crowdsourced datasets. Despite these efforts, there remains a challenge in the unsupervised, data-driven induction of event pairs that exhibit a plausible contingent relationship, particularly in the context of complex and densely structured narratives such as film scenes. In this paper, we focus on the unsupervised induction of such contingent event pairs from film scene descriptions. We take inspiration from multiple lines of prior work and adapt them into a framework that leverages statistical patterns in natural language to hypothesize event causality or dependency. A key innovation in our method is the integration of web search counts to refine the event pairs, effectively harnessing the implicit patterns of interest and co-occurrence found in global language use. We evaluate our approach by collecting human judgments of contingency between the inferred event pairs, using this as a grounded, empirical measure of effectiveness. The results validate the utility of our methods, showing that the incorporation of web search data significantly boosts average accuracy to 85.64%, well above the baseline of 50%, and notably higher than the 75.15% obtained without such integration. Through this work, we contribute a novel framework for modeling narrative expectations and demonstrate the practical feasibility of learning contingent event pairs in real-world, unannotated scenarios. Recent advancements in natural language processing (NLP) have underscored the importance of paraphrasing—transforming a sentence into an equivalent alternative while preserving its meaning—as a foundational capability for a wide range of text-to-text generation tasks. Paraphrasing is particularly crucial for tasks such as text simplification, data augmentation, machine translation, and sentence compression, all of which benefit from the ability to generate syntactically diverse yet semantically equivalent expressions of a given text. A particularly promising source for learning paraphrase patterns has been bilingual parallel corpora, where aligned sentences in two languages can reveal how the same meaning is expressed through different syntactic or lexical choices. Earlier work has primarily focused on extracting  phrasal  paraphrases from such corpora, where short segments of text are aligned across languages and used to learn word- or phrase-level variants. However, the extraction of  sentential  paraphrases—transformations that apply to full sentences and may involve complex syntactic restructuring—remains less explored in this context. This paper addresses this gap in the literature by extending the use of bilingual parallel corpora to the extraction of syntactic-level paraphrase patterns. We argue that such corpora, despite being traditionally viewed as primarily useful for cross-lingual tasks, can still be effectively harnessed for learning general, language-internal paraphrase transformations. We demonstrate that from these corpora, one can learn a range of fairly sophisticated, grammar-based paraphrase operations, such as passivization, dative shift, and topicalization. These are not only structurally complex but are also essential for generating natural and fluent paraphrases. Our approach not only focuses on the extraction of these patterns but also on how the model can be fine-tuned for practical applications through the adaptation of its feature set, development data, and parameter estimation techniques. We validate the utility of our model by applying it to the task of sentence compression—a canonical text generation problem where the input sentence is rewritten in a more concise but meaning-preserving form. Our experiments show that the paraphrase model derived from bilingual data is competitive with state-of-the-art systems in this domain. These results highlight the potential of bilingual corpora for training paraphrase models that are not only linguistically rich but also academically and industrially impactful across a spectrum of text-to-text transformation tasks. Through this work, we contribute a novel and effective method for leveraging bilingual resources in the service of monolingual generation tasks, opening new avenues for paraphrase-based system design without the need for extensive in-language parallel corpora.

The exponential growth of scientific publications in the modern digital age has led to a pressing demand for advanced techniques to effectively analyze and understand the rhetorical structure of scientific discourse. Scientific writing is not merely a conduit for factual reporting, but a persuasive medium where authors construct arguments, support claims with evidence, and situate their work within larger scholarly conversations. Understanding the rhetorical strategies and argumentative structures used in scientific texts is therefore essential for tasks ranging from literature summarization and recommendation systems to transcriptional information extraction and automated evaluation of scientific quality. A central challenge in the rhetorical analysis of scientific documents lies in their multi-layered nature: scientific texts are composed of rhetorical components (e.g., claims, enabling conditions, questions, rhetorical questions), citation contexts (e.g., citing to support, challenge, or background the current work), and argumentative elements (e.g., premises, claims, evidence). The interactions among these elements define how ideas are structured and justified. However, most prior work on rhetorical analysis has been conducted in isolation from argumentation, while relatively little effort has been devoted to the integration of these complementary perspectives. In this paper, we address this gap by investigating the relationship between argumentation and rhetorical structures in scientific publications. Our primary contributions are two-fold: First, we enrich an existing annotated corpus of scientific publications with fine-grained argumentation annotations, providing a new multi-dimensional data resource for the community. Second, we explore the potential of neural multi-task learning (MTL) frameworks that jointly model rhetorical and argumentative tasks. We hypothesize that by training models to simultaneously extract argumentative components and classify rhetorical functions, the models can leverage shared patterns and contextual cues, leading to a more holistic understanding of scientific discourse. Our experimental results demonstrate that a multi-task architecture consistently and significantly outperforms single-task baselines across a range of rhetorical and argumentation-related tasks. These findings not only underscore the importance of argumentation in scientific reasoning and communication, but also open new avenues for the joint modeling of argumentation and rhetoric in natural language processing. By providing tools and techniques to better analyze the persuasive and structural aspects of scientific communication, our work contributes to the advancement of knowledge extraction and the development of more accurate, interpretable, and domain-aware NLP systems for scientific literature. In doing so, it paves the way for more intelligent and context-aware approaches to the computational analysis of scientific discourse.

Neural Machine Translation (NMT) has emerged as a powerful paradigm for automatic translation, leveraging deep learning architectures to learn end-to-end mappings between source and target languages. Recent advancements in NMT have demonstrated that incorporating attentional mechanisms significantly improves translation performance by enabling the model to dynamically focus on relevant parts of the input sentence during decoding. Unlike traditional sequence-to-sequence models, where the entire source context is compressed into a fixed-length vector, attention-based systems allow the decoder to query and contextualize information from the source sentence in a more flexible and meaningful way. This selective focus helps address the limitations of fixed-length representations, particularly when dealing with long or complex source sentences. Despite the promising results of attention mechanisms, there remains a lack of comprehensive exploration into architectural choices for effectively implementing attention in the context of NMT. Most prior work has focused on specific application scenarios or made limited architectural expansions, leaving room for broader investigation of attentional strategies. In this paper, we present and evaluate two distinct mechanisms that offer promising improvements: a  global attention  model, which attends to all source words at every decoding step, and a  local attention  model, which restricts attention to a localized subset of the source sequence, inspired by human-like visual focus. These approaches are designed to be conceptually simple yet effective, as we recognize that complex attentional formulations are not always necessary for significant performance gains. By comparing the behavior of these models on large-scale and challenging translation tasks—specifically the WMT 2014 and 2015 English-German translation benchmarks—we demonstrate the empirical value of careful architectural design in attention-based NMT. Our results show that the local attention mechanism yields a substantial improvement—5.0 BLEU points—over non-attentional models that incorporate standard regularization techniques like dropout. Furthermore, we explore the potential of ensemble methods by combining models with different attentional architectures. The most successful of these ensembles not only outperforms all known NMT-based systems but also sets a new state-of-the-art for the WMT’15 English-to-German task, achieving 25.9 BLEU points, a 1.0 BLEU point improvement over existing strong baselines. This paper provides not only strong experimental results but also insights into the properties of effective attention architectures that can inform future research and development in NMT. Our contributions are threefold: (1) a systematic evaluation of global and local attention mechanisms in NMT, (2) the design of a local attention model with a novel alignment function that reduces computational costs and improves performance, and (3) the establishment of a new state-of-the-art using an ensemble approach that

Recent advancements in natural language processing (NLP) have enabled impressive progress in detecting and analyzing opinions presented in textual data, especially in domains such as product reviews, social media monitoring, and sentiment analysis. Much of this progress has been driven by large-scale supervised learning models trained on carefully curated corpora, leveraging linguistic features, embeddings, and contextual information to categorize expressions as subjective or objective. However, these systems remain limited in their ability to account for a crucial but often overlooked aspect of opinion: the  subjectivity of what counts as opinion itself . This article explores the undertheorized role of  metasubjectivity  in the design and evaluation of opinion detection systems. At its core, opinion is a flexible, context-sensitive phenomenon, and what one speaker or system may classify as an opinion, another might dismiss as purely factual, or vice versa. Opinions are rarely isolated instances but are often nested in evaluative and interpersonal structures that make it difficult to classify them according to a fixed set of criteria. For example, phrases like “I think she finds the book compelling” or “He says the results are inconclusive” highlight not just the presence of a propositional attitude, but a recursive meta-layer of evaluation — about someone else's evaluation. Crucially, human annotators, who are essential in creating annotated datasets for machine learning models, also bring their subjective perspectives to the task of labeling opinions. This variability introduces not only noise but also a deeper epistemological issue: the lack of consensus on what constitutes an opinion reveals that subjectivity is not only present in the content of utterances but in the identification of what is to be read as a subjectively expressed claim. This phenomenon — which we term  metasubjectivity  — is a central but underexplored challenge in the field of opinion mining. Metasubjectivity has significant implications for the development of accurate and reliable opinion detection technologies. At the corpus level, it raises questions about the reliability of existing annotations and the representativeness of data for real-world processing. At the level of sentence- or document-level detection, it complicates the modeling of nested, higher-order opinion expressions that require an understanding not just of the speaker's intent, but of speaker models of other speakers’ intentions. In this paper, we propose a framework for addressing metasubjectivity in opinion detection. We argue that incorporating pragmatic and metapragmatic considerations into the pipeline of opinion-mining systems is both necessary and non-trivial.

Recent advancements in natural language processing (NLP) have spurred interest in both distributional vector representations and traditional lexical-semantic resources when tackling tasks such as machine translation (MT). Among these, the METEOR metric has gained popularity as a comprehensive approach to MT evaluation, incorporating not only surface-level matching but also approximate semantic similarity between system outputs and reference translations. METEOR has traditionally relied on lexical resources such as WordNet to identify synonyms and measure morphological similarity. However, with the rise of large-scale, data-driven methods like Word2Vec, which learn dense vector representations of words from vast corpora, new possibilities emerge for capturing semantic similarity in a more quantifiable, context-sensitive manner. This paper explores the question: Can the integration of distributed word representations serve as an effective substitute or complement to traditional lexical resources in the augmentation of MT evaluation metrics? Specifically, we investigate the use of Word2Vec as an alternative to DBnary (a lexical-semantic resource providing mapping of database lexicons such as BabelNet into multilingual lexical resources like WordNet, Lemma, and DBPedia) to enhance the METEOR metric. Our goal is to assess whether Word2Vec, which encodes semantic information through neural embedding techniques, can outperform or at least complement human-constructed resources such as DBnary when applied to METEOR’s existing similarity judgments. We conduct our experiments within the framework of the Metrics task of WMT 2014, a widely acknowledged benchmark in the MT community. This allows for a thorough and standardized evaluation of the proposed enhancements to METEOR. Our preliminary findings indicate that vector-based representations not only offer a viable alternative to lexical-semantic resources but also bring added value in terms of flexibility and the capture of nuanced semantic relationships that might be underrepresented in static lexical databases. The resulting augmented versions of the METEOR metric, which incorporate Word2Vec embeddings, are made publicly available on our GitHub page to encourage further research and replication of our experiments. This study contributes to the ongoing discourse on the integration of deep learning techniques into classical NLP metrics, offering a pragmatic perspective on where and how traditional lexical resources can be revisited or replaced by modern, data-driven models to improve the evaluation of MT output. Query segmentation is a critical first step in the broader task of query understanding, which is essential for a wide range of natural language processing (NLP) applications, including information retrieval, question answering, and semantic parsing. The goal of query segmentation is to break down a natural language query into meaningful syntactic or semantic units. While automated approaches using machine learning and rule-based techniques have been explored, the idea of leveraging human judgment via crowdsourcing has gained increasing attention in recent years. Crowdsourcing provides scalability and human-like nuance; however, it also introduces variability and potential systematic biases that affect the quality and reliability of the annotated data. Inter Annotator Agreement (IAA) is a fundamental tool used to assess the consistency of annotations and, by extension, the reliability of crowd-sourced data. Traditional IAA metrics, such as Fleiss’ κ or Krippendorff’s α, have been used to measure the degree of agreement among annotators, but often lack the specificity required when analyzing tasks with structure-sensitive outputs like query segmentation. In such tasks, the location, depth, and distribution of segmentation boundaries may have significant implications for the downstream understanding processes. This paper introduces a novel IAA metric tailored specifically for query segmentation tasks, particularly in the context of crowdsourcing. Our analysis of real-world crowdsourced data from Amazon Mechanical Turk (AMT) reveals a previously undocumented but striking bias among annotators: they exhibit a strong preference for dividing queries into roughly equal parts, often choosing a binary-like partitioning that minimizes depth and maximizes balance. This tendency persists even when the query’s natural structure suggests multiple or uneven segments. Furthermore, when faced with hierarchical or nested segmentation tasks, annotators tend to favor balanced binary tree structures over more complex or realistic alternatives. These findings suggest that the crowd may not fully grasp the structural nuances of query segmentation or may be conforming to task constraints that inadvertently encourage simplistic responses. The insights from this study not only contribute to the refinement of crowdsourcing strategies for structured annotation tasks but also highlight the need for task design that mitigates such biases. Moreover, the proposed IAA metric offers a more granular and task-specific method for evaluating the reliability of annotated data in crowdsourced settings, ultimately facilitating better-informed decisions about the usefulness of human-labeled data in machine learning and AI systems. By addressing these challenges, our work aims to improve the quality of annotations and promote the development of more robust query understanding models.

The task of constructing a comprehensive multilingual dictionary is of fundamental importance in fields ranging from computational linguistics and machine translation to language documentation and digital humanities. Traditional approaches often rely on curated dictionaries such asWiktionary, which, despite their breadth and depth, are inherently limited in coverage, particularly for low-resource languages. The challenge thus arises: can we extend the reach and utility of multilingual resources by automatically combining and inferring translations across them? This paper addresses that challenge through a novel approach that harnesses probabilistic inference to compose a massive, multilingual dictionary from multiple existing translation sources. When translating between languages, particularly in the absence of direct source-target dictionary entries, one faces a transitive inference problem. Suppose word  A  in language  L1  is translated to word  B  in language  L2 , and word  B  is further translated to word  C  in language  L3 . What is the probability that word  C  is a direct translation of word  A ? Answering this question requires reasoning in a probabilistic framework, where translation paths are not simply concatenated, but weighted by the reliability of the lexical links that compose them. By modeling the multilingual translation network as a graph and using probabilistic inference techniques, it is possible to derive indirect, yet plausible, translation pairs that are not explicitly present in any existing dictionary. The central contribution of this paper is a new algorithm that addresses the transitive inference problem at scale. We apply this algorithm to a comprehensive set of existing translation dictionaries and Wiktionary resources, covering over 1,000 languages. The resulting resource, PANDICTIONARY, is the largest publicly available multilingual dictionary to date. It is built by propagating translation relations with probabilistic confidence across the network of lexical links, and it offers about four times more translations than the largest Wiktionary at a high precision level (0.90), with over 200 million pairwise translations across more than 200,000 language pairs at precision 0.8. By enabling the synthesis of translation knowledge across disparate linguistic resources, this work opens the door to deeper cross-linguistic research, improved language processing systems, and enhanced accessibility of multilingual knowledge to both the academic and public spheres. More importantly, it demonstrates the power of probabilistic reasoning in the domain of language technology, where the imprecision of linguistic data need not be a barrier to large-scale discovery. Through PANDICTIONARY, we aim to provide the community with an indispensable tool for emerging research and application in multilingual computation.

The task of identifying and classifying emotions expressed in textual content has gained significant attention in recent years due to its relevance in a range of applications, including sentiment analysis, mental health monitoring, customer feedback analysis, and human-computer interaction. At the core of emotion classification lies the concept of  word-emotion association —the identification of words that are semantically or sentimentally linked to specific emotional states. While this task is traditionally approached using pre-defined emotion lexicons such as NRC Emotion Lexicon, ANEW, or EmoLex, these resources often suffer from limited coverage and are defined over a fixed set of emotion categories that may not generalize well to new or domain-specific scenarios. On the other hand, methods that rely on general-purpose semantic relatedness measures have shown poor adaptability when applied to the nuanced task of modeling word-emotion associations, resulting in suboptimal performance. Although recent advances in word embeddings and contextual language models have improved the ability to capture semantic relationships, they still often fail to capture the asymmetric and categorical nature of emotions. Emotions, unlike general semantic concepts, exhibit certain unique properties—most notably  mutual exclusivity . In practice, one dominant emotion often characterizes a situation, and the words that appear with strong emotional context do so in a way that is relatively exclusive to a specific emotional category. Leveraging this key insight, we propose an unsupervised method for learning word-emotion associations, termed  Selective Co-occurrences  (SECO). The method exploits the co-occurrence patterns of words in large text corpora, while imposing a constraint based on mutual exclusivity to prioritize associations that are most indicative of a given emotion. Our approach does not require extensive annotated data or pre-defined emotion lexicons and is instead capable of learning robust associations from raw text using only a small set of seed words per emotion category. Through extensive empirical evaluation across three diverse domains and a comparison with both traditional emotion lexicons and state-of-the-art semantic models, we demonstrate that SECO significantly outperforms existing techniques. Our results highlight the importance of incorporating domain-specific and linguistically grounded constraints—such as emotional exclusivity—into unsupervised learning models for emotion classification. This work contributes to the broader goal of building more adaptive, interpretable, and domain-aware emotion detection systems from natural language text. In the following sections, we present the theoretical foundations of SECO, the algorithmic details, and the experimental setup used to validate its effectiveness.

The task of constructing effective word semantic representations has been a central focus in natural language processing for decades. A wide range of word relatedness measures has been proposed, often stemming from diverse linguistic, cognitive, or computational perspectives such as distributional statistics, psycholinguistic norms, or expert annotations. These measures offer unique yet complementary insights into the relationships between words and can be represented as word similarity matrices. However, synthesizing these multiple perspectives into a coherent and unified semantic representation remains a significant challenge, particularly when the matrices are noisy, incomplete, or vary in scale or scope. Traditional methods for integrating multiple similarity sources often rely on heuristic averaging or concatenation strategies, which can obscure the underlying relationships or make the resulting representations less flexible for downstream tasks. In this paper, we present a novel Bayesian probabilistic tensor factorization approach for learning rich and flexible word semantic representations directly from multiple word similarity matrices. Our model synthesizes a single latent word vector representation while simultaneously estimating per-perspective linear transformations for each input matrix. By modeling this synthesis in a probabilistic framework, we are able to regularize and generalize across the given similarity perspectives, recovering a more consistent and reliable semantic space even in the presence of missing or conflicting data. Crucially, the Bayesian formulation allows us to incorporate prior knowledge and uncertainty, enabling robust inference and better generalization to out-of-vocabulary words. Our model is capable of effectively integrating heterogeneous similarity sources, including both traditional handcrafted semantic resources and modern neural embeddings. This integration allows us to disentangle nuanced semantic relationships, such as synonyms and antonyms, which are often conflated in single-source embeddings. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach on the GRE antonym dataset, a benchmark that requires deep semantic understanding to resolve fine-grained lexical relations. The results show that our method achieves state-of-the-art performance, outperforming existing methods that use single similarity sources or simple combination heuristics. This paper makes three key contributions: (1) we introduce a principled Bayesian framework for unifying multiple sources of word similarity into a single semantic vector space; (2) we propose a novel use of probabilistic tensor factorization for integrating per-perspective transformations, enabling accurate approximation and regularization of individual similarity matrices; and (3) we demonstrate the practical effectiveness of our model with competitive empirical results on a challenging antonym recognition task. By enabling the fusion of diverse semantic perspectives in a statistically sound and interpretable manner, our approach offers a new direction for building more robust and semantically informative word representations in language modeling and downstream NLP tasks.

The task of identifying taxonomic relations between terms—specifically, determining whether one term is a taxonomic hypernym (e.g. car with respect to Toyota) or a taxonomic hyponym, and distinguishing such relations from unrelated or sibling terms (e.g. Toyota and Honda)—is a foundational challenge in natural language processing (NLP). Understanding and modeling these hierarchical relationships is critical for many NLP applications, including question answering, summarization, and recognizing textual entailment. In these tasks, the ability to reason about the semantic differences and inclusions among terms often hinges upon correctly identifying the nature of their taxonomic relationships, which in turn underpins effective logical inference and enhanced robustness in semantic processing. Over the years, the development of large-scale stationary knowledge sources like WordNet, FrameNet, and more recently, large knowledge graphs such as ConceptNet and YAGO, has shown promise in providing the hierarchical backbone for such tasks. However, these resources often suffer from several limitations. First, they tend to have limited coverage, especially for domain-specific or newly coined terms. Second, they can be noisy, resulting in incorrect or conflicting hierarchical relations. Third, these resources are static, often constructed for general-purpose use, and are not adaptable or extensible as new terms and relationships emerge in context. These shortcomings restrict their generalizability and reliability in real-world, dynamic environments. In response to these limitations, recent research has shifted focus towards dynamic, data-driven methods that are more adaptable and scalable. In this paper, we present a novel approach to taxonomic relation classification that avoids the pitfalls of static knowledge sources by using machine learning techniques. Our system takes as input two terms and classifies the relation between them as either hierarchical (e.g., hypernymy) or sibling using a predictive model grounded in features derived from context and existing knowledge bases. However, rather than treating such classification as a purely local decision process, we formulate the problem as a global constraint optimization task. This allows us to incorporate domain knowledge to enforce relational consistency across terms and ensure that the predicted relations do not violate known hierarchical constraints. By integrating a constraint-based inference mechanism with knowledge alignment from an external repository, we are able to refine classifications and achieve significant improvements in accuracy over existing approaches. This paper presents the design, implementation, and evaluation of this novel architecture, demonstrating the efficacy of our method on a benchmark dataset. We further emphasize the importance of incorporating such inference capabilities in systems that aim to model taxonomic relations at scale and in line with the evolving semantics of language.

Historical understanding is often facilitated through the study of event chronicles — structured narratives of significant occurrences presented chronologically. These chronicles serve as compressed narratives of the past, allowing users to grasp complex temporal sequences with clarity and ease. With the exponential growth of digital information, the ability to automatically generate event chronicles has become increasingly valuable for education, journalism, and historical research. However, one important challenge remains: how to automatically create event chronicles on a specific topic during a target period, given that a human-written or previously generated reference chronicle exists for a different period. While current systems are capable of detecting and summarizing events, they typically operate under the assumption that the reference chronicle represents the  only  source of knowledge about the relevant topic and time span — an assumption that limits their flexibility and applicability. In this paper, we address this critical shortcoming by introducing the first novel approach for automatically generating   topically relevant event chronicles   for a target period using a reference chronicle from a different period as a guide. This task, which we refer to as   chronicle adaptation  , is particularly important for enabling the creation of period-specific, context-preserving chronicles without manually curating each one from scratch. Our approach is two-pronged. First, we develop a   time-aware hierarchical Bayesian model   that identifies events during the target time period, leveraging both temporal coherence and semantic similarity with the reference chronicle. Second, we employ a   learning-to-rank model   to prioritize and select the most salient events identified by the Bayesian model, thereby constructing a concise and informative final chronicle. By combining probabilistic modeling with retrieval-based ranking, our framework not only identifies relevant events with greater accuracy than traditional methods but also aligns the output chronicle with the thematic structure of the reference, ensuring both coherence and relevance. We validate the effectiveness of our approach using both quantitative and qualitative evaluations, and demonstrate that it significantly outperforms baseline methods in generating event chronicles that are both topically consistent and temporally coherent. This work opens new avenues for automated history-aware systems, enabling richer, faster, and more adaptable access to historical knowledge through the automatic construction of accurate and thematically relevant event chronicles. As such, it brings us one step closer to the vision of 'bringing you to the past' with unprecedented efficiency and clarity. Through this approach, users can swiftly navigate and understand the context of any historical period of interest, simply by aligning it with a well-curated reference chronicle.

Recent advancements in deep learning have significantly enhanced the performance of image captioning systems, particularly through the use of encode-decoder architectures. These systems leverage the power of neural networks to encode visual content and decode it into human-readable descriptions. A key challenge in this domain lies in generating captions that are both visually detailed and semantically comprehensive. While visual attention mechanisms have demonstrated remarkable success in capturing fine-grained details from images, semantic attention has shown prowess in incorporating a broader contextual understanding from textual topics or narratives. Unfortunately, most existing image captioning models emphasize one form of attention over the other, leading to a trade-off between visual accuracy and semantic richness. To address this challenge, we introduce the Stepwise Image-Topic Merging Network (simNet), a novel framework designed to concurrently integrate visual and semantic attention during the caption generation process. The core innovation of simNet lies in its adaptive merging strategy, which dynamically combines the features extracted from image regions with those derived from textual topics at each decoding step. This approach enables the model to selectively focus on relevant visual elements while ensuring the generated captions remain contextually rich and semantically coherent. By aligning the image representation with topic-based semantic structures, simNet not only enhances the visual fidelity of the captions but also improves their overall coherence and specificity. Our framework operates on the principle that context is critical to successful caption generation. During the decoding process, simNet maintains a continuous context vector that summarizes the linguistic cues and visual features gathered thus far. This vector guides the adaptive fusion of visual and semantic cues at each step, allowing the model to maintain consistency in the evolving narrative of the caption. We implement this mechanism through a dual-stream attention module, where one stream focuses on the image and another on the predicted topics or semantic structures. The outputs from these streams are then merged in a context-dependent manner, resulting in a richer and more comprehensive caption. We evaluate the effectiveness of simNet on two widely used benchmark datasets, where it consistently outperforms existing state-of-the-art models in both qualitative and quantitative assessments. The results demonstrate that simNet excels at generating captions that are not only detailed in visual information but also rich in meaning and context. Furthermore, our analysis highlights the flexibility of simNet in adapting to different domains and caption styles, showcasing its robustness and generalizability.

Semantic Textual Similarity (STS) is a core task in Natural Language Processing (NLP), with applications in a wide range of domains, including machine translation, information retrieval, question answering, and dialogue systems. The goal of STS is to assess the degree to which two pieces of text are semantically equivalent. Given the importance of this task, numerous STS systems have been developed, each employing different algorithms, linguistic resources, and machine learning techniques. However, despite the proliferation of STS models and methods, NLP practitioners often face a critical challenge: selecting the most appropriate system for a specific task. This problem is further compounded by the fact that different tasks may require different aspects of semantic similarity—such as lexical, syntactic, or compositional similarity—to be prioritized. The traditional method for evaluating the performance of STS systems is intrinsic evaluation, where the system's output is compared to human judgments of semantic similarity. The most commonly used metric in this approach is the Pearson correlation coefficient, which measures the linear relationship between model predictions and human scores. While Pearson correlation has become a de facto standard in the field, this work challenges its adequacy for reliable system selection across different downstream tasks. We conduct a comprehensive analysis across three common STS-dependent tasks, demonstrating that high Pearson correlation scores do not always correspond to better performance on the target task. Indeed, in several cases, systems with lower Pearson scores outperformed those with higher scores, indicating that the correlation metric may not be task-aware or sufficient to capture the nuances required for specific applications. This discrepancy raises critical concerns about the reliability of current intrinsic evaluation practices in the STS domain. In response to these findings, we propose a framework for conducting task-oriented intrinsic evaluations of STS systems. Our framework emphasizes the importance of aligning the evaluation strategy with the properties and requirements of the target task. By taking into account task-specific characteristics, this approach allows for a more meaningful and actionable comparison of STS systems. We also provide guidelines for assessing the validity of intrinsic evaluations, advocate for the use of alternative evaluation measures when appropriate, and highlight the importance of understanding the relationship between STS and the tasks it supports. Our ultimate aim is to move beyond a one-size-fits-all evaluation paradigm and promote a more principled, task-driven approach to intrinsic evaluation in the STS domain, thereby enabling NLP practitioners to make more informed system choices.

Recent years have witnessed a surge in the development and deployment of large-scale unsupervised latent variable models (LVMs) of text, such as Latent Dirichlet Allocation (LDA) and Hidden Markov Models (HMMs). These models have become essential tools in natural language processing (NLP) and computational linguistics due to their ability to uncover hidden structures in text corpora. Given the exponential growth in the size of available text data, training these models has increasingly moved to large computational clusters to harness parallel processing capabilities. However, a key roadblock in scaling LVMs lies in the memory bottleneck: the memory required to store the model parameters often becomes a limiting factor, preventing the training of more powerful and accurate models. In distributed settings, the memory consumption of LVMs is primarily determined by the number of unique words (vocabulary size) assigned to each computational node. Existing approaches to parallel training distribute documents evenly across nodes, but often retain the full vocabulary on each node, resulting in inefficient memory usage. This inefficiency limits the number of topics or hidden states that can be included in the model and necessitates approximations that degrade model performance. In this paper, we address the problem of memory consumption during distributed training of LVMs by introducing a novel greedy document partitioning strategy. Our approach partitions the training corpus in a way that minimizes the number of unique words assigned to each node, thereby reducing the memory footprint required to store and update model parameters. This optimization not only allows larger and more expressive models to be trained within the same memory budget, but also improves training efficiency by reducing the volume of data that must be read from and written to memory. Our experimental evaluation on large-scale text corpora demonstrates the effectiveness of this strategy: memory consumption during training is reduced by over 50% compared to existing approaches. Furthermore, the reduced memory pressure allows for faster computation, with training times improving by up to three times. Notably, the quality of the resulting models remains comparable to those trained using traditional methods. Our work provides a scalable and practical solution to the memory bottleneck problem, opening the door to training richer LVMs on ever-larger datasets. This contribution is particularly timely given the increasing importance of memory-efficient training in both academic research and industrial applications of machine learning on text data. In the following sections, we describe the problem in more detail, present our greedy partitioning algorithm, and provide a comprehensive evaluation of its impact on training memory and speed.

The identification of verb–noun combinations (VNCs) is a crucial task in computational linguistics and natural language processing (NLP), with applications in areas such as machine translation, text summarization, and information extraction. VNCs are highly informative units that often carry coherent semantic and syntactic structures, reflecting specific patterns of how humans express actions, modifications, and relationships in language. These combinations are particularly valuable as they are abundant in real-world text and can serve as meaningful units for language modeling and semantic representation. While VNCs have been studied extensively in English, investigations into their behavior across different languages remain sparse, especially when considering the linguistic peculiarities of morphologically rich languages like Spanish. In this paper, we present a cross-linguistic study on the identification of VNCs in both English and Spanish, drawing on rich linguistic data to explore the structure, patterns, and identification of these combinations in multilingual settings. Our work is driven by the hypothesis that better characterizing the lexico-semantic and morphosyntactic features of VNCs across languages can lead to more robust and precise identification methods. We begin by conducting a detailed linguistic analysis of a representative sample of frequent VNCs in both English and Spanish. The selected VNCs are annotated and categorized based on their semantic roles, syntactic behaviors, and morphological properties. Through this analysis, we establish a reliable method of annotation with high inter-annotator agreement, reflecting the feasibility and importance of linguistic insights in VNC identification. Building on this annotation work, we then propose a method for VNC identification that leverages not only the linguistic information derived from the annotation but also syntactic dependencies and chunking features extracted from parsed sentences. The results of our experiments demonstrate that incorporating linguistic knowledge significantly enhances the performance of VNC detection systems, particularly in identifying additional valid VNCs that are often missed by simpler, rule-based or statistical methods. Our approach achieves high precision while expanding the overall coverage of VNCs, underscoring the importance of linguistic resources and processing in improving NLP systems across languages. By demonstrating the effectiveness of a linguistically informed method, this work contributes to the growing field of cross-linguistic NLP and encourages deeper exploration of language-specific patterns in syntactic construction extraction. This paper is structured as follows: in the next section, we provide a brief overview of related work on VNCs in both monolingual and cross-linguistic settings. We then describe our annotation framework, followed by the technical details of our identification method.

The notion of information status is central to the effective processing of discourse, as it informs how speakers and hearers manage and interpret referents within a conversation. Information status classifies a discourse entity as  old  (already mentioned in the preceding discourse),  mediated  (not directly mentioned but inferable from contextual knowledge), or  new  (not previously introduced). This classification is critical for tasks such as reference resolution, discourse modeling, and natural language understanding. A fine-grained approach to this classification—often grounded in modeling the information flow as it emerges incrementally—can offer insights into how humans and computational models maintain coherence in dialogue. In traditional approaches to information status classification, researchers have mostly relied on hand-crafted features involving the discourse history and linguistic cues to make predictions. These models, while effective, often require substantial feature engineering and domain-specific knowledge, limiting their scalability and adaptation to new domains. With the advent of deep learning, neural architectures, particularly those based on Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) networks, have shown promising results in modeling long-range dependencies and discourse dynamics without requiring extensive feature engineering. However, effectively capturing the incremental, context-sensitive nature of information status classification using deep neural models remains a significant challenge. In this paper, we introduce an attention-based LSTM model for  incremental fine-grained information status classification . Our model is designed to process the input in a left-to-right manner, mirroring the way human interlocutors track discourse as it unfolds. The core of our approach lies in the integration of attention mechanisms, which allow the model to dynamically assess the relevance of different parts of the preceding context when predicting the status of the current mention. By doing so, the model implicitly learns the cues and dependencies necessary for differentiation among  old ,  mediated , and  new  entities. Our experimental investigation is conducted on the well-established ISNotes corpus (Markert et al., 2012), which is annotated for fine-grained information status. Our analysis reveals two main insights. First, despite relying only on word embeddings for input representation, our model demonstrates that it can acquire a considerable amount of semantic knowledge essential for classification. Second, when incorporating a few carefully selected additional features, such as part-of-speech tags or syntactic dependencies, the model not only matches but also outperforms state-of-the-art approaches like that of Hou et al. (2013), which heavily depends on manually engineered feature sets.

Recent advancements in natural language processing (NLP) have increasingly focused on cross-lingual tasks, where models are required to transfer knowledge across languages and understand meaning in a language-independent way. Such tasks include cross-lingual information retrieval, multilingual question answering, and multilingual machine translation. A central challenge in this context is the construction of language-independent semantic representations, which enable the alignment of concepts across languages without relying on explicit annotations or direct supervision. The ability to identify and group semantically equivalent expressions across languages, especially in the absence of parallel corpora or human annotations, represents a significant step toward achieving this goal. In this paper, we address the problem of inducing cross-lingual semantic relations—specifically, relations between referring expressions—through an unsupervised approach that does not require parallel text or explicit cross-lingual annotations. Our method leverages the contextual co-occurrence of named entities in large monolingual corpora in English and French to cluster expressions that are semantically equivalent. The underlying intuition is that relations between referring expressions in a text, such as "worked for" or "lived in," manifest consistent patterns of argument usage—especially with named entities—which can serve as a proxy for their meaning. By aligning these patterns across languages, we derive clusters of expressions that correspond to language-independent semantic relations. This work is the first of its kind to propose an entirely unsupervised framework for inducing such semantic relations, setting it apart from previous methods that rely on parallel corpora or strong assumptions about translation equivalence. We demonstrate the utility of our induced relations in two tasks: cross-lingual question answering and machine translation. On a cross-lingual question answering benchmark, our clustering approach outperforms a baseline that uses machine translation as a means of aligning semantic relations across languages. Moreover, we show that these induced semantic relations can be effectively incorporated into a reranking model for machine translation, leading to significant improvements in translation quality. These results suggest that unifying meaning representations across languages is not only possible without explicit supervision but also beneficial for downstream multilingual tasks. Our approach opens new avenues for building robust, language-agnostic semantic systems, which are essential for the next-generation global NLP applications. Our contributions are as follows: (1) the first unsupervised method for inducing cross-lingual semantic relations between referring expressions, (2) an empirical evaluation on a cross-lingual question answering task, where our method outperforms a strong baseline, and (3) a novel reranking approach that leverages the induced relations to enhance machine translation.

Sequence labeling is a fundamental task in natural language processing (NLP), encompassing applications such as part-of-speech tagging, named entity recognition (NER), and text chunking. In these tasks, the goal is to assign labels to a sequence of words based on certain syntactic or semantic roles—often in the form of contiguous segments rather than individual words. Conventional approaches to sequence tagging, such as Conditional Random Fields (CRFs), typically focus on modeling at the word level. While effective in many settings, word-level modeling can limit the expressiveness of these models as they do not explicitly consider the structure of the segments themselves, which often carry rich contextual information crucial for accurate labeling. Semi-Markov Conditional Random Fields (Semi-CRFs) were introduced to directly model variable-length segments, allowing for more flexible and accurate sequence labeling. By explicitly accounting for the duration of states, Semi-CRFs can better capture local dependencies and avoid the label bias problem common in traditional CRFs. However, despite this advantage, existing Semi-CRF-based models still heavily rely on carefully engineered segment-level features to capture meaningful representations of segments. The manual design and extraction of such features are both time-consuming and require domain-specific knowledge, which can be a significant limitation as the complexity and variety of real-world NLP tasks continue to grow. In this paper, we propose a novel approach known as Gated Recursive Semi-Markov Conditional Random Fields (grSemi-CRFs), which addresses the limitations of existing models by integrating deep learning techniques with the structural advantages of Semi-CRFs. Our model is designed to not only directly model segments but also automatically learn segment-level representations using a gated recursive convolutional neural network. The architecture combines a recursive component to capture hierarchical structure within segments and a gating mechanism to regulate information flow and ensure effective representation learning. This enables the model to dynamically attend to different aspects of the input and generate meaningful features without the need for explicit feature engineering. We evaluate our proposed model on two standard sequence labeling tasks: text chunking and named entity recognition. Our experiments show that grSemi-CRFs consistently outperform existing neural models, including both traditional CRFs and other neural-sequence modeling approaches. This demonstrates the effectiveness of directly modeling segments and learning their representations in an end-to-end fashion. More importantly, our approach advances the state of the art by opening a new direction for combining the strengths of structured prediction and deep learning for improved sequence modeling.

Recent advancements in natural language processing (NLP) and machine learning have been driven by significant progress in distributed word representations, particularly in the form of word embeddings. These representations facilitate the modeling of term similarity, syntactic, and semantic relationships by projecting words into low-dimensional continuous vector spaces, where words with similar usage patterns are positioned closely together. Prominent pre-trained word embeddings, such as those produced by   word2vec   (Mikolov et al., 2013) and   GloVe   (Pennington et al., 2014), are derived from extensive general-domain corpora, capturing broad linguistic regularities. Such representations have been invaluable in a wide spectrum of applications, from sentiment analysis to machine translation, where understanding word relationships across diverse contexts is crucial. In   ad hoc information retrieval  , one of the enduring challenges is the   query ambiguity   and   semantic mismatch   between user queries and relevant documents, often due to the use of insufficient, overly concise, or ambiguous search terms.   Query expansion  , a long-standing retrieval technique, aims to address this issue by adding synonyms or semantically related terms to the original query to improve the recall and precision of retrieval systems. Effective query expansion depends heavily on the quality of the term representations and the contextual relevance of the embedded terms in relation to the target documents. While existing approaches often rely on general-purpose embeddings for query expansion, this paper investigates the benefits of   training word embeddings locally  —that is, on domain-, corpus-, and query-specific data rather than leveraging pre-trained global embeddings. We carry out an empirical evaluation comparing the performance of query expansion strategies based on global embeddings like word2vec and GloVe with those trained locally on a corpus or query-specific data. Our results suggest that   locally-trained embeddings consistently outperform global embeddings   in retrieval effectiveness for the task of query expansion. This finding is especially significant for information retrieval settings where domain-specificity and data uniqueness are key determining factors. Our analysis not only highlights the limitations of general-purpose embeddings in domain-specific query settings but also points to broader implications: many machine learning tasks currently relying on global embeddings might benefit from   domain-adapted or locally trained models   to improve performance and contextual relevance. This paper contributes to the growing literature on the intersection of word embeddings and information retrieval, emphasizing the importance of   adaptation of representations to the specific characteristics of the target data  . In the following sections, we elaborate on the motivations, methodology, experimental design, and implications of our findings.

Recent years have witnessed a substantial surge of interest in question-answering (QA) tasks grounded in visual content, especially in images and text. These tasks often require a system to integrate visual perception, linguistic comprehension, and logical reasoning to accurately answer a question. Despite the progress in image-based QA, video-based QA remains a much less explored and challenging domain. This is partly due to the complexity involved in handling multi-modal temporal signals, the high computational demand of processing video content, and the scarcity of human-annotated video QA datasets. As a result, research in this area lags behind the advances made in image-based tasks, limiting the development of systems that can understand complex video content. In this paper, we aim to address this gap by introducing   TVQA (TV Series Question Answering) -- a localized, compositional video QA dataset   derived from six popular TV shows. Our dataset contains   152,545 QA pairs   extracted from   21,793 video clips  , amounting to a total of   460 hours of video  , making it, to the best of our knowledge, one of the largest and most diverse video QA datasets to date. The questions in TVQA are intentionally designed to be   compositional  , requiring systems to perform multiple, intertwined tasks: localizing relevant segments within a clip, understanding the textual content from subtitles, and recognizing important visual entities and events in the clip. This design reflects the complexity of real-world QA tasks over video, where the answer may rely on heterogeneous information from both audio and visual modalities. The TVQA dataset is unique in its   temporal localization component  , which explicitly requires the system to identify the relevant moment in the video that contains the answer. This is in contrast to many QA tasks in the literature, where context about the relevant region is often implicitly given or the task is limited to static images. By requiring localization, TVQA encourages research that better integrates visual perception and temporal reasoning -- key components in developing video understanding systems. Additionally, the dataset offers rich semantic annotations and multi-step reasoning challenges, making it a valuable benchmark for pushing the boundaries of video-centric AI. To enable future research, we provide   several baseline models as well as a multi-stream, end-to-end trainable neural network framework   tailored for the TVQA task. Our work represents a meaningful step toward building systems that can effectively comprehend and reason about real-world video content.

Recent advancements in natural language processing (NLP) have underscored the importance of effective feature representations for building robust and generalizable models. While fully supervised approaches have yielded impressive results on various NLP tasks, their performance is often constrained by the availability of large annotated datasets. On the other hand, unsupervised methods can leverage vast amounts of unlabeled data to learn meaningful word representations that capture important syntactic and semantic relationships. This paper explores how efficiently combining these unsupervised word representations with traditional supervised models can yield substantial improvements in downstream tasks, without requiring task-specific training of the representations. Our central hypothesis is that word representations derived from unsupervised learning can provide useful features to enhance the performance of existing supervised NLP systems, in a general and task-agnostic manner. To validate this hypothesis, we evaluate three well-known forms of unsupervised word representations: Brown clusters, the word embeddings from Collobert and Weston (2008), and the Hierarchical Hidden Markov Model with Logistic Regression (HLBL) from Mnih and Hinton (2009). These representations, though obtained through different algorithms and assumptions, all aim to encode semantic or syntactic similarity between words. We experiment with two classic NLP tasks—Named Entity Recognition (NER) and Chunking—both of which benefit from accurate local context modeling. Our work is grounded in the use of strong, near state-of-the-art supervised baselines, and we demonstrate that the integration of these unsupervised word representations consistently improves model performance across both tasks. Moreover, we find that the performance gains are even greater when different representations are combined, suggesting that these representations capture complementary aspects of word meaning and usage. This approach exemplifies a practical and effective semi-supervised learning paradigm: leveraging powerful unsupervised representations to enhance the performance of supervised systems, without the need to retrain or fundamentally alter those systems. We present an open and reusable resource where the community can download the word representations and the corresponding code, facilitating plug-and-play integration into existing NLP pipelines. Our results suggest that even simple integration of such unsupervised features can lead to accurate, state-of-the-art performance across a variety of NLP applications. Through this work, we emphasize the value and effectiveness of semi-supervised learning in bridging the gap between abundant unlabeled data and the limited but high-quality labeled data required for learning high-performance NLP models. Downloadable features and code are available at http://metaoptimize.com/projects/wordreprs/. Finally, we hope that this paper inspires further exploration into the design and utilization of unsupervised representations for NLP, both as standalone tools and in combination with traditional supervised models.

The identification of metaphors in natural language remains a core challenge in computational linguistics, with broad implications for applications in semantic comprehension, language modeling, and text analysis. Metaphors are more than mere stylistic choices—they are fundamental constructs that allow speakers and writers to communicate abstract or complex ideas by mapping them onto more concrete or familiar domains. However, their abstraction makes them notoriously difficult to detect automatically, especially within the diversity of expressions found in unrestricted text. Traditional approaches to metaphor identification have often relied on large amounts of annotated data or domain-specific knowledge resources, which are expensive to create and limited in scope. In this paper, we propose a novel solution to the problem of metaphor recognition that is both efficient and effective, leveraging unsupervised learning techniques grounded in linguistic patterns. Our system is designed to identify metaphorical expressions by exploiting the rich contextual structure found in verb-noun relationships. Central to our approach is the idea that metaphorical language emerges when an expression, while sharing syntactic structure with a literal counterpart, deviates from the conventional semantic associations of its constituents. Starting from a small, manually annotated seed set of metaphorical expressions, our method iteratively expands this set by clustering verbs and nouns based on their distributional properties across a large corpus. This clustering process allows us to uncover and isolate metaphorical usages that align in syntactic form but differ semantically from their literal equivalents. What sets our approach apart is its reliance solely on data-driven, unsupervised methods, avoiding the need for hand-crafted linguistic rules or extensive annotated corpora beyond the initial seed. This not only makes our system more scalable but also more adaptable to diverse linguistic contexts. To evaluate the effectiveness of our method, we applied it across a variety of unrestricted texts, and the results demonstrate robust metaphor identification with a precision of 0.79. Given its accuracy and minimal reliance on external resources, our system represents a significant advancement in the field of metaphor detection and opens new avenues for understanding and processing figurative language at scale. This step toward fully automated metaphor identification is an important milestone in improving machine understanding of human communication. By bridging the gap between figurative language and computational analysis, our work contributes to a broader vision of natural language processing systems that can not only parse but also truly comprehend the full spectrum of nuanced and metaphorical expressions in written and spoken language.

The task of labeled segmentation has received significant attention in the field of document analysis, particularly for structured documents such as books, reports, and academic papers. Printed books often have a well-defined yet complex structure, with sections such as the table of contents, preface, chapters, appendices, and index playing critical roles in navigation and comprehension. However, despite the importance of these structural elements, systematic and large-scale efforts to automatically identify and classify these components remain limited. A fundamental challenge lies in the variability of layouts, typographic diversity, and differences in structural arrangement across historical and modern printings. This paper addresses this gap by introducing the task of  book structure labeling , which involves segmenting page boundaries and assigning a fixed structural label to the content found on each page. Our work is motivated by the growing interest in applying machine learning techniques to digitized books—from early modern English literature to 20th-century historical texts—for tasks such as archival preservation, knowledge extraction, and document exploration. However, such efforts are hindered by the lack of annotated data that captures the structural components of printed books at a granular level. To this end, we present a large, manually annotated dataset comprising 294,816 pages from 1,055 printed books, evenly sampled across the period 1750–1922.
