The annotations are structured around a fixed set of categories, including but not limited to TABLE OF CONTENTS, PREFACE, CHAPTER, INDEX, and others that reflect the depth and variety of internal book structures. To evaluate the feasibility of automated book structure labeling, we conduct an empirical study comparing the performance of several machine learning models. Among the approaches considered—ranging from traditional rule-based methods and supervised classifiers to sequence models—we find that a bidirectional long short-term memory (LSTM) network with rich linguistic and typographic features achieves the highest performance. Notably, this model attains an overall accuracy of 95.8%, a class-balanced macro F-score of 71.4%, and demonstrates strong robustness across different book genres and formats. These results indicate a promising foundation for building scalable tools that can automatically infer document structure in large collections of printed books, enabling numerous downstream applications in digital humanities and library science. This paper contributes both a new annotated dataset for book structure labeling and an evaluation framework for learning-based methods in this domain. More broadly, it serves as a stepping stone for advancing our understanding of how to model and classify the structural language of printed materials.

Parsing a sentence accurately is a central task in computational linguistics, enabling a wide range of downstream applications from machine translation to information extraction. Over the years, numerous approaches have been proposed, yet the challenge of balancing model complexity, accuracy, and interpretability remains. Among these approaches, Data-Oriented Parsing (DOP) stands out for its empirical foundation and ability to capture linguistic variability by using syntactic fragments observed in treebanks as building blocks for a generative parser. Despite its theoretical appeal, DOP has sometimes struggled with scalability due to the large number of fragments it can incorporate and the associated computational and statistical challenges. In this paper, we present a novel DOP-inspired parsing model designed to address these challenges. Our approach, termed   Double-DOP  , leverages syntactic fragments of arbitrary size extracted from a treebank to analyze new sentences. However, to ensure the model remains tractable and focused on generalizable patterns, we impose an important constraint: we retain only those fragments that appear at least twice in the training data. This filtering criterion allows us to preserve a small but representative set of tree fragments, resulting in a compact Tree-Substitution Grammar (TSG) that can serve as the backbone of a probabilistic generative model. In turn, this compact TSG facilitates more efficient computation while preserving the linguistic richness of larger grammatical units. To integrate our DOP model with established methodologies, we develop a transform-backtransform approach, allowing the application of standard Probabilistic Context-Free Grammar (PCFG) inference techniques. This not only improves the efficiency of our model, but also ensures compatibility with widely-used parsing frameworks and enables straightforward comparison with other state-of-the-art systems. Our implementation simplifies replication and is grounded in a clear generative probabilistic interpretation, which offers both theoretical and practical advantages. According to standard parsing evaluation metrics such as the Parseval measures, the resulting model achieves performance comparable to a number of leading parsing systems. More importantly, it provides complementary benefits, such as a transparent generative process, an explicit representation of grammatical structure at multiple levels, and a leaner grammar that reflects frequent patterns in the data. These characteristics make   Double-DOP   a compelling alternative for researchers and practitioners seeking accurate and interpretable parsing solutions. Through our experiments, we demonstrate that a more selective and principled use of treebank data can yield strong, interpretable models that capture the essence of syntactic structure in a novel and effective way.

Recent advancements in transfer learning have significantly mitigated the dependency on large-scale annotated data for training machine learning models in new domains. These techniques have shown remarkable success in scenarios where the source and target domains share similar label sets or task structures, effectively leveraging pre-trained knowledge to boost performance in the target domain. However, a critical challenge remains unaddressed in many real-world applications: the problem of cross-domain text classification when the source domains and the target domain involve disparate label sets in terms of both the quantity and semantic meanings of the labels. In such scenarios, direct application of conventional transfer learning or domain adaptation methods is not only suboptimal but often impractical. This paper introduces a novel transfer learning approach to tackle cross-domain text classification involving multiple source domains and a target domain with a disparate set of labels. Unlike existing approaches that either implicitly assume label alignment or operate within the constraints of a single source domain, our framework is specifically designed to handle heterogeneous label spaces, enabling the discovery and aggregation of transferable patterns from multiple domains to support learning in a new target domain. The core idea of our approach is to selectively extract informative labeled instances from the multiple source domains, based on semantic relevance and domain adaptivity, and combine them into an auxiliary training set that aligns with the target domain's learning objectives. The proposed methodology is centered on three key components: (1) a domain-invariant representation learning module capable of encoding semantic meaning while reducing domain bias; (2) a label alignment mechanism that identifies and captures cross-domain semantic correlations even when the label sets are heterogeneous; and (3) an adaptive classification framework that leverages the auxiliary training set to improve generalization to the target domain. By designing a flexible architecture that does not assume label consistency across domains and can scale with an increasing number of source domains, our approach provides a significant step forward in addressing the complexities of multi-domain, cross-label transfer learning. To demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach, we conduct extensive experiments using two widely-used and representative datasets: a real-world social media dataset, where the multi-domain and multi-label settings are more reflective of real-life heterogeneity, and the 20 Newsgroups dataset, a classical benchmark for text classification. The experimental results not only confirm the robustness of our method across different domain-label configurations but also show a substantial performance improvement over existing state-of-the-art approaches, including both traditional domain adaptation methods and recent multi-task learning baselines.

Coreference resolution (CR) is a fundamental task in natural language processing (NLP) that aims to identify expressions in a text that refer to the same entity or concept. While significant progress has been made in monolingual CR systems, particularly for well-resourced languages like English, the problem remains challenging in low-resource scenarios or for cross-lingual settings. This paper presents a novel approach to   cross-lingual coreference resolution of pronouns  , where CR is performed on   bitexts  —parallel sentences in two languages. Specifically, we introduce a machine learning-based method to resolve English pronouns using information from the Czech side of a parallel corpus, marking, to our knowledge, the first attempt at tackling CR in this cross-lingual context. Traditional monolingual CR systems rely on linguistic features derived from within a single language. These features include part-of-speech tags, syntactic dependencies, semantic similarity between candidates, and rules for anaphoric relations. However, when dealing with parallel texts, multilingual resources offer additional opportunities to enhance coreference modeling. By integrating knowledge from another language, we can leverage cross-lingual lexical and semantic cues that may not be present or as discriminative in the monolingual context. In this work, we focus on   pronouns  , which are often ambiguous and require strong contextual and semantic understanding for accurate resolution. Our approach involves constructing a cross-lingual feature set by extending the standard monolingual CR feature space with features derived from the aligned Czech sentence. These include syntactic and semantic features extracted from the Czech side, such as agreement patterns, semantic roles, and word senses. Additionally, a key component of our system is the   supervised pronoun aligner  , which improves the quality of cross-lingual links between pronouns in the two languages. This aligner significantly outperforms a GIZA++ baseline on both intrinsic and extrinsic evaluations, highlighting the importance of accurate alignment in cross-lingual modeling tasks. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our cross-lingual CR system by comparing it against a monolingual English CR system as well as a cross-lingual projection system, where CR is performed in one language and then projected to the other. The results show that our integrated, supervised approach leads to a substantial performance improvement, confirming the value of incorporating cross-lingual information for resolving pronoun coreference. More broadly, this work contributes novel methods and insights into the challenges of leveraging parallel corpora for coreference modeling, opening promising avenues for future research in multilingual NLP.

Answer selection is a critical task in community question answering (CQA), where the goal is to identify the most suitable answer to a given question from a pool of candidate responses. CQA platforms, such as Stack Overflow or Quora, are essential resources for knowledge sharing, and improving answer selection mechanisms enhances the efficiency and user experience of these platforms. Typically, the input to an answer selection system includes the question and the possible answers. In practice, most community questions consist of two major components: the subject and the body. The subject is a concise summary, typically presented as a title, while the body provides detailed contextual information. Although these two components serve different functions in conveying the content of a question, traditional approaches often concatenate them as a single textual input without considering their distinctiveness. This one-size-fits-all concatenation approach may not reflect the underlying structure of how the question is constructed or how information is processed by readers. A growing body of research in natural language processing emphasizes the importance of explicitly modeling structural and semantic relationships between different parts of a text in order to achieve superior performance. Inspired by this, we argue that treating the question subject and body as separate entities and modeling their relationships could lead to a more accurate understanding of the question, thereby improving the quality of selected answers. In this paper, we introduce the Question Condensing Networks (QCN), a novel model that harnesses the relationship between the subject and body of community questions to enhance answer selection. Specifically, QCN treats the subject as the primary source of information and conditionally incorporates the body through a similarity and disparity-aware mechanism, which captures both what aligns with and what complements the subject. This approach effectively condenses the question into a rich and contextually appropriate representation that better discriminates among candidate answers. To validate the effectiveness of our approach, we conduct extensive experiments on two widely used CQA datasets. Our results demonstrate that QCN consistently outperforms state-of-the-art baselines, achieving superior accuracy in answer selection. These findings not only highlight the importance of modeling the structural composition of questions but also open new directions for designing domain-aware architectures in CQA systems. By leveraging the latent relationships within community-generated content, our work contributes to a more principled approach for selecting high-quality answers in real-world Q&A environments. lunches to students and parents from the school.

Recent advancements in machine translation (MT) have emphasized the importance of evaluating translation quality through multiple metrics, each highlighting different aspects of fluency, accuracy, and adequacy. However, despite the availability of diverse metrics, such as BLEU, METEOR, and TER, most MT systems are typically optimized for a single metric at a time. This approach limits the system's ability to balance the trade-offs between the different aspects of translation quality that these metrics aim to capture. In this paper, we propose a novel approach to MT training and decoding by formulating the optimization as a multi-objective problem. Rather than relying on a subjective or potentially suboptimal linear combination of metrics, we leverage the theoretical foundations of Pareto Optimality to generate a set of non-dominated hypotheses that represent the best possible trade-offs between multiple metrics. This method is not only more principled but also offers greater flexibility and robustness compared to ad hoc approaches. Our approach is built upon the MERT (Minimum Error Rate Training) and PRO (PRObability optimization for ROUGE) frameworks, which are widely used in MT, and is simple to implement in existing systems. We demonstrate that by relaxing the assumption that the model must optimize a single objective, we can achieve better overall translation quality across a range of evaluation metrics. Furthermore, we explore the issue of metric tunability and show that our Pareto-based method is more effective at incorporating new metrics into the optimization process, making it a more scalable and adaptable solution for future MT evaluation and optimization efforts. Importantly, our experiments confirm that the Pareto multi-objective approach consistently outperforms traditional linear-aggregation methods in both standard evaluation settings and under conditions where new or domain-specific metrics are added to the optimization. These findings highlight the potential of multi-objective optimization techniques in MT and set the stage for more sophisticated approaches to translation quality modeling. By explicitly considering multiple aspects of translation quality during training and decoding, our method represents an important step toward more holistic and robust evaluation-driven MT systems. In the following sections, we provide a detailed formulation of the multi-objective optimization framework and evaluate its effectiveness on several standard MT benchmarks. Our contributions include a novel application of multi-objective optimization in MT, an analysis of its advantages compared to existing approaches, and empirical evidence of its superior performance and adaptability to new metrics.

Strategic conversation is a fundamental aspect of human interaction in complex decision-making scenarios, especially in environments where outcomes are interdependent and competitive. In such settings, negotiation often serves as the primary mechanism through which participants exchange information, build alliances, and make compromises. A core challenge in understanding the dynamics of these conversations is how to extract actionable insights from spoken or written dialogue to predict the resulting strategic decisions. This task is particularly challenging in zero-sum or win-lose domains where the preferences of one participant may directly oppose those of another, and each communication move can carry hidden or explicit strategic intentions. This paper focuses on the problem of predicting the trades that players execute in a win-lose board game, The Settlers of Catan, through the analysis of their negotiation dialogues. The game offers a rich, semi-structured environment where players negotiate resource trades to achieve their individual objectives, and the conversations they conduct often serve as a window into their underlying strategies and preferences. Unlike previous work that has incorporated dialogue in collaborative or cooperative domains, our task emphasizes the competitive setting and the need to account for dynamic preference shifts, as each participant's leverage and willingness to trade evolve based on the game state and the actions of other players. To address this problem, we introduce a novel framework that dynamically models each player’s preferences based on the negotiation dialogues they produce during the game. Our method incrementally updates these preference models as new dialogue turns are observed, capturing how players signal their priorities and respond to the arguments and proposals of others. We then apply equilibrium reasoning from game theory to anticipate plausible trades that are consistent with the current distribution of strategic value and the estimated utility each player can gain. By combining real-time dialogue analysis with strategic prediction, our approach enables a deeper understanding of the interplay between language and decision-making in competitive settings. We evaluate our method against four baselines to assess the importance of tracking evolving preferences and integrating equilibrium reasoning. Our results highlight that both components are essential to accurately predicting the trades that players will ultimately execute. This work contributes a proof-of-concept methodology for grounding strategic conversation in computational models of negotiation and shows promise for broader applications in domains such as negotiation support systems, personalized tutoring, and strategic game AI. Ultimately, the paper demonstrates that dialogue can serve as both a means of communication and a nuanced source of strategic insight in competitive human interaction.

Natural language generation (NLG) is a pivotal component in spoken dialogue systems, where it directly affects the user experience by shaping the language that systems use to interact with users. An effective NLG system must produce responses that are not only semantically accurate but also fluent, natural, and contextually appropriate. Traditional approaches to NLG in dialogue systems have largely relied on rule-based and template-driven methods, which often result in rigid outputs that lack the natural variation and flexibility of human language. While these systems offer precise control, they are labor-intensive to develop, difficult to adapt across domains, and resistant to scaling for multilingual or complex scenarios. As user expectations for conversational agents continue to rise, there is a pressing need for data-driven and easily adaptable solutions that can produce high-quality and diverse natural language responses. In recent years, deep learning models have shown considerable promise in generating fluent and contextually coherent language. Among these, Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) networks have emerged as a powerful tool for modeling sequential data in natural language tasks due to their ability to preserve long-term dependencies and generate coherent, context-aware outputs. This paper advances the state-of-the-art by introducing a statistical NLG model based on semantically conditioned LSTM networks that generate surface realizations while explicitly considering high-level semantic content. Unlike many prior approaches, this model does not require explicit alignment between semantic representations and sentences. Instead, it jointly optimizes sentence planning and surface realization, making the system more flexible and scalable. A core contribution of this work lies in its use of a simple cross-entropy objective that enables end-to-end training of the generator using unaligned data. This not only simplifies the training process but also reduces the need for domain-specific heuristics, making the model more generalizable. Furthermore, the proposed system introduces variability in generated utterances through sampling from output candidates, which mimics the diversity found in human language. Evaluation results on two distinct test domains demonstrate that the semantically conditioned LSTM-based generator achieves improved performance in terms of both informativeness and naturalness compared to existing approaches. A human evaluation study further supports these findings by showing higher preference for the LSTM-generated responses. This paper thus marks an important step toward more robust and natural NLG for spoken dialogue systems, providing a compelling alternative to traditional hand-crafted and static models by leveraging the power of deep learning and semantic control.

Recent advancements in natural language processing (NLP) have enabled models to not only understand surface-level language but also reason about deeper semantic structures embedded in text. One crucial step towards this goal is the parsing of natural language into formal meaning representations that accurately capture the logical and referential structure of discourse. Discourse Representation Theory (DRT; Kamp and Reyle 1993) provides an expressive framework for formalizing the meaning of utterances, represented as Discourse Representation Structures (DRSs), which encode predicates, logical relationships, referents, and their interactions. While DRT was originally proposed for compositional semantics in formal semantics research, its applicability to computational NLP tasks has motivated recent efforts to develop flexible, accurate models for DRS parsing. Traditional approaches to DRT parsing are typically rule-based or rely on symbolic methods, which are limited in scalability and domain adaptability. In recent years, neural network-based approaches have shown promise in encoding compositional and contextual information for semantic tasks. However, the complexity of DRS representations — which include nested structures, variable binding, and predicate-argument relationships — poses significant challenges for neural parser design. One key challenge is the decomposition of the parsing process into manageable subtasks while preserving the full expressiveness of DRT. Most early approaches tend to treat DRS parsing as a single, monolithic task, which can obscure the interpretable relationships between the various semantic elements in the meaning representation and complicate the model’s learning process. In this work, we propose a novel structure-aware method for DRS parsing that addresses these limitations. We first introduce a transformation that maps DRSs into tree representations, which facilitates the application of tree-based neural architectures. Building upon this, we develop a multi-stage decoding model that explicitly disentangles the parsing process into three distinct stages: predicting the basic hierarchical structure of the DRS, inferring the predicates and their logical roles (condition prediction), and determining the referents and their connections (referent prediction). By structuring the parsing process in this way, the model can independently refine its predictions at each stage, improving both accuracy and effectiveness. Our model is fully differentiable and does not rely on domain-specific resources or manually curated templates. We evaluate our approach on the standard benchmark for DRS parsing: the Groningen Meaning Bank (GMB). Experimental results demonstrate that our method achieves a significant improvement over strong baseline models, including both traditional DRT parsers and recent neural architectures. This work not only advances the state of the art in DRS parsing but also provides a flexible framework that facilitates further research into open-domain semantic parsing and deeper compositional reasoning in NLP tasks.

Recent advancements in statistical machine translation (SMT) have focused heavily on optimizing translation output with respect to one primary evaluation metric, such as BLEU or METEOR. However, these single-metric approaches often ignore the nuanced trade-offs that exist across multiple evaluation criteria, each capturing different aspects of translation quality — fluency, adequacy, and grammatical correctness, among others. This one-dimensional optimization can lead to suboptimal translations when multiple quality dimensions are considered simultaneously. As such, the need for methods capable of handling multi-metric optimization (MMO) has become increasingly evident in the MT community. MMO in SMT poses unique challenges. Optimization over a single metric is already complex, but when multiple metrics are involved, the problem becomes multi-objective in nature. Traditional approaches to this problem have either relied on scalarization techniques, where metrics are combined into a single weighted objective, or heuristics that prioritize one metric at the expense of others. Both strategies suffer from limitations. Scalarization requires careful and often arbitrary weight selection, while heuristic-driven baselines lack theoretical guarantees of optimality. In this paper, we adopt a formal approach to MMO based on the concept of Pareto-optimality, a well-established framework in multi-objective optimization. Here, a solution is considered Pareto-optimal if no other solution can improve one metric without worsening another. By viewing MMO through this lens, we are able to fairly represent the trade-offs inherent in optimizing multiple evaluation objectives. More importantly, this perspective allows us to explore the space of possible optimal solutions and combine them effectively, rather than being constrained to a single point in the objective function space. To this end, we present several novel methods for multi-metric tuning, including a new ensemble tuning approach that explicitly searches for Pareto-optimal solutions. This approach avoids the need to preprocess or combine metrics a priori, allowing the different models to contribute to the final translation outcome in a balanced and interpretable manner. We evaluate our proposed methods on a variety of datasets with both multiple and single reference corpora, demonstrating that our multi-metric ensemble decoding techniques yield significant improvements across multiple evaluation metrics such as BLEU and RIBES, without performance degradation on others. In contrast to traditional single-metric tuning approaches, which often improve one metric at the expense of others, our human evaluation results also support that multi-metric optimization results in better overall translation quality. This insight underscores the importance of holistic evaluation in machine translation and highlights the promise of ensemble tuning as a practical solution to the multi-objective optimization problem in SMT.

Event detection and classification is a crucial task in natural language processing, enabling the extraction of structured knowledge from unstructured text. Events, typified by specific actions or phenomena such as "attack," "rescue," or "flood," are essential for building robust semantic representations of textual content and are widely used in downstream applications such as information retrieval, question answering, and knowledge base population. Despite the increasing interest and advancements in event detection, particularly with the rise of neural network-based approaches, there remains a gap in a comprehensive empirical comparison of how different model architectures perform under rigorous experimental setups. Most works to date either treat event detection in isolation or rely on a limited set of experimental configurations without robust statistical validation. This is particularly important as slight variations in training settings can lead to significant differences in model performance, potentially misleading conclusions about architectural efficacy. In this paper, we address this gap by presenting a focused and comprehensive empirical evaluation of neural network architectures for event detection, using the widely adopted ACE2005 dataset. To this end, we propose a novel architecture based on Gated Recurrent Units (GRUs) that integrates both syntactic and temporal features through an attention mechanism. Syntactic information, derived from parse trees, is leveraged to enhance the model's understanding of event triggers and their contextual roles within sentences. Temporal features are incorporated to capture the sequential nature of event mentions and their relationships within a document. This dual focus on syntax and temporal structure aims to provide a richer representation that is better suited for event detection than models that use either modality in isolation. We conduct extensive empirical evaluations comparing our GRU-based model against a suite of established architectures including vanilla recurrent neural networks (RNNs), long short-term memory (LSTM) networks, and transformer-based approaches under multiple experimental conditions. Specifically, we evaluate model performance across different random initializations and training-validation-test splits of the data to ensure the consistency and generalizability of our findings. Our empirical results highlight the competitive performance of the proposed model in terms of both precision and recall, while offering insights into how various architectural choices impact event detection metrics. Beyond benchmarking performance, this paper also emphasizes the importance of methodological rigor in neural network evaluations, advocating for reproducible and robust evaluation practices in NLP research. Our findings contribute to a better understanding of what architectures are most effective for event detection and set a precedent for more systematic and comprehensive comparisons in the field.

The task of canonicalizing named entity mentions—mapping mentions of entities in text to a standardized identifier or record in a knowledge base—is a central challenge in natural language processing. As real-world text collections grow in size and diversity, the ability to accurately link surface forms such as "Barack Obama", "Obama", or "President Obama" to a normalized representation becomes increasingly important for applications such as information extraction, entity disambiguation, and knowledge base population. Traditional approaches often rely on agglomerative clustering or dictionary-based mapping, but these methods can be brittle or limited in their ability to handle ambiguous or noisy input. In this paper, we address the task of canonicalization through a novel probabilistic model that integrates several complementary sources of information into a unified framework. Specifically, our model considers the context in which entities appear, the surface forms of mentions, and the relationships between attributes (e.g., names and descriptions of entities). These attributes are often structured, with dependencies between their parts (e.g., a person’s full name likely has a relation to their title or location), and we incorporate these dependencies explicitly to improve inference. Additionally, the model includes a built-in mechanism for detecting and handling noisy or ambiguous data, a feature critical for robustness in real-world settings. A key innovation of our approach is the use of transductive learning, where inference and learning are combined from a small initial set of known (seed) entities and a collection of unlabeled mention tokens. By treating the process as a joint learning and inference problem within a probabilistic generative framework, our model seamlessly integrates principles from Bayesian inference and conditional estimation. This allows the system to iteratively refine its understanding of entities and their canonical representations, capitalizing on the structure of the data as a whole. We evaluate our model on two distinct datasets drawn from political blogs and sports news, domains known for their rich but often ambiguous mentions of entities. Our experiments demonstrate that the proposed model achieves superior performance compared to both a straightforward agglomerative clustering baseline and to previous work, highlighting the effectiveness of the joint probabilistic modeling approach. These results suggest that incorporating contextual, structural, and inferential knowledge through a principled probabilistic framework is a promising direction for advancing canonicalization methods in NLP. This paper is organized as follows: Section 2 introduces the canonicalization task and formalizes our model, Section 3 details the transductive learning algorithm, Section 4 presents the datasets and experimental setup, and Section 5 compares our approach with baseline and prior work.

Stock movement prediction remains one of the most challenging problems in quantitative finance due to the inherently stochastic nature of financial markets, the complex interplay of numerous influencers, and the requirement to make temporally-dependent predictions from often noisy or chaotic data sources. Traditional models often focus solely on historical price data and technical indicators, but recent advances in natural language processing and deep learning have highlighted the potential of alternative data, such as social media content, in capturing market sentiment and improving predictive performance. However, integrating text-based features from financial social media, such as tweets, with historical time series data presents significant challenges, particularly in adequately modeling the inherent uncertainty and temporal dependencies. This paper addresses these challenges through the introduction of a novel deep generative model designed to jointly exploit textual and price signals for stock movement prediction. Unlike discriminative models, which directly model the output distribution given the inputs, or topic modeling approaches that infer hidden topical structures, our model employs recurrent, continuous latent variables to better capture the stochastic nature of stock price movements. This structure allows us to model temporal uncertainty dynamically and flexibly over time. Additionally, we address the intractability of the posterior distribution in such models by applying neural variational inference, a powerful deep learning technique that approximates the true posterior with a learnable inference network. To further enhance the model's ability to capture predictive dependencies across time, we introduce a hybrid objective function that incorporates temporal auxiliary tasks. This hybrid formulation allows the model to learn both the immediate prediction objective and intermediate temporal representations, enabling richer learning and better generalization. Our experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach by achieving state-of-the-art performance on a newly collected dataset for stock movement prediction. This dataset integrates real-time stock price movements with rich textual content from social media platforms, and as such provides an important benchmark for future research. Our work bridges the gap between financial time series analysis and social sentiment modeling, offering a flexible and scalable framework for leveraging alternative data in stock prediction. Going forward, we hope this model will serve as a foundation for more sophisticated financial forecasting systems that can better adapt to the constantly evolving nature of global markets. The integration of economic intuition with modern deep learning methods presents a promising path forward in the accurate and interpretable prediction of financial events.

The interaction between syntax and semantics has long been a core focus in natural language understanding, with researchers exploring how syntactic structure can enhance semantic representations and aid in downstream tasks. While syntactic dependencies are often considered crucial for interpreting meaning, explicitly constructing and processing syntactic trees at inference time incurs substantial computational costs and introduces error propagation from flawed syntactic parsers. To address this challenge, we propose an innovative approach: the syntactic scaffold — a framework for encoding syntactic knowledge into semantic models without the need for explicit syntactic analysis during inference. Traditional methods typically rely on explicit syntactic trees either as feature inputs or through joint models, but these methods often require full syntactic parsing at inference time, limiting scalability and robustness, particularly for out-of-domain or resource-constrained settings. My approach circumvents this by integrating syntactic patterns into a semantic model during training, using the parallel information from a treebank as part of a multitask learning objective. These syntactic scaffolds allow the model to implicitly learn structure-sensitive semantic representations, without the need to generate syntactic trees at runtime. This decoupling provides both computational efficiency and a more flexible representation of semantic phenomena. Our key insight is that semantic tasks can benefit from syntactic patterns that are embedded into a model through training, rather than explicitly parsed at inference time. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach on a range of semantic tasks — from semantic role labeling in PropBank to frame semantics and coreference resolution — achieving improvements over strong baselines on all tasks. Crucially, the method does not modify the inference pipeline; instead, it enriches the semantic representation with syntactic patterns during training, enabling the model to effectively mimic syntactic dependencies through learned representations. These results highlight the potential of syntactic scaffolds as a scalable and robust alternative to traditional syntactically-driven semantic models. By removing the dependency on syntactic parsing at inference time, this approach opens new avenues for efficient and accurate semantic modeling that better aligns with the practical needs of real-world natural language processing systems. In the following sections, I will detail the architecture of syntactic scaffolds, present experiments on representative semantic tasks, and analyze their impact on model performance and interpretability. Through this work, I aim to bridge the syntactic-semantic divide in a way that is both theoretically grounded and practically advantageous.
