Importantly,  PATTY  is designed with open accessibility in mind. The resource is freely available for both interactive exploration and bulk download, making it a powerful tool for NLP researchers and developers alike.

Accurately estimating word similarity from textual data is a foundational task in natural language processing (NLP). Traditional approaches such as latent semantic analysis or word embedding models often rely on computationally intensive operations that process vast amounts of text data, sometimes requiring multiple passes over the data or large memory footprints. These characteristics can become bottlenecks in real-time or streaming environments, where data arrives continuously and efficiency is paramount. As the demand for scalable NLP systems grows, especially in information retrieval, document summarization, and chatbots, there is a pressing need for methods that can estimate word similarity in a lightweight and online fashion. In this paper, we present a novel and resource-efficient method for mining word similarity from streams of text data. Our approach centers on the observation that word similarity can be effectively approximated by analyzing   second-order co-occurrences   between words. Whereas traditional co-occurrence-based methods compute similarity by comparing how words appear together in a fixed context window (first-order co-occurrence), we propose a method that captures richer relational patterns by considering co-occurrences of co-occurring words. This allows us to infer indirect lexical associations that are strong indicators of semantic relatedness. The core idea is to maintain lightweight buffers that store co-occurring words for each term as the stream is processed in a single pass. By leveraging these buffers, we compute second-order co-occurrence statistics efficiently, reducing the need for expensive pairwise similarity calculations among huge vocabularies. This method not only minimizes the computational overhead but also ensures linear scalability with the size of the input stream, making it suitable for online NLP tasks. We demonstrate that our algorithm not only matches the performance of state-of-the-art word embeddings in capturing word similarities but also possesses several practical advantages: it converges rapidly, adapts gracefully to streaming data, and exhibits robust behavior under various parameter settings. By trading memory for accuracy in a clever and principled fashion, we open new avenues for similarity-based NLP tasks in environments where resources are limited and data arrives continuously. Our experiments across diverse linguistic tasks confirm that this approach can be a minimal-cost yet high-impact alternative to traditional embedding models, paving the way for scalable, real-time similarity computation in NLP pipelines. Through this work, we aim to rethink the cost–accuracy trade-off in word similarity estimation, advocating for a paradigm where semantic understanding is not the domain of vast neural networks or complex models, but can instead be achieved efficiently using clever statistical patterns derived in a streaming context.

Recent advancements in natural language processing have focused on improving translation systems through richer syntactic representations. Tree-to-string translation, which takes a syntactic tree as the source input and generates a string as the target output, has emerged as a promising alternative to traditional phrase-based and sequence-to-sequence translation models. These tree-to-string approaches leverage hierarchical syntactic structures to better model source language nuances while benefiting from the efficiency of tree-based decoding algorithms. Most of these systems rely solely on tree substitution operations—where one subtree is replaced by another in a single derivation step—for building the translation. While substitution effectively captures local syntactic patterns, it is inherently limited in expressing long-distance dependencies and structural reordering, both of which are critical for high-quality machine translation, especially across highly divergent language pairs. In this work, we address this limitation by extending tree-to-string translation with adjoining operations from the formalism of tree adjoining grammars (TAG). TAGs are an extended class of tree rewriting grammars capable of generating more complex structure through both substitution and adjoining operations. The inclusion of adjoining allows for non-local transformations that can reinsert subtrees at multiple points in the derivation, directly modeling complex syntactic phenomena like wh-movement, scrambling, and subject extraction that are problematic for substitution-only models. While early works in TAG-based translation explicitly reconstructed TAG derivations for machine translation, such methods are computationally intensive and hinder real-time inference. To this end, we introduce a method for learning tree-to-string translation rules from aligned source and target syntactic trees without explicitly reconstructing TAG derivation structures. Our rule extraction algorithm directly identifies useful tree-to-string rules that include both substitution and adjoining transformations, effectively capturing global structural dependencies. Due to the tree-based nature of decoding in our framework and the fact that adjoining is integrated into the derivation as part of the rule set rather than through complex derivation reconstruction, our system maintains the efficiency of standard tree-to-string decoders. Our experiments demonstrate that the inclusion of adjoining operations improves translation quality by up to +0.7 BLEU over the baseline substitution-only system on NIST Chinese-English test sets, with only a minimal increase in decoding time (less than 2 times slower). These results highlight the effectiveness of integrating adjoining into tree-to-string translation as a viable and efficient enhancement for modeling complex syntactic structures in machine translation.

Recent advancements in natural language processing (NLP) have enabled impressive progress in open-domain and domain-specific question answering (QA) systems. However, the healthcare domain remains particularly challenging due to the complexity, diversity, and specific constraints of electronic medical records (EMRs). EMRs are the cornerstone of modern clinical practice, yet the heterogeneity in writing styles, use of jargon, and patient-specific context makes EMR-based QA a non-trivial task. The lack of large, high-quality QA datasets from actual clinical notes has been a major bottleneck in advancing EMR-focused QA research. Several works have sought to address the problem of building QA systems within the EMR domain, but these have typically relied on either small manually annotated datasets or the use of crowdsourcing platforms, which are prone to errors and domain mismatches. The scarcity of high-quality training data has led to limited generalization, especially when developing models that can extract structured information from unstructured clinical narratives. This problem is exacerbated by the need to extract both factual answers and underlying logical representations (e.g., database queries, ontological terms) that can be used for deeper analysis and integration within clinical decision support systems. To overcome these challenges, we propose a novel methodology for generating large-scale domain-specific QA datasets by  re-purposing  existing NLP annotations from EMR datasets. Instead of collecting new data from scratch, we leverage the rich – but task-specific – annotations present in existing EMR corpora to automatically derive QA examples. This methodology not only reduces annotation costs but also ensures the generated QA examples are grounded in the principles and structures of clinical documentation. As an instantiation of this approach, we introduce a new large-scale QA dataset for EMRs called   emrQA  , constructed from the widely used i2b2 shared-task datasets. By converting existing expert annotations about patient records (e.g., named entities, problem lists, coding annotations) into question-answer pairs, we create a resource that supports both QA over clinical text and logical form generation tasks. The emrQA dataset contains over 1 million question-logical form mappings and 400,000+ answer-evidence pairs, significantly expanding the amount of QA resources available for the medical domain. In addition to describing the construction of emrQA, we analyze the qualities and characteristics of the dataset, such as its coverage of clinical concepts, question types, and difficulty levels. We also investigate its utility in training deep learning models for end-to-end QA over EMRs, presenting baseline results for both question-to-answer and question-to-logical-form mapping tasks.

Semantic Role Labeling (SRL) is a core task in natural language understanding, aiming to identify and classify the semantic roles that syntactic constituents play in relation to a predicate, such as "agent", "theme", or "location". It is a crucial step toward deeper syntactic and semantic representation of language, with applications in question answering, information extraction, and machine translation. Traditionally, SRL has leveraged syntactic structures—particularly dependency parses—extensively, under the assumption that semantic roles are closely tied to syntactic patterns. This assumption has been supported by a long line of research demonstrating that features derived from syntax, such as grammatical relations or tree structures, significantly improve SRL accuracy. However, with the advent of deep learning and the increasing success of sequence-to-sequence and transformer-based models, there has been a notable shift away from explicitly incorporating syntactic features in neural SRL architectures. Some modern models achieve strong performance with purely lexical or contextual features, raising questions about the necessity of syntactic information in deep learning frameworks for SRL. This paper revisits this debate, focusing on the role of syntax in dependency-based SRL, and attempts to quantify its contribution. We argue that, despite the impressive performance of syntactic-agnostic models, syntactic information remains a valuable and non-redundant asset in SRL, especially when effectively modeled. To support this claim, we introduce an enhanced argument labeling model, which explicitly leverages syntactic information while maintaining compatibility with deep learning pipelines. In conjunction with this model, we propose an extended k-order argument pruning algorithm, which systematically explores the syntactic neighborhood of predicates to identify promising argument candidates. This algorithm enhances the model's ability to generalize over syntactic variations and reduce noise in the training process. To validate our approach, we conduct extensive experiments on the CoNLL-2008 and CoNLL-2009 benchmarks for both English and Chinese. Our model not only achieves state-of-the-art performance but also provides empirical evidence of the quantitative contributions of syntactic information to semantic understanding. Moreover, through a comprehensive comparison with existing neural SRL models, we highlight the scenarios in which syntactic features are most beneficial, shedding light on their operational role in neural models of SRL. Our findings affirm that syntax, when properly modeled, continues to offer meaningful improvements in semantic parsing tasks, even in the age of deep learning. This insight challenges the common perception that syntax is becoming obsolete and offers a more nuanced view of the relationship between syntax and semantics in neural architectures.

Recent years have witnessed a growing interest in the task of sentence-level sentiment analysis, where the goal is to predict the emotional or evaluative stance of a text with respect to a predefined set of sentiment labels. Traditionally, most approaches have focused on predicting a single binary or multi-class sentiment label, often neglecting the nuanced and multi-faceted nature of human sentiment expression. Real-world text, however, often conveys multiple overlapping emotional reactions that are better characterized by a distribution over labels rather than a single point label. Capturing this distribution provides a richer and more accurate representation of sentiment, particularly in the absence of clear-cut polarities or the presence of mixed emotions. To address this challenge, we propose a novel semi-supervised machine learning framework based on recursive autoencoders (RAEs) tailored for the task of predicting sentiment distributions. Our method learns hierarchical, compositional vector space representations for multi-word phrases directly from raw text, without relying on predefined sentiment lexicons or hand-crafted linguistic rules—such as polarity shifts—which are frequently domain-specific and hard to generalize. By leveraging the structure of natural language and the recursive nature of sentence composition, our approach captures semantic and syntactic regularities, enabling it to infer consistent and context-sensitive distributions of sentiment labels. A key contribution of this work is the demonstration that our model significantly outperforms several state-of-the-art approaches on standard benchmark datasets, such as movie reviews, while maintaining a semi-supervised learning setting—using only a small amount of labeled data. This result highlights the effectiveness of the proposed recursive autoencoding framework in extracting meaningful, low-dimensional representations useful for downstream sentiment tasks. Additionally, we introduce a new dataset derived from confessions on the Experience Project, a real-world repository of personal narratives. This dataset is unique in that it consists of user-generated texts annotated with multiple labels corresponding to emotional reactions, forming aggregate multinomial distributions that reflect diverse human responses. Our model is shown to outperform several competitive baselines in predicting these sentiment distributions, further validating the applicability of our framework to real-world emotional analysis tasks. In summary, this paper presents a novel, semi-supervised approach for representing and predicting sentiment distributions using recursive autoencoders. The method's performance on both established and newly introduced datasets underscores its robustness and adaptability, offering a promising new direction for models that seek to capture the complex, multi-dimensional nature of sentiment in natural language.

Bilingual lexicons play a crucial role in various natural language processing tasks, notably in machine translation and cross-lingual information retrieval. These resources provide essential mappings between equivalent terms in two languages and help bridge linguistic and cultural divides. However, the manual construction of high-quality bilingual lexicons is a resource-intensive process that demands in-depth knowledge in both languages and is typically limited to widely spoken language pairs and general vocabulary. As the demand for cross-lingual systems grows, especially in less commonly supported language pairs and specialized domains, there is a pressing need for scalable and robust methods to augment or replace manual construction. Automatic methods for building bilingual lexicons have gained traction as a viable alternative. These approaches mostly rely on parallel corpora, static dictionaries, or cross-lingual word embeddings. Although these methods offer some level of automation, they often suffer from limitations relating to language coverage, domain specificity, and the reliance on high-quality training data. In many cases, they are constrained to a small number of widely studied language pairs and lack the flexibility to adapt to domain-specific terminology, which is essential in specialized fields such as medicine, law, engineering, and environment. In this paper, we introduce a novel and efficient method for constructing bilingual lexicons in specific domains using a large-scale multilingual and structured knowledge base: Wikipedia. As one of the largest repositories of human knowledge in multiple languages, Wikipedia is inherently rich in content, covering a vast array of domains, making it an ideal source for automatic lexicon construction. Our approach leverages the cross-lingual links and page structures in Wikipedia to extract and align domain-specific terminology between two languages. This enables the creation of bilingual lexicons not only for well-documented language pairs but also for under-resourced and less commonly studied language pairs. We test our approach on four specialized domains and compare it with three state-of-the-art methods using the English-French and English-Romanian language pairs. Our results demonstrate that the proposed method consistently outperforms existing techniques across all tested configurations. This work underscores the potential of leveraging large-scale background knowledge like Wikipedia to build domain-specific bilingual lexicons, paving the way for more inclusive and adaptable cross-lingual NLP resources. The implications of this approach are far-reaching, providing scalability, domain adaptability, and multilingual coverage that are essential for the next generation of multilingual systems.

The digital transformation of political discourse has led to an explosion of user-generated content, particularly in the form of online political blogs and their associated comment sections. These comment sections offer unique insights into public sentiment, engagement, and the evolution of political opinions over time. However, analyzing and understanding the dynamics of these discussions is a challenging task due to their sheer volume, the complexity of the language used, and the interdependencies between posts and comments. Most approaches focus on either the primary content (i.e., the blog posts) or the user reactions (i.e., the comments); yet, political discourse is inherently a dialogue. In this paper, we take a step toward modeling these interactions by leveraging topic modeling, a powerful class of probabilistic models for uncovering latent themes in text corpora. Traditional topic models, such as Latent Dirichlet Allocation (LDA), are well-suited for analyzing textual data and have been widely applied to news articles, scholarly papers, and social media. However, when applied to political blogs, these models often fail to capture the nuanced interplay between the opinions expressed in blog posts and the resulting community responses in the form of comments. In this work, we extend LDA to account for additional contextual features inherent in political blogs, including authorship patterns and the content of user comments. Our contributions include a suite of topic model variants that jointly model the generation of blog posts and the associated comments, with the express goal of understanding and, crucially, predicting the responses of individual users. To validate our models, we introduce a novel comment prediction task: given the content and authorship of a blog post, predict which users are likely to comment. This task is both practical and informative—practically, it can help content creators and politicians anticipate audience engagement; informatively, it can reveal patterns in user behavior and content preferences. In addition to our quantitative evaluation, we conduct a qualitative analysis of the models' inferred topics and their relationships to user engagement. This analysis provides insight into the types of posts that are most likely to spark response within a political blog community. By integrating generative modeling with a pragmatic understanding of political discourse, this work represents a foundational step toward more sophisticated models of online political engagement. As such, it has broad implications for both computational social science and applied machine learning in the domain of digital politics. We believe our approach not only advances the state of the art in topic modeling but also contributes to a deeper understanding of how political opinion is formed and transmitted in online environments.

Gender inference from online social data has gained significant attention in the field of natural language processing and social media analysis. Accurately determining the gender of users based on their textual content and social interactions is a fundamental task with numerous applications, including personalized content delivery, targeted advertising, and demographic analysis. However, traditional fully supervised approaches to gender classification often struggle due to the scarcity of high-quality labeled data, which is necessary to train accurate models. In many practical scenarios, only a small subset of user data is annotated, while a much larger amount of unlabeled data is available. This creates a compelling case for the application of semi-supervised learning methods, which aim to exploit both the limited labeled data and the abundant unlabeled data to improve classification performance. Semi-supervised learning techniques are well-suited for such problems because they attempt to implicitly or explicitly utilize the structure or patterns present in the unlabeled data, which can provide valuable information for modeling. In the context of gender classification, several approaches have been explored that leverage either textual content or social network features in isolation. However, the human social web is inherently multimodal, combining both the textual expressions of users and their complex social relationships. By combining these two complementary modalities, it is possible to build a more comprehensive understanding of user characteristics and enhance the accuracy of gender classification. In this paper, we propose a semi-supervised approach to gender classification that explicitly models both textual features and a particular type of indirect social relationship among users, which we refer to as "same-interest" links. These links are based on the idea that users with similar interests tend to interact more frequently or in similar patterns, even if not directly connected. To effectively integrate these two types of information, we introduce the Textual and Social Factor Graph (TSFG), a principled probabilistic framework that models the joint dependencies between textual features and social signals. The TSFG allows us to propagate gender information not only through the textual evidence of each user but also through the indirect links formed by shared interests, thereby exploiting latent social structures. Our empirical evaluation on real-world social media datasets demonstrates that the proposed approach significantly outperforms existing methods, confirming the utility of integrating textual and social information in a semi-supervised framework for gender classification. This work opens up promising directions for future research on leveraging multimodal social data to improve various downstream tasks.

The task presented involves creating a skip list from an unsorted list of integers, where each node has a 50% chance of having a forward pointer to the next node on the same level. This implementation will provide a data structure that allows for faster searches with a time complexity of $ O(\log n) $ on average, in contrast to the linear time $ O(n) $ for a standard linked list. 1. Each node will be initialized with a value and the number of levels it can have. Since the maximum number of levels is unpredictable, setting an upper bound, say 16 levels (as the highest probability will be $ 1/2^{\textbf{level}} $), is practical for implementation. 2. If it's greater, it will drop to the next lower level to continue the search. 5.   Delete Method  : The delete method will perform a search to find the node containing the value to be deleted and then update the links in all levels where this node exists to skip over the deleted node. 6.   Random Level Generator  : A helper function will be used to randomly decide the number of levels the new node should span. Starting from level 1, the level is increased as long as a randomly generated boolean is true, up to the maximum level of 16. 7.   Putting It All Together  : Now, the complete class implementation for the skip list will be structured with the defined classes and methods. The testing procedure will involve inserting multiple values, searching for specific values, and validating the correctness of deletions.

Minimum error rate training is a crucial component to many state-of-the-art NLP applications, such as machine translation and speech recognition. However, common evaluation functions such as BLEU or word error rate are generally highly non-convex and thus prone to search errors. In this paper, we present LP-MERT, an exact search algorithm for minimum error rate training that reaches the global optimum using a series of reductions to linear programming. Given a set of N -best lists produced from S input sentences, this algorithm finds a linear model that is globally optimal with respect to this set. We find that this algorithm is polynomial in N and in the size of the model, but exponential in S. We present extensions of this work that let us scale to reasonably large tuning sets (e.g., one thousand sentences), by either searching only promising regions of the parameter space, or by using a variant of LP-MERT that relies on a beam-search approximation. Experimental results show improvements over the standard Och algorithm. The dynamic and ever-evolving nature of the Twitter platform makes it a rich yet challenging source of data for summarization and real-time analysis. With millions of tweets being posted every day across a broad spectrum of topics, distilling meaningful and concise summaries is a crucial task for applications ranging from social media monitoring to event detection. Traditional summarization approaches often fall short in capturing the topical nuances of Twitter content, especially when it comes to identifying key representative terms that encapsulate the central themes under discussion. In this context, keyphrase extraction presents a powerful alternative as it offers a structured and interpretable way to summarize the content while preserving the essential topical semantics. Keyphrase extraction from Twitter, however, is not without its challenges. The informal, short-form, and often noisy nature of tweets poses significant obstacles to traditional natural language processing (NLP) techniques. Moreover, the need to identify keyphrases that are not only relevant but also interesting and contextually aligned with the underlying discussion requires a more sophisticated approach than simple term frequency or keyword extraction. This is particularly important when analyzing trending topics, where topical dynamics can change rapidly and the resulting keyphrases need to reflect both accuracy and temporal relevance. In this paper, we address these challenges by proposing methods that enhance topical keyphrase extraction from Twitter. Our contribution includes two primary components: a context-sensitive topical PageRank method for keyword ranking, and a probabilistic scoring function that jointly optimizes for the relevance and interestingness of extracted keyphrases. By combining graph-based ranking with probabilistic modeling, our method ensures that the extracted keyphrases are not only statistically significant but also aligned with the discussions they aim to represent. We evaluate our methods on a large-scale Twitter dataset and demonstrate that the proposed techniques significantly outperform baseline approaches in terms of both precision and topical coherence. This work provides a robust foundation for summarizing Twitter content using topical keyphrases and opens up avenues for further research in dynamic and context-aware NLP methods. By enabling more accurate and meaningful analysis of social media content, our approach has the potential to support a wide range of real-world applications, including crisis management, marketing intelligence, and event tracking. Through this paper, we aim to contribute to the evolving landscape of social media text mining and Twitter-based NLP systems. Our experiments with large-scale data demonstrate the practical efficacy and scalability of the proposed approaches, reinforcing their value for real-world deployment.

The acquisition of language is a multifaceted process in which children develop sensitivities to multiple levels of linguistic structure simultaneously, including phonology, morphology, and syntax. Among these, morphology and syntax play particularly crucial roles in the formulation of a coherent grammatical system. Morphology constitutes the rules governing word formation and inflection, while syntax coordinates how these words are combined into meaningful utterances. Notably, children encounter this linguistic input as an undifferentiated stream—a transcription of child-directed speech containing no explicit segmentation or labels. Despite this, they manage to extract both morphological and syntactic patterns from the very early stages of language development. This suggests a deeply integrated learning process, in contrast to many computational models that isolate linguistic learning tasks and treat them sequentially. A prevailing challenge in computational models of language acquisition is the implicit assumption that levels of structure—such as morphology and syntax—are learned in isolation, each with its own dedicated learning mechanisms. However, recent theoretical and empirical advances in developmental psychology and computational linguistics have begun to question this modular view. The idea that language learning is inherently joint—that morphological, syntactic, and phonological patterns co-evolve and inform one another—has gained increasing traction. Modeling this joint learning process not only aligns better with observed developmental patterns but may also be more computationally efficient, as insights from one level can inform and improve task performance at another. In this paper, we explore the feasibility and efficacy of joint morphological and syntactic learning from raw child-directed speech. Our model integrates two previously established learning algorithms—each capable of capturing morphological structure and syntactic distributional patterns independently—into a single system. By jointly inducing syntactic categories and morphological boundaries, our approach aims to simulate a more holistic language learning process. We evaluate the model on a corpus of child-directed speech in two typologically distinct languages: English, characterized by relatively limited morphology, and Spanish, a highly inflected and morphologically rich language. The results highlight the potential benefits of a joint learning framework. In English, the model produces improved morphological segmentations, whereas in Spanish, it shows better syntactic performance. These findings provide empirical support for the hypothesis that joint learning can be more effective than single-task approaches, while also suggesting that the specific advantages may vary by language type. Our work contributes to a growing literature on the simulation of developmental language learning, shedding light on how interaction between the multiple levels of structure may enhance the overall learning process.

Coreference resolution is a fundamental task in natural language processing (NLP) that aims to identify expressions within a text that refer to the same real-world entity. A substantial body of research has approached this problem by recasting it as a two-class classification task, where the model must determine whether two mentions in a text are coreferent or not. While this approach has enabled the development of powerful models capable of handling complex linguistic phenomena, it often falls short in aligning training objectives with final evaluation metrics. In particular, conventional supervised learning algorithms, which aim to minimize classification errors on individual instances, do not directly optimize the evaluation metrics, such as MUC or B-CUBED scores, that are used to assess coreference resolution systems. Consequently, there is a growing need for training paradigms that bridge this gap between instance-level loss functions and task-specific evaluation metrics. This paper introduces a novel training strategy designed to directly optimize for the evaluation metric used in coreference resolution tasks. Our approach, referred to as  Maximum Metric Score Training , dynamically weights training instances and integrates beam search techniques to maximize the metric score on the training data during the learning process. Unlike traditional methods that optimize for cross-entropy or hinge loss, which are not directly tied to the desired evaluation criteria, our framework encourages the model to produce outputs that best adhere to the evaluation standards. This is achieved through careful reweighting of the training examples based on their contribution to the metric, combined with an end-to-end optimization procedure during beam search to ensure global consistency in the generated clusters. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach through extensive experiments on widely adopted benchmark datasets for coreference resolution: two MUC corpora and three ACE corpora. Our evaluations are conducted using two prevalent metrics—link-based MUC and mention-based B-CUBED—to ensure a comprehensive assessment of system performance. Experimental results show that the proposed method consistently outperforms state-of-the-art models, highlighting the benefits of directly optimizing for the evaluation metric. These findings not only demonstrate the practical value of aligning training objectives with evaluation criteria but also suggest a broader paradigm shift in how NLP systems should be evaluated and optimized. By focusing on metric-aware training, we open new avenues for improving performance in coreference resolution and propose a promising direction for future research in machine learning and NLP tasks with similar evaluation requirements.

The human ability to process and understand language in real time is a remarkable cognitive feat, involving a complex interplay of syntactic, semantic, and pragmatic mechanisms. A long-standing goal in psycholinguistics has been to build computational models that accurately capture the cognitive processes underlying sentence comprehension, particularly in discourse contexts where contextual expectations play a key role in guiding interpretation and processing effort. Recent advances in the application of probabilistic models to language processing have provided a promising approach to this challenge by allowing us to quantify the human processor’s expectations and the information-theoretic surprise associated with different input elements. This has led to the development of models that use surprisal—a measure quantifying the inverse of the probability of a word token given its linguistic and discourse context—as a predictor of human processing difficulty. In this paper, we introduce a new psycholinguistic model of sentence processing that simultaneously integrates structural and referential information within a single probabilistic framework. Our model combines two state-of-the-art statistical learning systems: a Hidden Markov Model (HMM)-based noun phrase chunker, which is responsible for incrementally building structural predictions, and a co-reference classifier, which tracks referential relationships between utterances and discourse entities. These components are tightly integrated in a fully incremental framework to compute the probability of upcoming linguistic inputs as they are parsed and disambiguated. The joint probability distribution gives rise to a continuous stream of surprisal predictions, which can then be evaluated against human processing data. The central contribution of our work lies in demonstrating that incorporating co-reference information is essential for capturing the full range of human processing behavior. While syntax-based models have shown success in accounting for a number of aspects of sentence processing, they often fail to capture the complexity of discourse-level dependencies that influence processing effort. Using the Dundee corpus of eye-movement data, we validate our model by showing that the inclusion of co-reference leads to more accurate predictions of fixation times and regression patterns than previous syntax-only models. This not only supports the theoretical value of integrating referential dependencies into sentence processing models but also highlights the computational feasibility of doing so within a probabilistic information-theoretic framework. By offering a more comprehensive account of human language comprehension, our model contributes to the broader goal of building cognitively plausible theories of language processing. Our paper is structured as follows: We begin by reviewing existing models of surprisal and their application to psycholinguistic data.

Recent advancements in machine translation (MT) have largely focused on formal and well-structured textual genres, such as news articles or legal documents, where the language is often standardized and predictable. However, natural human communication, especially in conversational settings, is far more complex, often characterized by informal language, idiosyncratic expressions, discourse particles, and vocal cues that influence meaning in subtle ways. Despite the centrality of dialogue in human interaction, the field of statistical machine translation (SMT) has given limited attention to modeling and translating conversation-like text, particularly in the domain of fictional dialogues present in literature, films, or scripts. Fictional dialogues, as a unique genre, pose a special challenge for translation due to the expressive and genre-specific nature of the language used. Characters speak with distinct voices, influenced by their personality, social background, gender, and emotional state. Translation of these subtleties requires not just linguistic accuracy but also fidelity to the pragmatic and performative aspects of speech acts and register. Existing MT systems lack in-depth modeling of these conversational characteristics, resulting in potential losses in both meaning and stylistic elements when translating from one language to another. In this paper, we take a significant step toward addressing this research gap by investigating the impact of conversational aspects on machine translation quality in the domain of fictional dialogues. We focus on four key dimensions that inherently define the structure of dialogues:   dialogue acts  ,   speakers  ,   gender  , and   text register  . These variables have scarcely been studied in the context of machine translation, despite their foundational role in natural language processing and discourse analysis. To facilitate this investigation, we create and release a new multilingual corpus specifically designed for this purpose, consisting of movie dialogues annotated with the aforementioned aspects. Our analysis reveals that incorporating these features into translation models significantly improves the translation quality, as measured by standard evaluation metrics such as BLEU. We also observe that certain variables—such as speaker gender—have a measurable impact on the difficulty of translation, with male characters exhibiting higher frequencies of vulgar language, which is often lost or altered in translation. These findings underscore the importance of adapting MT systems to the unique properties of dialogues and suggest promising directions for future research on conversational language translation. More broadly, our work highlights the need to move beyond formal text genres in MT evaluation and modeling, toward a richer understanding of the context and function of language in communicative tasks.

Recent advancements in machine translation (MT) have emphasized the role of syntactic features in improving translation quality and fluency, especially in syntactic decoding and beyond. While traditional MT systems rely heavily on probabilistic models built upon surface phenomena such as n-grams, the integration of syntactic information has been explored as a means to better capture the structural and hierarchical relationships within source and target languages. However, the practical deployment of syntactic features in real-time translation systems has been largely limited by parsing efficiency. Parsing algorithms, particularly those modeling longer-distance dependencies and grammatical relations, often exhibit high computational complexity, which poses a challenge for integration into the decoding process under stringent performance requirements. One promising alternative is the use of maximum spanning tree (MST) algorithms for dependency parsing, which were formalized by McDonald et al. (2005b) and demonstrated to offer a compelling balance between parsing efficiency and accuracy. The MST parsing approach leverages an Edmonds’ Blossom algorithm to achieve a quadratic-time complexity relative to the sentence length, making it significantly faster than cubic-time dependency parsing methods while maintaining high parsing accuracy, particularly for languages with free word order. Despite its computational advantages and robust performance, MST parsing has not yet been widely adopted in the context of machine translation decoding frameworks. This paper explores the utility of MST-based dependency parsing in the machine translation domain, focusing on how it can be integrated into a phrase-based MT system to provide effective and efficient syntactic guidance during decoding. Specifically, we incorporate dependency language model (DLM) scores generated by the MST parser into the translation model, allowing the decoder to favor target phrase segments that align with grammatically coherent syntactic structures. By doing so, the model implicitly integrates long-range syntactic dependencies and improves the fluency and structure of the generated translations. To evaluate the effectiveness of this approach, we conduct comprehensive experiments using a state-of-the-art phrase-based MT system and a collection of five NIST Chinese-English evaluation test sets. Our results demonstrate that the integration of the MST-based dependency language model leads to statistically significant improvements in translation quality, as measured by TER (improvement of 0.92%) and BLEU (increase of 0.45%). These results suggest that quadratic-time MST parsing not only provides a viable pathway to efficiently incorporate syntactic features in MT but also offers a practical route toward delivering higher quality translations in real-time applications.

Transliteration — the process of converting a text from one script to another — is a crucial yet challenging task in natural language processing. It plays a vital role in cross-lingual applications such as dictionary compilation, cross-lingual search, and machine translation, particularly when dealing with languages that use different writing systems. Traditional transliteration approaches have primarily focused on either  character-level  models, which transduce phonetic or orthographic information from the source character sequence to the target, or  word-level  dictionaries, which map words directly between scripts. Both paradigms have their own limitations: the former can struggle with out-of-vocabulary (OOV) words due to lack of dictionary support, while the latter is often static and unable to generalize to new or misspelled input. Recent advances have sought to bridge this gap by combining the strengths of both paradigms into what is known as discriminative character transduction (DCT). These systems learn a discriminative model for character-level alignments while leveraging contextual features derived from the source and target sequences. However, even the most effective DCT models to date have not fully exploited the potential of lexical resources that are commonly available for transliteration tasks — namely, a list of known words in the target language. Such a list is essential for constraining the hypothesis space in decoding and for providing semantic or phonetic context from the known vocabulary, which can significantly improve transliteration accuracy. In this paper, we present a new decoding mechanism that builds on the DCT framework and incorporates a known target-language dictionary as a resource for substring matching during inference. Our approach is a full decoding strategy that integrates substring retrieval from the dictionary with character transduction, thereby enabling rich interactions between the generated transliteration hypotheses and real-word constraints. We evaluate our approach on a key transliteration task: Japanese katakana to English Roman characters. Importantly, we demonstrate a relative 28.5% improvement in transliteration accuracy compared to the state-of-the-art Sherif and Kondrak (2007b) decoder. In addition to model design, we analyze the impact of different feature paradigms in discriminative training, including indicator-based features and hybrid generative features. Contrary to expectations, our experiments reveal that hybrid generative features can outperform their purely discriminative alternatives, even when the latter have access to a richer source context. Finally, we investigate the downstream impact of transliteration systems on machine translation. Our results confirm that higher-quality transliterations lead to improved overall system performance, with a 0.5-point increase in human evaluation scores on a 4-point scale.

Recent advancements in statistical machine translation (SMT) have enabled models to capture a broader range of linguistic phenomena, particularly through the development of hierarchical phrase-based (HPB) methods. HPB systems extend traditional phrase-based translation by allowing non-contiguous phrases and hierarchical structures to be considered, enabling the modeling of both short- and long-distance reordering during decoding. This increased flexibility has led to significant improvements in translation fluency and accuracy. Nevertheless, most HPB systems suffer from a critical limitation: they do not adequately incorporate contextual information into the reordering process. Conventional HPB systems typically rely on fixed reordering rules during the training phase, which often fail to capture the dynamic nature of phrase boundaries and reordering preferences based on surrounding linguistic context. Phrase reordering is a crucial aspect of SMT, especially in asymmetric language pairs (e.g., Chinese-to-English), where source and target language structures often differ substantially. Reordering decisions must take into account not only the structural properties of phrases, but also their context within the source and target sentences. Failing to do so can lead to overly literal or ungrammatical translations that ignore discourse-level cues or semantic coherence. In this paper, we propose a novel context-dependent phrase reordering approach that enhances the HPB translation model by introducing contextual features through the Maximum Entropy (MaxEnt) framework. The core idea of our approach is to build a MaxEnt model for each reordering pattern, allowing the decoder to dynamically select the most appropriate reordering strategy based on the surrounding context. These models are trained using a rich set of features derived from both the source and target language, including word alignments, surrounding phrase types, and sentence position indicators. By integrating these context-based reordering models into the HPB decoding process, we aim to make reordering decisions more adaptive and context-sensitive. We validate the efficacy of our approach on large-scale Chinese-to-English translation tasks using state-of-the-art evaluation metrics such as BLEU. Experimental results demonstrate that incorporating the MaxEnt-based reordering model leads to significant improvements in translation quality compared to traditional HPB systems. Specifically, we observe absolute BLEU score improvements ranging from 1.2 to 2.1, highlighting the effectiveness of our method in capturing contextually appropriate reordering patterns. In summary, this work contributes a novel approach to context-sensitive phrase reordering for hierarchical phrase-based translation. By incorporating the MaxEnt model into the reordering framework, we show that contextual features can dramatically enhance the performance of modern SMT systems, especially for highly asymmetric language pairs.

Keyphrases play a vital role in a variety of natural language processing (NLP) tasks, including document indexing, information retrieval, and text summarization. The ability to automatically extract meaningful and representative keyphrases from a text is a challenging yet essential problem in NLP. Evaluating the performance of automatic keyphrase extraction systems relies heavily on well-defined and accurate evaluation metrics. Traditionally, n-gram-based metrics have been used in NLP evaluation tasks such as machine translation and summarization, and they are increasingly being applied to keyphrase extraction evaluation due to their simplicity and computational efficiency. However, the applicability of these metrics to the specific domain of keyphrase extraction is relatively underexplored. Current evaluation practices in keyphrase extraction often focus on exact n-gram matching between the automatically extracted keyphrases and those provided by human annotators. While this approach is straightforward and widely accepted, it lacks the ability to account for near-misses – instances where a keyphrase is almost correct, but not an exact match. These near-misses are especially important in keyphrase extraction, where minor variations, ordering differences, or the substitution of synonyms may still convey semantic equivalence. Standard evaluation metrics, which ignore such nuances, may therefore provide an incomplete or even misleading assessment of system performance. To address these limitations, we conducted a feasibility study on the adaptation and evaluation of n-gram-based metrics from domains such as machine translation and summarization, and also explored the application of the R-precision metric, traditionally used in keyphrase evaluation. Our goal is to assess the suitability of these metrics for capturing the nuances of keyphrase extraction beyond exact matches. In doing so, we examined how different configurations of the metrics affect their ability to align with human judgments and to account for varying degrees of semantic similarity. Our key findings indicate that the R-precision metric achieves the highest correlation with human annotations, suggesting that it is well-suited for evaluating keyphrase extraction systems. Furthermore, we observed that the semantic similarity between partially matching keyphrases is not uniform and depends on the position of the matching component words. This insight highlights the importance of evaluation metrics that can capture such alignment dependencies. This paper contributes to the broader discourse on keyphrase evaluation by offering a comparative analysis of existing n-gram-based metrics and their applicability to the unique demands of the keyphrase extraction task. Through our study, we aim to inform the development of more sensitive and robust evaluation protocols that better reflect the semantic and contextual qualities of extracted keyphrases.

Document-level sentiment inference is a crucial task in natural language processing, particularly in understanding how sentiment is expressed and directed in complex real-world texts. Unlike sentence-level sentiment analysis, which is concerned with the affective tone of specific phrases or clauses, document-level sentiment inference considers the broader narrative, aiming to predict directed opinions—specifically, who feels positively or negatively towards whom—for all entities mentioned within an entire document. This task is challenging as it requires not only identifying localized sentiment cues but also contextualizing them across a social, factional, and discourse landscape, which is often opaque and deeply interdependent. Despite significant progress in sentence-level emotion and sentiment analysis, document-level sentiment remains underexplored. Existing methods typically focus on pairs of entities co-mentioned in a sentence, leaving relationships that span longer texts uncovered. Yet, in many domains—such as political analysis, corporate sentiment, or social media monitoring—understanding document-wide patterns of directed opinion is essential for accurate interpretation and insight. For instance, tracking sentiment between a CEO and their company or between political factions across a news article can provide meaningful insights into underlying social dynamics or strategic alignments. To address these challenges, we present a novel approach that combines a variety of contextual signals—spanning sentence-level, discourse-level, factional, and social contextual cues—into a unified inference framework. Our model integrates a range of input features, including local sentiment expressions, discourse connectives, and factual cues derived from entity roles or memberships. These features are organized within an integer linear programming (ILP) formulation that enforces global consistency through social science principles such as homophily (the tendency for similar individuals to associate), social balance (the idea that favorability should align between interconnected entities), and reciprocity (the expectation that positive relationships are often reciprocated). By incorporating these principles, our model enables coherent and comprehensive sentiment predictions across interrelated entities, even when direct evidence is sparse or absent. For example, if two individuals are known to belong to the same faction and have aligned statements in the text, the model will favor expressing similar sentiments about their actions and relationships with others. This joint modeling is particularly valuable in scenarios with densely interwoven social or organizational structures, where the sentiment of one node can inform predictions of others within the same network. We evaluate our approach on a newly curated dataset that provides exhaustive supervision for all pairwise relationships in a document, moving beyond the co-mention-only coverage of previous work.

Dependency parsing is a core task in natural language processing, aiming to represent the syntactic structure of a sentence as a set of directed edges encoding grammatical relations between words. While much progress has been made in parsing projective dependency structures — where all arcs can be drawn without crossing lines over the words as arranged on a line — non-projective parsing remains a challenging task, especially in languages with free word order and extensive use of scrambling or inversion. Traditional transition-based dependency parsers have been highly effective in handling projective structures, but modeling non-projectivity requires adapting their mechanisms to account for arcs that cross between constituents. Transition-based parsers rely on a sequence of atomic actions to incrementally build a dependency structure, offering appealing trade-offs between speed and accuracy. In the case of non-projective parsing, several methods have been proposed, including the left-right variants of transition systems, the arc-eager or arc-standard pushdown automata, and hybrid parsers that combine rules for both arcs and vertex labels. However, integrating non-projectivity directly into a transition system often complicates the action space, leading to a higher number of invalid configurations and a less efficient parsing algorithm. This paper introduces a novel three-step transition-based system for non-projective dependency parsing that avoids these challenges by decomposing the parsing process. The first step is a classical projective dependency parsing phase, capturing all projective relations. The second and third steps then perform inverse parsing: one focusing on left non-projective arcs and the other on right non-projective arcs. This split parsing method ensures that each transition-based phase can be optimized independently and retains the efficiency of linear-time processing. By breaking the parsing into three algorithmically distinct but linguistically meaningful tasks, the approach is able to achieve higher accuracy on both projective and non-projective dependencies in comparison to existing state-of-the-art non-projective parsers. Furthermore, the clear modularization of the parsing process allows for easier analysis and potential extension to additional parsing components or linguistic theories. The evaluation on universal dependencies corpora demonstrates significant performance gains, validating the effectiveness of this structural decomposition for non-projective dependency parsing. This work contributes a novel framework that combines the interpretability of modular design with the performance efficiency of transition-based parsing, offering a promising path forward for building more accurate and efficient non-projective dependency parsers across diverse linguistic typologies.

The semantics encoded within ontologies are a foundational component of many natural language processing (NLP) systems, particularly in domain-specific applications like biomedical text analysis. Ontologies such as the Unified Medical Language System (UMLS) provide structured knowledge that can be leveraged for tasks such as word-sense disambiguation (WSD), in which the goal is to select the correct meaning of an ambiguous word within a given context. Traditionally, these ontologies are constructed through human knowledge engineering and semantic modeling, but their efficacy in downstream NLP tasks is not always predictable. A critical challenge in the application of ontologies to NLP lies in evaluating their fit to a target domain and identifying potential biases or imbalances that may impact their performance. This paper addresses this challenge by proposing a novel method for assessing and improving ontologies through the principle of spreading activation over their graph structure. By representing instances of ontology concepts and their relationships as nodes and edges in a graph, we can simulate the flow of semantic influence using domain-specific text corpora. Spreading activation, a cognitive modeling technique inspired by human memory, allows us to estimate the relevance and salience of each concept within a target NLP task, thereby quantifying the extent to which the ontology aligns with the domain’s semantic landscape. Our method offers several advantages over traditional ontology-based evaluation metrics, which often measure structural completeness without regard to functional relevance or task appropriateness. By incorporating domain text, we uncover areas of the ontology that may be underdeveloped, overrepresented, or semantically disconnected—providing actionable insights for targeted refinement. Our approach further enables the automated optimisation of the ontology graph to better support the NLP task at hand, without requiring manual intervention. To demonstrate the utility and effectiveness of this method, we apply it to the UMLS ontology in the context of biomedical WSD. We show that using the activation scores computed from our model significantly outperforms existing graph-based methods for WSD in this domain. Moreover, when we introduce a fall-back mechanism that incorporates word-sense probability estimates, we achieve a state-of-the-art unsupervised performance of 0.89 accuracy. Altogether, our work bridges the gap between static knowledge representation and dynamic task-oriented adaptation of ontologies in NLP, offering a scalable and interpretable strategy for ontology evaluation and enhancement. Through this approach, we advance the goal of making human-constructed semantics go further in the domains where they are most needed.

The study of semantic representation has long occupied a central place in cognitive science and computational linguistics. Traditionally, the dominant paradigm has favored distributional models of meaning, which posit that word meanings are learned entirely from their linguistic environments. These models are driven by the Distributional Hypothesis, which suggests that words occurring in similar contexts tend to have similar meanings. While effective in capturing certain linguistic regularities, such models often overlook the role of perceptual and sensorimotor experience in shaping human semantic understanding. This discrepancy raises important questions: To what extent is linguistic meaning influenced by perceptual and embodied experiences? Can computational models replicate the kind of rich, multimodal semantic knowledge that seems to underlie human comprehension? Recent research in cognitive science and developmental psychology has shown that human concepts are deeply rooted in perceptual and sensorimotor systems. The embodied cognition framework argues that language is grounded in the interactions between the body and the environment. These findings challenge purely linguistic approaches to meaning and call for models that integrate perceptual and action-based information. Despite this growing recognition, the development of computational models that effectively bridge these domains remains limited. Most existing work either treats linguistic and perceptual cues as separate and independent, or naively combines them through concatenation without exploring the structure of their shared and unique contributions to meaning. In this paper, we propose a novel approach to semantic representation that reconciles linguistic and perceptual grounding. We present a comparative study of different models that learn semantic representations using both linguistic corpora and perceptual feature norms extracted from human ratings. These feature norms reflect the sensorimotor experiences and conceptual attributes people associate with words. Our core contribution lies in proposing a variety of integration mechanisms for combining these two modalities and investigating the degree to which these mechanisms improve the model’s ability to approximate human semantic judgments. We argue that a superior representation is achieved not by concatenating the modalities, but by uncovering latent information that is shared between them. This approach better aligns with the hypothesis that meaning emerges from the intersection of multiple, interacting sources of knowledge. Our experimental results demonstrate that latent alignment between textual and perceptual data significantly enhances the model's ability to capture human-like semantic patterns, highlighting the potential of grounded models in the quest for deeper and more accurate semantic representations. This work contributes to a growing effort to bridge the gap between formal models of meaning and the complex, embodied nature of human language..

Parameter tuning is a critical component in the development of statistical machine translation (SMT) systems. The performance of these models heavily depends on the proper assignment of weights to various features, such as phrase probabilities, language model scores, and lexical translation probabilities. A robust and efficient tuning method is essential, as it directly influences the quality of the translation output and the overall effectiveness of the system. Traditional tuning methods, such as Minimum Error Rate Training (MERT) (Och, 2003), have long served as the standard due to their effectiveness in optimizing decoding parameters. However, these methods are often limited in their scalability, struggling with models that have a high number of features, even in the order of thousands. This shortcoming limits their applicability in modern SMT frameworks where the number of features has grown substantially to capture increasingly complex translation behaviors. Recent works have explored alternative approaches, drawing from algorithms like the MIRA optimizer (Watanabe et al., 2007; Chiang et al., 2008b), which aim to enable the tuning of systems with thousands of features. While these methods offer improved scalability, they can be complex to implement, often requiring careful tuning of their own set of hyperparameters or custom software. The pursuit of a simple, effective, and scalable tuning method motivates us to explore a new perspective on the parameter optimization problem. In this paper, we introduce a novel and efficient approach to SMT parameter tuning that reframes the task as a pairwise ranking problem. Our method, Pairwise Ranking Optimization (PRO), directly optimizes translation parameters by treating improvements in translation quality as a ranking problem, a technique inspired by the pairwise approach to ranking proposed by Herbrich et al. (1999). By doing so, we are able to leverage the simplicity and widespread availability of linear binary classifiers such as SVM or logistic regression tools, eliminating the need for custom-built optimization engines. This not only makes the method easy to implement but also enhances its scalability and robustness for high-dimensional feature spaces. The PRO algorithm demonstrates competitive performance against both MERT and MIRA across both phrase-based and syntax-based translation systems, across multiple language pairs, and in the presence of large-scale training data. This work presents a significant step forward in making parameter tuning more accessible and efficient, particularly in the context of large, feature-rich SMT models. The proposal of PRO as a viable alternative to existing tuning mechanisms contributes not only to the advancement of tuning techniques in machine translation but also to the broader field of machine learning through the application of ranking principles to optimization problems.

Neural Machine Translation (NMT) has achieved remarkable success through the use of deep learning techniques, particularly in modeling the word-level language phenomena using sequence-to-sequence architectures. These models typically rely on Maximum Likelihood Estimation (MLE) training with teacher forcing, where each word in the target sentence is predicted one at a time based on the ground-truth previous words. While teacher forcing is effective for training, it introduces well-documented limitations, including exposure bias — a discrepancy between training and inference where the model during inference generates words based on its own previously generated outputs, unlike during training where it uses gold-standard context — and an improper evaluation of translation fluency and coherence, as it treats translation as a word-by-word process. To address these limitations, recent research has explored sequence-level training frameworks, such as those based on reinforcement learning (RL). These methods attempt to optimize the translation quality based on sentence-level metrics like the BLEU score, thus offering a more holistic evaluation. However, reinforcement learning-based training often suffers from high variance in gradient estimation, leading to unstable performance and slow convergence. This has motivated the exploration of alternative training frameworks that maintain the benefits of sequence-level modeling without the drawbacks of RL. In this paper, we propose a novel approach to NMT training that is based on probabilistic $n$-gram matching. Our method formulates a differentiable sequence-level training objective inspired by $n$-gram overlap, a common metric for evaluating translation quality. Instead of relying on reinforcement learning to model sentence-level rewards, we directly optimize toward maximizing the probability of matching $n$-grams between the model's output and the reference translation. This formulation effectively bridges the gap between the training and inference stages, allowing for a more fluent and accurate translation process. A key contribution of our approach is the use of greedy search during training, where the generated words are used as the input context for future predictions. This mimics the inference stage and helps to reduce exposure bias by better aligning the training and decoding conditions. The differentiability of the objective function ensures that the model can be trained using standard gradient-based optimization techniques without the need for reinforcement learning. Our experiments on the NIST Chinese-to-English translation tasks demonstrate that our method not only overcomes the instability issues of RL-based models but also achieves a significant improvement in translation quality, with an average increase of 1.5 BLEU points over a strong baseline.

Recent advancements in natural language processing (NLP) have increasingly focused on the acquisition and application of inference knowledge for tasks such as semantic reasoning, text simplification, and knowledge base construction. This knowledge is often represented in the form of   entailment rules  , which specify logical consequences between different textual expressions, and   paraphrase rules  , which capture equivalence between semantically identical but syntactically varying expressions. These rules are applied over syntactic or semantic representations of sentences, enabling systems to infer new knowledge from existing text. However, as the scale and complexity of such rule sets grow, the computational efficiency and scalability of inference mechanisms become significant challenges. Traditional approaches to inference often rely on explicit rule application over large-scale syntactic structures, such as dependency trees or semantic graphs. While these methods are effective in capturing complex linguistic patterns, they often suffer from inefficiencies, particularly when the number of rules and their application permutations grows exponentially. As a result, scalable inference engines often require compact representations and optimized algorithms to manage both memory and time complexity without sacrificing the correctness or completeness of the inference process. In this paper, we propose   A Compact Forest for Scalable Inference over Entailment and Paraphrase Rules  , a novel framework designed to address these challenges. Our framework introduces a   packed data-structure  , which we term the   entailment forest  , that compactly represents the application of multiple entailment and paraphrase rules over a given input. The structure is designed to avoid the redundancy and inefficiencies inherent in traditional unfolding mechanisms, thereby enabling large-scale inference over rule sets that were previously infeasible to process within acceptable time bounds. Building on a formalism for entailment-rule application, we present a   corresponding inference algorithm   that operates directly on the compact structure. This algorithm guarantees   correctness by construction  , preserving all necessary rule applications while avoiding redundant computations. We theoretically analyze the efficiency of our approach and demonstrate its superiority over existing baselines using   both analytical and empirical evaluations   on standard datasets for entailment and paraphrase tasks. Our results indicate that the proposed method not only scales better but also maintains the ability to infer precise and meaningful relationships between textual elements. By introducing a unified and scalable solution for inference over hybrid rule sets, our work bridges a critical gap in the application of rule-based reasoning over large-scale textual data, with potential implications for semantic search, automated reasoning, and knowledge-based NLP systems.

Recent advancements in machine translation have significantly improved the fluency and accuracy of cross-lingual systems. However, the performance of these systems is often constrained by upstream preprocessing steps, particularly tokenization. This issue is particularly pronounced in languages with less explicit word boundaries, such as Chinese and Korean, where tokenization is inherently ambiguous. Traditional pipeline approaches typically apply a separate tokenization step before translation, making the system susceptible to tokenization errors that can cascade into translation mistakes. A commonly adopted mitigating strategy involves using lattices to encode multiple possible tokenization paths, offering the translation model more flexibility in navigating ambiguity. While this strategy considerably elevates the robustness of translation systems, it is still fundamentally a phased approach that tackles tokenization and translation as separate tasks. In this paper, we propose a more integrated approach by performing tokenization and translation in a joint manner, eliminating the need for explicit tokenization preprocessing and enabling translation features to directly influence the tokenization process. This approach is particularly valuable when the source text is provided as a continuous sequence of atomic units—such as characters for Chinese or Korean—that can be combined into words in multiple ways. By treating tokenization and translation as coupled inference problems, we design a joint decoder that takes such sequences as input and simultaneously generates both the source-side tokenization and the translation hypothesis on the target side. This method naturally captures the interdependencies between tokenization choices and translation decisions, allowing for a more coherent and informed decoding process. To support this joint decoding framework, we employ a discriminative model that integrates features from both tokenization and translation within a unified probabilistic framework. Experimental results on Chinese-English and Korean-Chinese translation tasks demonstrate that our joint model significantly outperforms baseline systems that rely on 1-best tokenizations or lattices. Notably, as a byproduct of the joint model, the derived tokenization results are also of high quality, outperforming established monolingual tokenizers for Chinese. These findings highlight the potential of unifying preprocessing and translation steps within a joint framework, offering new directions for improving machine translation robustness in languages with complex segmentation challenges.
