The second component classifies the extracted words into concepts using a hand-crafted rule set that maps linguistic patterns to predefined categories. These rules are based on linguistic observations as well as empirical analysis of question datasets. One of the key contributions of this work is the integration of syntactic and semantic cues, which, when combined, provide a more accurate and robust classification mechanism than either would alone. Importantly, our rule-based system achieves a classification accuracy of 97.2%, significantly outperforming the previous state-of-the-art machine learning-based system by 6 percentage points. This is a substantial gain and highlights the effectiveness of a carefully designed rule-based approach in a domain that remains challenging even for modern statistical models. We hypothesize that such a rule-based system can serve as a strong baseline and even complement machine learning approaches. By generating high-quality, unambiguous feature vectors that encapsulate key syntactic and semantic properties of questions, our method can be used as a preprocessing step to enhance the input for any supervised learning model. We conclude that accurate rule-based question classification is not only feasible, but also highly competitive with more complex learning-based methods, with the potential for synergy when the two paradigms are combined. Through this work, we advance the goal of building interpretable and high-performing NLP systems for real-world question classification tasks.

The global rise in the prevalence of Alzheimer’s Disease (AD) has spurred a critical need for early and accurate assessment tools that can identify individuals at risk and monitor disease progression. Alzheimer’s Disease and related dementias pose a major public health challenge, with cognitive decline often progressing insidiously and being difficult to detect in the early stages. As a result, there is increasing interest in leveraging multimodal data and machine learning techniques to improve the accuracy of dementia detection and tracking. However, one of the major challenges in developing such methods is the limited availability of comprehensive and annotated clinical datasets, which are essential for training reliable models. In many cases, these datasets not only lack sufficient sample size but are also sparse and heterogeneous, spanning multiple views such as linguistic, behavioral, and neuropsychological assessments. To address these challenges, this paper explores the potential of learning multiview embeddings for capturing the complex, multi-faceted nature of cognitive impairment in AD patients. Specifically, we focus on the DementiaBank dataset, which contains multiview data representing different aspects of cognitive decline. We employ generalized canonical correlation analysis (GCCA), a multiview learning technique, to learn embeddings that integrate heterogeneous features and preserve the underlying relationships across different data views. The core idea is to encode complementary and discriminative patterns from multiple data sources in a shared latent space, thereby improving both task performance and interpretability. In this work, we evaluate the effectiveness of our learned multiview embeddings in two downstream tasks: binary classification to identify individuals with AD and regression to predict clinical scores that quantify the severity of cognitive impairment. Using these embeddings in conjunction with standard classifiers and regressors, we achieve an F1 score of 0.82 and a mean absolute error of 3.42, respectively, which demonstrates the utility of incorporating multiview information. Moreover, our experiments indicate the generalizability of this approach, as we show that multiview embeddings can be effectively derived from other related datasets as well. This suggests the potential for transferring the learned representations to new settings or augmenting data-limited scenarios. By bridging the gap between multiview data and dementia assessment, this work contributes to the development of robust and generalizable models for early detection and monitoring of cognitive decline. Our findings highlight the importance of leveraging the intrinsic multimodal structure of clinical datasets and set the stage for more effective machine learning approaches in the domain of Alzheimer's research.

Recent advancements in natural language processing (NLP) have seen a growing focus on structured prediction tasks, particularly in domains such as abstractive text summarization and neural machine translation. In these settings, generating a coherent and semantically aligned sequence of tokens is crucial for achieving high-quality outcomes. One of the most commonly adopted approaches for training such models is maximum-likelihood estimation (MLE). Under MLE, the model is trained to maximize the probability of a correct next word given a preceding sequence, typically using a cross-entropy loss objective. Despite its effectiveness in training models to generate fluent and locally consistent outputs, MLE suffers from several known limitations. Among them is the exposure bias problem, where the model during training is fed with ground truth tokens, while during inference it relies on its own generated tokens, leading to error propagation. Another significant issue is the well-documented problem of misaligned objectives, where models are optimized for the MLE loss but are evaluated based on discrete sequence-level metrics such as ROUGE or BLEU scores. These metrics measure the similarity between the generated output and reference texts, often capturing global structural alignment and relevance aspects that MLE does not account for. To overcome these limitations, recent work has explored policy-gradient methods that aim to optimize the final evaluation metrics directly. These methods treat the sequence generation task as a reinforcement learning problem, where the model learns from the reward signals derived from discrete evaluation metrics. While policy gradient-based approaches have shown promising improvements in evaluation performance, they introduce new challenges, including high variance in the gradient estimates and the instability that arises from sampling-based exploration during training. These issues make the training process more computationally intensive and less reliable, especially for complex sequence generation tasks with long-term dependencies. In this paper, we propose an alternative approach to bridge the gap between word-level training and sequence-level evaluation metrics. We introduce CALCS (Continuously Approximating Longest Common Subsequence), a novel differentiable objective function that captures the sequence-level similarity between the predicted output and the target reference. CALCS is constructed as a continuous relaxation of the longest common subsequence (LCS) measure, a classic metric for representing the alignment between sequences. By directly incorporating this relaxed objective into the training process, CALCS enables models to learn to optimize for discrete metrics in a more stable and sample-efficient manner, without relying on the simulation-based sampling of policy gradients.

Recent advancements in natural language processing (NLP) and machine learning have emphasized the importance of learning meaningful and generalizable representations of textual and structured data. Central to many NLP applications are entities and documents, which often reside within structured knowledge bases (KBs) that provide semantically-rich annotations. These KBs, such as Wikipedia, not only offer unstructured textual content but also include rich annotations that indicate entity mentions, relationships, and hierarchical structures. This paper addresses the challenge of learning joint distributed representations of entities and documents directly from a knowledge base by leveraging both the textual and structural information provided in the KB content. We propose   TextEnt  , a neural network model that learns to map entities and documents into a shared continuous vector space. Given a document associated with a set of entity annotations—commonly found in structured KB entries—the model’s primary objective is to predict the entity the document describes while simultaneously learning representations that place the document and its corresponding entity in close proximity within the vector space. This dual objective enables the model to capture rich semantic relations between textual content and the entities they describe, while also encoding document-level semantics for effective downstream tasks. A key advantage of TextEnt is its ability to integrate both contextual information from surrounding text and entity-specific knowledge from annotations during the representation learning process. This integration is particularly crucial in tasks where entities are not only labeled by name but are also associated with complex relationships and categorical information. By training the model on a large corpus of Wikipedia documents, we ensure that the learned representations are robust and generalizable across a wide range of KB entries. We evaluate the effectiveness of the proposed model on two representative tasks:   fine-grained entity typing  , which assesses the model's ability to identify the precise semantic category of an entity, and   multi-class text classification  , which evaluates the model’s performance in assigning labels to documents based on their content. Experimental results demonstrate that TextEnt achieves state-of-the-art performance on both tasks, validating the value of joint entity and document representation learning from KB descriptions. Furthermore, to promote reproducibility and further research, we make the code and pre-trained models publicly available. This paper contributes not only a novel approach to KB representation learning but also a practical tool for leveraging KB content in a wide range of NLP applications.

Natural language inference (NLI), also referred to as textual entailment, is a fundamental task in natural language processing (NLP) that aims to determine the logical relationship—entailment, contradiction, or neutrality—between a pair of sentences: a premise and a hypothesis. This task is critical for a wide range of downstream applications, including question answering, machine translation, and dialogue systems, as it enables models to reason about the semantic implications of text. Recent advances in deep learning have led to a significant shift in NLI research, with attention-based models becoming the dominant paradigm. These models, such as the widely successful Bidirectional Encoder Representations from Transformers (BERT) and its variants, leverage attention mechanisms to compute flexible, context-aware interactions between token representations of the premise and hypothesis. By dynamically focusing on relevant parts of the input, attention mechanisms enable the model to capture the interactions that are crucial for determining the relationship between the two sentences. However, while attention-based models are powerful and effective, they are often computationally intensive and lack a certain inductive bias that could enable the extraction of interaction patterns of arbitrary structural complexity. In this paper, we explore an alternative modeling approach for NLI, challenging the notion that attention is the only viable mechanism for sentence interaction. We propose the  Convolutional Interaction Network  (CIN), a model that leverages convolutional operations to dynamically generate filters for sentence encoding. Inspired by the success of convolutional neural networks (CNNs) in pattern recognition tasks, CIN introduces a novel way to model the relationship between two sentences by encoding one sentence using filters that are dynamically generated based on features of the other. This design allows the model to implicitly learn a variety of interaction patterns—based on different filter sizes and numbers—without relying on explicit attention weights. The main contributions of this paper are as follows: 1.   The Proposal of CIN  : We present the first NLI model that utilizes convolutional operations for learning sentence interactions. CIN is a general-purpose framework that can be trained for various NLI tasks and offers an alternative to traditional attention mechanisms. 2.   Flexible Interaction Pattern Learning  : CIN's dynamic filter generation enables the model to capture a broader range of interaction patterns than is typically possible with attention alone. The architectural flexibility allows the network to learn both local and long-range dependencies in the text. 3.   Empirical Validation  : We evaluate CIN on three large-scale NLI datasets: SNLI, MultiNLI, and SciTail.

Extracting opinion targets is a crucial task in the field of opinion mining, especially in the context of online reviews, where understanding which aspects of a product or service users are expressing opinions about can provide valuable insights for businesses and researchers. With the rapid growth of user-generated content on social media and review platforms such as Amazon, Yelp, and TripAdvisor, there is an increasing demand for automated systems that can identify and classify opinion targets accurately and efficiently. Opinion mining systems often rely on two major approaches for this task: syntax-based methods and alignment-based methods. Syntax-based approaches leverage syntactic patterns—such as dependencies or clauses—within sentences to pinpoint the targets of opinions. These methods often depend heavily on parsing, which, while powerful, can introduce noise and errors when applied to the informality and variability of online language. On the other hand, alignment-based methods bypass syntactic parsing altogether by using word alignment techniques, which are particularly effective for matching expressions between source and target opinions, and are generally more robust when dealing with informal or noisy text. Despite the growing adoption of these two paradigms, there is a lack of systematic investigation into the relative effectiveness of syntax- and alignment-based methods across different data characteristics—such as corpus size, domain specificity, and language. Understanding whether to prioritize one method over the other based on these factors is critical for optimizing opinion mining systems. This paper addresses this gap by providing an empirical comparison of these two methodologies under varying conditions, including different sizes, domains, and languages of corpora. Furthermore, we propose a method that combines the strengths of both domains within a partially supervised framework, aiming to harness improvements in performance while reducing dependence on high-quality annotated data. Our experimental results demonstrate that the proposed combination approach is particularly effective in the case of corpora with small and medium sizes, offering a promising direction for practical applications where large annotated datasets are not available. By systematically evaluating different methods and their combinations, this work contributes to the advancement of opinion mining techniques and provides actionable insights for future research and development efforts. The Introduction for the paper "Syntactic Patterns versus Word Alignment: Extracting Opinion Targets from Online Reviews" is as follows: --- Extracting accurate opinion targets from online reviews is a foundational task in opinion mining that enables the systematic analysis of user sentiments with respect to specific aspects of products, services, or experiences.

Transliteration — the process of mapping a text from one script to another — is a crucial yet challenging task in natural language processing, particularly in the context of statistical machine translation (SMT). This task becomes even more complex when bootstrapping is involved, where only raw bilingual corpora are available and no parallel sentence-level or sub-sentence alignment resources are at hand. In recent years, bootstrapping statistical machine transliteration (SMT) has attracted significant attention because it mitigates the need for human-annotated data, enabling the development of transliteration models in resource-constrained scenarios. However, when transliteration models are bootstrapped using automatically extracted phrase pairs, they are highly susceptible to contamination by noisy examples, which include nontransliterate parts, misspellings, and correspondences that are semantically related but not phonetically aligned. Thus, robust noise detection during the alignment process is essential to the success of such bootstrapping systems. In this paper, we propose a novel   noise-aware character alignment   method designed for bootstrapping statistical machine transliteration from automatically extracted phrase pairs in bilingual corpora. Our approach builds upon a Bayesian many-to-many character alignment framework, which is capable of modeling probabilistic relationships between characters from the source and target scripts. To address the issue of noise in automatically generated phrase pairs, we extend the model to explicitly distinguish between transliteration segments and nontransliteration (noise) parts. By incorporating this noise-aware component, the model is better able to ignore spurious correspondences and focus on the genuine transliteration patterns within the data. Experimental evaluation was conducted in the Japanese-to-English transliteration domain using a patent bilingual corpus, which is representative of a technical domain with a high degree of named entity usage. The results demonstrated that the proposed noise-aware character alignment model significantly outperformed baseline methods in the bootstrapping task, especially when the input phrase pairs were noisy. Our method not only improves the quality of the transliteration alignments but also contributes to the robustness of the bootstrapping process by reducing the impact of faulty examples. The proposed approach has wide potential applications in domains where parallel alignment resources are scarce, and accurate transliteration is critical, such as cross-lingual Named Entity Recognition (NER) and domain-specific terminology mining. Overall, this paper contributes a robust and effective framework for statistically bootstrapping transliteration models from bilingual corpora by incorporating explicit noise detection into the alignment process. This innovation allows for more accurate and reliable transliteration in real-world scenarios where clean, human-annotated data is often unavailable.

Recent advancements in natural language processing (NLP) have enabled models to perform a wide range of language understanding tasks, such as document classification, information extraction, and question answering. These models benefit from large-scale datasets that provide diverse and representative examples of real-world language use. However, the development of such datasets for structured knowledge inference from unstructured text remains relatively limited. This paper introduces WIKIREADING, a novel large-scale language understanding task that addresses this gap by leveraging the information contained within Wikipedia and its structured counterpart, Wikidata. The task involves predicting textual values from the Wikidata knowledge base by reading and understanding the unstructured text of the corresponding Wikipedia articles. With over 18 million instances, WIKIREADING provides a rich and diverse testbed for evaluating and training end-to-end deep learning models in natural language processing. The WIKIREADING task encompasses a range of sub-tasks, including classification and extraction, making it an ideal benchmark for assessing the capabilities of modern deep neural network (DNN) architectures in continuous, end-to-end settings. The diversity of the task reflects the complexity of natural language understanding and the challenges posed by real-world tasks that require both syntactic and semantic comprehension of text. These challenges include handling out-of-vocabulary words, resolving ambiguities, and inferring non-explicit relationships within textual data. The dataset spans multiple domains, from biographical information to scientific facts, further enhancing its applicability across a wide variety of application contexts. To explore the effectiveness of current state-of-the-art models in tackling the WIKIREADING task, we conduct a comprehensive evaluation of various DNN-based architectures. Our analysis highlights the importance of a model's ability to support a rich answer space, such as generating word or character sequences. In particular, we find that sequence-to-sequence models, equipped with mechanisms for copying out-of-vocabulary words, are especially effective. Our best-performing model achieves an accuracy of 71.8%, demonstrating the feasibility of applying modern NLP techniques to the task of structured knowledge inference from unstructured text. By making the WIKIREADING dataset publicly available, we aim to encourage further research and development in the field, promoting the creation of more robust and generalizable language understanding models that can effectively navigate the complexities of bridging structured and unstructured information sources. This work not only introduces a valuable new resource for the NLP community but also underscores the importance of goaldirected tasks that reflect real-world challenges in language processing.

Recent advancements in natural language processing (NLP) have enabled impressive capabilities in data-driven sentence generation, particularly in modeling and generating surface syntactic structures and linearized sequences of tokens. However, many traditional generation systems rely on fixed, isomorphic structures—where hierarchical trees or grammatical representations mirror the sentence's final output. In practice, however, the hierarchical and semantic source structures used in linguistic generation, such as those found in PropBank-style semantic role labeling (SRL) frames, often lack functional syntactic nodes, such as prepositions, determiners, or auxiliaries. In contrast, the surface-syntactic or parsed structures (e.g., those provided by phrase-structure trees or dependency parsers) contain these functional elements, which are crucial for generating grammatically well-formed and fluent sentences. This discrepancy results in a significant challenge: the need to project from source structures that are sparse in functional elements to richer target structures that must be complete for surface realization. This mapping task is complicated by the fact that source and target structures are often non-isomorphic—differing not only in content, but also in topological structure and node count. Such non-isomorphism has long been a barrier in data-driven generation approaches, particularly in statistical and machine learning models that assume a one-to-one alignment between source and target structures. As a result, many existing generation systems either bypass non-isomorphic projections by manually enriching the source, constraining the generation to template-like outputs, or simply avoiding the learning of structural differences through handcrafted rules. In this paper, we address the challenge of generating from non-isomorphic source structures using a fully stochastic approach. Our proposed system starts from PropBank-like semantic representations and generates surface syntactic structures in a way that accurately accounts for the differences in structure between the input and output. Central to our approach is a cascade architecture composed of support vector machine (SVM) classifiers, each responsible for incrementally transforming the source data through a series of structural transitions. By decomposing the generation process into a sequence of subtasks, our system can learn to model the mapping between structurally dissimilar representations without requiring any manual alignment or rule-based guidance. We evaluate our generator on English data from the Penn Treebank and Spanish data from the multi-layered Ancora-UPF corpus, demonstrating its ability to produce syntactically valid and semantically coherent sentences from non-isomorphic semantic frames. Through these experiments, we show that our approach contributes a novel and effective solution to the problem of projection between non-isomorphic structures in data-driven generation, offering a pathway to more flexible and domain-independent linguistic generation systems.

The digital transformation of global communication has equipped researchers with an unprecedented amount of data, especially through social media platforms like Twitter, enabling new avenues for understanding and modeling international relations. As nations increasingly influence and are influenced by their citizens' expressions online, the study of political sentiment becomes vital not only for policymakers and diplomats but also for the social sciences. This paper addresses the challenge of identifying political sentiment between nation states by leveraging the vast and real-time information present on social media. A novel approach to large-scale sentiment analysis is proposed, offering insights into how the populace perceives and discusses foreign nations, and how these sentiments align—or differ—with the formal bilateral relations declared by their governments. The emergence of robust natural language processing (NLP) techniques has enabled the extraction of nuanced information from unstructured text at scale, opening the door for cross-disciplinary research in political science. While much of the current research in NLP and social media has focused on predictive tasks such as estimating election outcomes or gauging sentiment on specific policy issues, this work deviates from that narrow scope. Instead, it moves towards a broader, more exploratory use of sentiment modeling that aims to illuminate the fluctuating terrains of political opinion and national sentiment across borders. Our work poses two core questions: Do the sentiments expressed by the citizens of one country toward another correlate with the formal political relations between those countries? And when such sentiments diverge—particularly over time—can social media serve as an early indicator of these shifts, and what might be the underlying causes? To answer these questions, this paper outlines a comprehensive approach for detecting and analyzing political sentiment directed at foreign nations using Twitter. We explore a variety of machine learning techniques, including state-of-the-art contextual sentiment analysis models, in addition to practical learners designed to filter noisy or irrelevant content from the data stream. Crucially, we validate our models not only using standard sentiment datasets but also by comparing our findings with established public opinion polls and current international alliance data. This cross-validation strengthens the credibility of our approach and demonstrates its applicability to real-world political dynamics. The implications of such an approach are significant for political scientists and international relations researchers seeking to understand the evolving nature of national identities, public diplomacy, and the soft power of states.

The automated detection of political ideology from textual sources such as news articles has gained increasing importance in the era of information overload and growing misinformation. With the proliferation of digital media platforms, understanding the political leanings of content becomes crucial for purposes such as content moderation, media literacy, and fact-checking. News articles often convey political ideologies not only through their textual content but also through metadata attributes such as the structure of associated links (e.g., references to other articles) and the presentation of information within the article titles. However, conventional methods for political ideology detection predominantly rely on textual analysis and neglect the rich contextual cues present in the non-textual aspects. This paper addresses the limitations of prior approaches by introducing a  multi-view model  that integrates the textual content of news articles with additional contextual features such as their metadata and network structure. Our approach is inspired by recent progress in attention-based neural networks, which have demonstrated effectiveness in jointly modeling heterogeneous data sources. By assembling a unified representation from multiple views of a document—such as the article title, body text, and link structure—we aim to capture a more comprehensive picture of the political ideology embodied by the news content. Our model leverages recent advancements in natural language processing (NLP) and network science to extract meaningful features from both unstructured textual data and structured network information. For textual components, we employ state-of-the-art transformer-based architectures known for their ability to learn deep contextual representations. For the network-based components, we incorporate graph-based feature extraction techniques to model the web of interconnected news articles. These features are then integrated using a cross-attention mechanism that dynamically adjusts the importance of each view in predicting political ideology. We evaluate our multi-view model against a variety of competitive baselines on a benchmark dataset and demonstrate a significant improvement in ideology detection performance, achieving a 10 percentage point boost in F1 score compared to the current state of the art. Our results underscore the importance of leveraging multi-dimensional information for ideological classification and highlight the potential of attention-based fusion for cross-domain modeling. This work contributes both methodologically and empirically toward more robust and context-aware systems for understanding political orientation in digital news content. This study not only advances the field of political ideology detection but also opens new avenues for integrating diverse views of data in downstream NLP tasks.

Question answering (QA) systems rely heavily on effective representation learning to understand and match the semantic content of questions and potential answers. Traditionally, such systems have utilized general-purpose lexical models like word embeddings to measure relatedness between questions and candidate responses. These models are trained to capture broad, context-agnostic relationships among words, presuming that semantic proximity implies relevance. However, this assumption can be misleading in task-specific contexts, where the relevance of an answer is not solely determined by general semantic similarity but by a specific relationship to the question’s information need. To address this limitation, we propose a shift from general-purpose embeddings to task-specific, or  causal , embeddings that model the relationships that are specifically relevant to the question at hand. In this paper, we focus on the domain of causality, a key aspect of human reasoning frequently involved in QA systems—from medical diagnosis to policy decisions or event explanations. We argue that a good answer to a causal question is not just related to the question semantically, but is  causally  related in a relevant and task-specific manner. To operationalize this, we present a method to create  causal embeddings  that directly model the cause-effect relationships embedded within natural language text. Our approach is designed with scalability and minimal supervision in mind, bridging the gap between human-curated causal datasets and the vast amounts of unlabeled text available online. The method proceeds in three stages: first, we cost-effectively generate a dataset of cause-effect pairs by bootstrapping from free text using a small set of seed patterns; second, we train task-specific embeddings in which the contextual relationships are explicitly defined by cause-effect pairings; and third, we integrate these causal embeddings into a state-of-the-art reranking framework for QA, enhancing its ability to detect causal implications. This builds a novel, yet practical pipeline for causal QA that can leverage weak supervision and augment unsupervised learning. We evaluate this approach both directly, using a causal implication task, and indirectly, through a downstream QA task using data from Yahoo! Answers. Our experiments demonstrate that task-specific causal embeddings significantly improve QA performance, achieving a 7.7% increase inPrecision@1 (P@1) over a strong baseline. These results illustrate the value of tailoring embedding models to explicitly encode task-relevant relationships—here, causality—and open new avenues for embedding learning informed by domain-specific reasoning. More broadly, the work contributes a scalable method for injecting task-specific knowledge into QA pipelines with minimal annotation effort, making it especially relevant for domains where traditional labeled data is scarce.

Recent advancements in natural language processing (NLP) have enabled impressive improvements in sentiment analysis, particularly in the context of social media platforms like Twitter, where informal, often unfiltered language provides a rich source of subjective content. Despite these achievements, existing models often overlook the nuances of demographic language variations, which can play a critical role in shaping the meaning and tone of user-generated content. Gender, one such key demographic characteristic, has been shown to influence language use in subtle yet important ways. These differences in subjective expression, including the use of emoticons, hashtags, and affective language, are particularly evident in informal communication environments where users are more likely to express personal opinions and emotions freely. While much prior research has focused on linguistic patterns in the general population, less attention has been given to the cross-lingual and cross-demographic variability that can arise when modeling sentiment across multilingual social media data. Given the global reach of social platforms and the increasing interest in cross-cultural and multilingual analyses, it is essential to investigate whether incorporating demographic awareness—specifically gender—can improve the performance of sentiment classification tasks, even across different languages and cultures. This is especially relevant in multilingual NLP, where language-specific nuances can mask or amplify demographic distributions in the data. In this paper, we investigate how gender differences manifest in the subjective language of English, Spanish, and Russian Twitter users. We explore variations in emoticon use, hashtag prevalence, and lexical patterns that correlate with gender, and examine how these differences impact the performance of polarity and subjectivity classification tasks. Our experiments demonstrate that leveraging gender as a feature in sentiment analysis models leads to significant improvements in classification accuracy. Specifically, we observe statistically significant relative F-measure increases over the gender-independent baseline in all three languages, with improvements ranging from 0.5% to 5% across polarity and subjectivity tasks. These results underscore the importance of accounting for demographic language variations in multilingual sentiment analysis, paving the way for more informed and representative NLP models for social media. Our findings not only contribute to the growing body of work on demographic-aware language modeling but also highlight the need for further interdisciplinary research that combines sociolinguistic insights with machine learning techniques to develop more culturally and cognitively sensitive sentiment analysis tools. By explicitly modeling the intersection of language and demographic factors, we open up new avenues for building more accurate, fair, and contextually aware computational models of human communication in multilingual domains.

The study of poetic meter has long occupied a central place in literary criticism and linguistic analysis. Meter, the rhythmic structure that underlies a poem, serves as both a formal constraint and a creative tool, shaping the expression and emotional impact of poetic language. In English poetry, metrical patterns such as iambic pentameter, trochaic tetrameter, and others form a systematic framework that writers use to craft their works. However, the same structural consistency that makes meter analyzable also invites deviation, where poets stretch, fracture, or entirely reconfigure the expected rhythm to produce expressive effects. Such metrical fluidity poses a significant challenge not only for literary scholars but also for computational linguists seeking to automate metrical identification and scansion. Recent advances in natural language processing (NLP) have enabled machine learning (ML) models to excel in a wide range of linguistic tasks, from syntactic parsing to semantic disambiguation. These successes suggest the potential for applying ML techniques to the more specialized and nuanced domain of poetry analysis. Nevertheless, the metrical structure of poetry hides complexities that are not always amenable to the assumptions and methodologies underpinning standard NLP approaches. For example, stress patterns—key to scansion—can be influenced by both phonetic and contextual factors that are inherently context-sensitive and sometimes non-arbitrary. Moreover, poets often employ ambiguity or variation at the lexical level (e.g., through enjambment or elision), further complicating the task of identifying consistent metrical signatures. In this paper, we explore the feasibility of applying machine learning to the metrical analysis of English poetry. Our work builds on a foundational corpus of classical poems manually annotated with scansion, allowing us to train and test a series of NLP models capable of identifying key metrical patterns. Central to our approach is the recognition that reliable scansion cannot be achieved without careful attention to the unique characteristics of poetic language. This paper not only presents a straightforward application of NLP tools to scansion but also underscores the complexities and challenges inherent in this task. By doing so, we aim to contribute a baseline for further research and encourage a deeper exploration of the intersection between machine learning and poetic form. Through this effort, we hope to foster both a practical resource for the automatic analysis of meter and a broader conversation about the limitations and potential of algorithmic approaches to poetry. This work will be of interest to researchers in computational linguistics, poetry studies, and digital humanities.

Entity retrieval is a critical task in information retrieval and knowledge base systems, where the goal is to find entities (e.g., people, organizations, or locations) that best match a user query. Traditional approaches to entity retrieval often rely on matching query terms with surface attributes of entities or their surface textual descriptions such as Wikipedia paragraphs. However, these methods may not fully capture the complex relationships between query terms and underlying entity attributes, especially when the queries involve abstract or context-dependent intent. Understanding how users construct entity queries and how to model these queries more effectively remains a central challenge in the field. Recent works have sought to model the query generation process as a decision-making task where users select distinguishing properties of entities and formulate these as factual descriptors (often called factoids) in their queries. Underlying the success of such approaches is the assumption that the generated queries reflect the structure of the knowledge about the entity itself, encoded in the features extracted from knowledge bases. However, many prior approaches treat factoids as flat, independent descriptors of an entity, overlooking the hierarchical and overlapping nature of the relationships between different facts. In this paper, we propose a novel framework for entity representation and retrieval that directly models the hierarchical structure of entity factoids. We argue that entity queries are generated through a two-step process: first, users identify distinguishing factoids that best characterize the target entity, and second, they select linguistic paraphrases or expressions for those factoids to form a query. Building on this insight, we introduce the  Entity Factoid Hierarchy  (EFH), a hierarchical tree structure that organizes factoids around an entity in different levels of granularity and relatedness. Each node in this hierarchy represents one or more factoids that describe the entity, and the tree structure captures the dependencies and generalization between these facts. To construct the Entity Factoid Hierarchy, we design a probabilistic model using a factor graph formulation, which enables efficient inference over complex dependencies between entity facts. The learning process is informed by a modified variant of the Multiple-try Metropolis algorithm for sampling and processing the entity knowledge graph. Once constructed, the Entity Factoid Hierarchy can be used for entity retrieval by decomposing queries into their constituent factoids and computing the likelihood of each entity as a function of the alignment between the query and the hierarchy nodes. Our experimental evaluations across multiple benchmark datasets demonstrate that the proposed approach significantly outperforms existing models in terms of retrieval accuracy and robustness to noisy or partial queries.

The task of sentiment analysis has become a cornerstone in natural language processing, with wide-ranging applications from social media monitoring to market research and opinion mining. At the heart of many sentiment analysis systems lies a  semantic orientation  or  sentiment lexicon , a resource that categorizes words (and often phrases) as either positively or negatively oriented. The availability of such lexicons is critical for both rule-based and machine learning-based sentiment analysis systems, especially in domains with limited annotated training data. While early semantic orientation lexicons, such as General Inquirer and SentiWordNet, have proven to be useful, they also suffer from limitations, including low coverage, especially for multi-word expressions, and a heavy reliance on manual curation or computationally intensive training pipelines. A prevailing method for semantic orientation lexicon construction involves leveraging WordNet and other semantic resources to propagate polarity scores to neighboring synsets or words based on semantic similarity or co-occurrence. However, these approaches often require substantial computational resources and, in the case of WordNet-based lexicons like SentiWordNet, are constrained by the structure and coverage of the underlying thesaurus. Moreover, lexical resources that rely heavily on context, such as corpora or manual labeling, are not always accessible, especially in low-resource languages or when real-time generation is required. In this paper, we propose a lightweight and effective alternative for building high-coverage semantic orientation lexicons with minimal reliance on external resources beyond a  Roget-like thesaurus  and a few  affix patterns . Our approach uses a small set of  overtly marked words —those with clear affixes such as  "un-", "dis-", "in-" —as seeds to generate a polarity-rich lexicon. By bootstrapping using the thesaurus, we expand the lexicon to include both single words and multi-word expressions without the need for large-scale annotation or copious corpora. Our method inherently supports the  Polyanna Hypothesis , which suggests that favorable words are more frequent in text processing, aligning with known patterns in human language. We evaluate our approach using the General Inquirer as a gold standard and demonstrate that our generated lexicon achieves a 14 percentage point improvement in accuracy over the widely used SentiWordNet. Additionally, we conduct an extrinsic evaluation on phrase polarity determination and show that our thesaurus-based method outperforms existing state-of-the-art systems. We also explore  visualization techniques  to help interpret the propagation of sentiment across the lexicon, further shedding light on the structure and performance of our approach.

The task of sentiment analysis has become a cornerstone in natural language processing, with a wide range of applications from social media monitoring to product reviews and customer feedback analysis. A fundamental assumption in many sentiment analysis models is that human-provided ratings, often on a star-based scale, accurately reflect the sentiment conveyed in the associated text. However, recent concerns about the reliability and consistency of these ratings—particularly when derived from crowdsourced platforms—have led to increased scrutiny. A central question remains: to what extent do these human-assigned ratings align with the expressed sentiment in the associated text, and can models effectively learn from them? This paper explores the reproducibility of sentiment ratings from text, focusing on three key research questions: (i) whether human readers are able to infer the sentiment rating from the text, (ii) how human performance compares with a machine learning model, and (iii) whether model performance is influenced by the source of the ratings—whether provided by the author of the text or a third-party annotator. To address these questions, we collect a dataset of movie reviews from IMDb, each originally accompanied by a rating assigned by the author. We then conduct large-scale human annotation studies, using both crowdsourced and trained annotators, to reproduce the sentiment ratings as independently as possible. Our findings reveal that while human annotators outperform standard machine learning models in reproducing the original ratings from the text, their agreement with the author's rating still falls short, with more than 5% of annotations significantly diverging from the original. Furthermore, we discover that models trained on the ratings provided by annotators outperform those trained on author-provided labels. These results challenge the assumption that author-provided ratings are inherently reliable signals for sentiment modeling, and raise important questions about their utility as training data. Our work provides a critical evaluation of the assumptions underlying sentiment analysis datasets and highlights the importance of carefully considering the source and reproducibility of human-provided labels. Understanding the gaps between author intent, reader interpretation, and model interpretation is key to building more reliable and robust sentiment analysis systems. In doing so, we encourage future research to further investigate the factors influencing rating coherence and model generalization, with a focus on improving the alignment between textual sentiment and numerical representations. The Rating Game—where ratings and text must align—is far from over. It is a game worth playing more carefully, with informed strategies and a keen eye for the human in the machine.

Coreference resolution is a fundamental task in natural language processing (NLP) that aims to identify expressions within a text that refer to the same real-world entity. As one of the first stages in deep language understanding, it plays a pivotal role in higher-level NLP tasks such as question answering, summarization, and machine translation. Despite its significance, coreference resolution remains a challenging problem, particularly in unsupervised settings where annotated training data is not available. Most existing approaches heavily rely on supervised learning from human-annotated data, which limits their applicability in low-resource or multilingual scenarios. Hence, there is a pressing need to explore models that can perform robust coreference resolution without supervision. In this paper, we present an unsupervised ranking model for entity coreference resolution that offers a novel approach by integrating resolution mode variables into a generative framework. Unlike traditional supervised or semi-supervised models, our method does not require annotated training data, making it highly scalable and adaptable across domains and languages. The resolution mode variables are key to dynamically modeling the uncertainty and diversity in the discourse structure, enabling the model to effectively rank and cluster mentions of the same entity. Despite the challenges inherent in unsupervised learning, our model demonstrates strong performance on coreference resolution as evaluated by the human-aligned CoNLL metric. Experimental results on the English data from the CoNLL-2012 shared task show that our system achieves an F1 score of 58.44%, outperforming the state-of-the-art deterministic method from the Stanford system (Lee et al., 2013) by 3.01%. This represents a meaningful improvement in the field of unsupervised coreference resolution and highlights the effectiveness of our model’s design in capturing the complexities of entity mentions without manual annotation. Our work contributes significantly to the advancement of unsupervised learning techniques in NLP. By achieving a competitive performance without any labeled data, we open new avenues for coreference resolution in environments where annotated resources are scarce. Additionally, the integration of resolution mode variables into the model introduces a novel mechanism for reasoning about discourse structure, potentially inspiring future research in both unsupervised NLP and generative modeling approaches. As such, this paper not only presents a practical improvement in coreference resolution performance but also advances the theoretical understanding of how coreference can be modeled in the absence of explicit supervision. The proposal of an unsupervised ranking model for entity coreference resolution offers a promising direction for further exploration in language modeling and deep language understanding tasks.

Referring expression generation (REG) is a vibrant area of natural language generation, where the goal is to create expressions that uniquely identify a particular object within a visual or textual context. In traditional settings, most research on REG has focused on the “one-shot reference” paradigm, where the task is to generate a single, sufficiently discriminative expression that eenables the listener or system to identify the target object. While this approach is well-suited for scenarios with clean and precise knowledge of the contextual domain, it often falls short in modeling the subtleties of natural human-to-human and human-to-system interactions. In real-world contexts, people frequently establish reference in “installments,” offering bits of information incrementally and adapting based on feedback until the target is unambiguously identified. This paper investigates how such incremental, or referential installments, can be beneficial in the domain of referring to objects in photographs, especially in the context of systems with uncertain access to object attributes and categories. We propose that integrating a strategy of stepwise expression generation can lead to substantial improvements in the accuracy and robustness of referring expression generation systems. Our study is grounded in the observation that semantic imprecision—particularly when drawing from ambiguous or noisy visual features—can lead to the generation of expressions that are either inadequate or misleading, even as they pass syntactic and grammatical standards. Indeed, when people interact with objects in real-world images, incorrect or vague object names (e.g., “a long object” instead of “a car,” or “a colored shape” rather than “a blue shirt”) are not only possible but often unavoidable given the limitations of low-level vision features. We draw inspiration from human task-oriented interaction to develop a novel approach to REG: a context-aware and adaptive method that uses referential installments to iteratively refine and disambiguate expressions. We extend a recently introduced model of grounded word meaning, training it on a dataset of referring expressions for objects in images. We learn to generate expressions that are both visually grounded and semantically accurate. Our results from a human evaluation reveal that human users are highly sensitive to semantically inappropriate or imprecise object names. Accordingly, we design and implement strategies for avoiding or repairing these inaccuracies as part of a larger, incremental referential process. Our experiments demonstrate that by incorporating referential installments into a word-based REFER model, the system achieves a significant improvement in referential success rates.

The dynamic nature of social media platforms has introduced an unprecedented opportunity for businesses to understand and respond to emerging trends in real time. Microblog platforms, such as Twitter or Weibo, are particularly valuable because they capture users' spontaneous expressions, including their intentions, preferences, and interests. These expressions often serve as early indicators of new trends, which can potentially translate into new business opportunities. For instance, the emergence of public interest in air pollution has been known to catalyze a surge in demand for products such as air purifiers and protective masks. For ecommerce companies, it is crucial to effectively detect these emerging trends and identify the associated products that might see a spike in commercial demand, allowing them to make rapid and informed business decisions. Identifying trend-related products is a non-trivial task. It involves accurately interpreting the implicit signals of commercial interest in user-generated content, which is often noisy, ambiguous, and lacks context. A major challenge lies in distinguishing general interest about a trend from explicit commercial intent, such as an expression of a desire to purchase or promote a particular product. Furthermore, as trends evolve, the scope of products they can affect also evolves, necessitating methods that can continuously learn and adapt. In this paper, we take the initiative to tackle the problem of identifying trend-related products by explicitly modeling commercial intents derived from microblogs. Our approach is grounded on the hypothesis that the way users express their intentions about trends can often be predictive of product relevance and consumer demand. To this end, we construct a comprehensive and carefully curated dataset that captures the association between trending topics and products. Moreover, our proposed method leverages a graph-based modeling approach that jointly considers the relevance of products to trends and their associativity with each other, allowing for a more holistic understanding of emerging market opportunities. This paper contributes to both the fields of social media mining and business intelligence by not only revealing insight from microblog data but also offering a robust and generalizable approach to transforming microblog data into actionable business insights. The evaluation of our method on extensive experiments demonstrates its effectiveness in identifying trend-related products, making it a valuable tool for businesses aiming to leverage the power of social media for commercial gain. In the following sections, we elaborate on the problem formulation, dataset construction, and the proposed methodology. Through our findings, we aim to inspire new research and practical applications in mining the vast potential of microblog data for identifying upcoming business opportunities.

Manually annotated corpora are invaluable resources in natural language processing (NLP), serving as training data for a wide range of tasks like syntactic parsing, semantic role labeling, and machine learning model development. These corpora require extensive human effort and domain knowledge to produce, often involving the annotation of sentence structures, part-of-speech (POS) tags, and morphological features. However, the creation and maintenance of such resources are hindered not only by the high cost and time but also by the diversity and incompatibility of annotation standards across different corpora. This presents a significant challenge in the field: when multiple corpora exist but with differing or incompatible annotation schemes, the human effort invested in annotating them is effectively siloed, limiting cross-corpus integration and knowledge reuse. The issue is particularly pronounced in annotation tasks like treebanking and sequence labeling, where the absence of a universal standard and the presence of task-specific nuances can make assembling a unified dataset difficult. In tasks such as Chinese word segmentation and POS tagging, for instance, the lack of explicit morphology means that different annotation standards can lead to substantial variations in the segmentation and classification of lexical units. For example, the Penn Chinese Treebank (CPTB) adheres to a tagset that is widely adopted and suitable for syntactic parsing, but its relatively limited size can hinder training performance in task-specific models. In contrast, the People's Daily (PD) corpus, while much larger, uses a different annotation convention and captures richer domain diversity, making it underutilized due to incompatibility with downstream NLP applications. Given this challenge, there is a pressing need for methods that enable the transfer of knowledge between corpora with different annotation standards—what we refer to as  automatic adaptation of annotation standards . Such methods could allow valuable data from one corpus to be repurposed for the benefit of another without the need for re-annotation. To this end, we propose a simple yet effective strategy that treats the adaptation problem as a cross-domain knowledge transfer task. Specifically, we develop a model that generates annotations in a target corpus's format (e.g., CPTB format) by leveraging a larger but differently annotated source corpus (e.g., the PD corpus). Our framework is designed to align word segmentation and POS tagging across corpora by capturing the underlying linguistic structure shared between them, while respecting the specific requirements of the target standard. This paper evaluates the efficacy of the proposed method in the domains of Chinese word segmentation and POS tagging.

The task of Open Information Extraction (OIE) is to automatically identify and extract relational facts from unstructured text in a domain-independent and largely unsupervised fashion. Unlike traditional information extraction approaches that rely on pre-defined schemas or ontologies, OIE systems aim to process raw text and extract surface-level triples — typically consisting of a subject, a relation, and an object — without prior linguistic or domain-specific knowledge. These extractions form the basis for a wide array of downstream applications, including knowledge base construction, semantic search, and question answering. As such, the effectiveness of OIE systems is measured not only by the accuracy of the extractions (in terms of precision and recall) but also by their utility and ease of integration into knowledge management systems. Despite significant progress in this area, many existing OIE systems suffer from a number of limitations. First, they often produce an overwhelming number of extractions, many of which are redundant, overly specific, or semantically ambiguous. This makes post-processing and integration into knowledge bases both computationally intensive and infeasible at scale. Second, while these systems typically extract the core relational facts, they often fail to convey important semantic nuances such as modality, polarity, attribution, and numerical quantities in a structured manner. In this paper, we introduce MinIE, a novel Open Information Extraction system that addresses these limitations by focusing on the dual goals of minimizing extractions while maximizing their semantic content and utility. MinIE aims to provide compact, semantically enriched extractions with high precision and recall. To achieve this, we leverage two key design principles: first, by representing complex semantic features — such as modality or attribution — as annotations rather than cluttering the core extraction structure; and second, by identifying and removing overly specific subcomponents that do not contribute to the overall meaning of the extracted relation. Experimental results across a range of real-world datasets demonstrate that MinIE not only matches or outperforms existing systems in terms of precision and recall but also delivers a significantly reduced and more semantically meaningful set of extractions. Our approach thus represents a step toward more scalable and practical open information extraction. We evaluated the efficacy of MinIE through a comprehensive experimental analysis using multiple datasets. We compared MinIE's performance with existing state-of-the-art OIE systems and found that it consistently achieves higher precision and recall while producing fewer, more meaningful extractions. Our analysis reveals that the system's structured approach to semantic enrichment and specificity reduction contributes to its effectiveness.

Recent advancements in natural language processing (NLP) have underscored the importance of leveraging large-scale data to enhance model performance. One particularly effective direction has been the incorporation of selectional preferences—linguistic constraints that guide the syntactic and semantic compatibility between words—into computational models, particularly in dependency parsing tasks. Selectional preferences have traditionally been studied in the context of word-to-class relations, where a syntactic element (e.g., a verb or preposition) is understood to constrain the semantic class of its arguments (e.g., a subject, direct object, or prepositional phrase). Such preferences have been crucial in constraining the decision space of probabilistic parsing models, helping them make linguistically well-formed predictions. However, real-world language is far more variable and context-dependent than traditional class-based models suggest. In particular, the specific interactions between individual words—rather than just word classes—often determine syntactic structure and semantic coherence. These  word-to-word  selectional preferences, though arguably more fine-grained and challenging to acquire in scale, are increasingly being recognized as a valuable resource, particularly when augmented with the vast amounts of textual data now accessible from the web. In this paper, we propose a novel framework for incorporating web-derived selectional preference information into statistical dependency parsing models. Our approach leverages distributional patterns extracted from web-scale corpora, capturing detailed and context-rich preferences between lexical items. By integrating this information into the parsing process, we demonstrate significant improvements in parsing accuracy, particularly for longer dependency distances, which are commonly underperformed in current parsing models due to the difficulty of maintaining structural coherence beyond a certain span. Furthermore, we show that web-derived selectional preferences are especially valuable when the parser operates in previously unseen domains. In such out-of-domain settings, where in-domain data may be sparse or lacking, our method helps maintain robustness and generalization by augmenting the model with a broad, data-driven understanding of syntactic agreement derived from the web. Our analysis also suggests that the performance benefits of using web-scale data scale log-linearly with the number of unique patterns extracted (e.g., N-grams), emphasizing the utility of larger and more diverse data resources in improving dependency parsing. This paper therefore not only advances the technical capacity of parsing models with web-derived data but also underscores the diminishing returns of conventional, class-based selectional preference learning in comparison to the richer, context-sensitive insight that web-scale corpora can provide.

Recent advancements in natural language processing (NLP) have enabled impressive improvements in a wide range of language understanding and generation tasks. One particularly challenging domain within NLP is grounded language learning, where systems must interpret and respond to language in physical or simulated environments. Tasks such as learning to follow navigation instructions—whether for robots or interactive agents—require not only parsing and understanding language but also coordinating with perceptual and motor components to achieve specific goals. In this context, the ability to interpret and execute language-based instructions accurately is crucial, and errors in understanding can lead to catastrophic failures in task completion. Traditionally, reranking methods in NLP have been used to refine the outputs of initial parsers by selecting the most probable structure from a set of candidate derivations. These methods typically rely on well-annotated datasets with gold-standard reference structures (e.g., parse trees or semantic graphs), enabling the model to learn discriminative features that distinguish correct from incorrect analyses. While effective, this reliance on high-quality, manually annotated data has limited the applicability of reranking techniques in grounded settings, where such annotated structures are typically not available due to the complexity and continuous nature of real-world environments. In this paper, we investigate how discriminative reranking methods can be adapted to the grounded language learning setting, specifically for the task of learning to follow navigation instructions. We hypothesize that in the absence of gold-standard reference trees, weak supervision signals—such as whether a task was successfully completed—can be instrumental in guiding the learning process. We propose a framework that leverages this form of feedback as an implicit, albeit noisy, supervisory signal to train a discriminative reranker. This approach effectively bridges the gap between traditional NLP reranking techniques and the data-scarce and partially observable nature of grounded language tasks. Our experimental results demonstrate that the performance of the reranking model trained using feedback-based weak supervision is comparable to models trained on gold-standard parse trees. This finding not only highlights the practical utility of weak supervision in grounded tasks but also suggests a promising direction for scaling language learning techniques to real-world scenarios where traditional annotation is infeasible. By adapting discriminative reranking to the grounded context, we open new possibilities for improving the robustness and accuracy of language understanding models in embodied systems. Our work contributes a methodology for leveraging minimal supervisory signals to regulate the interpretation of language in complex, interactive environments.

Recent advancements in robotics have led to a growing interest in enabling robots to follow natural language instructions for navigation tasks. In such scenarios, a robot must understand a human-generated instruction—such as “go to the living room, then turn left and enter the first kitchen you see”—and translate it into a sequence of motor behaviors that it can execute in a real or simulated environment. This task poses significant challenges due to the ambiguity and variability in human language, the need to map linguistic information to spatial knowledge of the environment, and the diversity of possible path-finding strategies that can be acceptable under different constraints. Hence, developing robust systems that can interpret and execute natural language navigation instructions remains a critical goal in human-robot interaction research. The core challenge lies in the translation of a high-level semantic instruction into a low-level executable plan. Traditionally, this translation process has relied on predefined grammar rules or handcrafted heuristics, which are often limited in their generalization and scalability. These systems perform well in controlled environments but struggle to cope with the complexity and variability present in real-world, non-deterministic navigation scenarios. Moreover, they often require extensive feature engineering, limiting their adaptability across different spaces and instruction types. In this work, we take a novel approach by leveraging end-to-end deep learning to address the translation of natural language instructions to high-level robot navigation plans. Our model integrates attention-based mechanisms to effectively link semantic content from the user instruction with a topological representation of the environment. This allows the model to dynamically focus on relevant parts of the instruction while leveraging the environmental structure to construct a coherent navigation plan. Crucially, the topological map is not merely an input modality but is treated as an external knowledge base that is essential for interpretation and reasoning. To support this work, we introduce a new, fully annotated dataset comprising 11,051 instruction-plan pairs collected from real robot navigation tasks. This dataset is specifically designed to enable research into data-driven translation models and is openly available to the community to foster future work. Experimental results demonstrate that our model outperforms traditional heuristic- and rule-based baselines as well as existing deep learning architectures on the task of instruction-to-plan translation. More broadly, this work contributes to the emerging field of semantic robot navigation by illustrating how deep learning can be used to integrate natural language understanding with topological spatial reasoning.

Recent advancements in activity recognition have significantly improved the ability of machine learning models to understand human actions from video and sensor data. However, most current approaches rely on labeled training data for the specific set of action classes considered, making them ineffective for categorizing activities that were not encountered during training—a key limitation in real-world deployment. Zero-shot activity recognition (ZSAR) addresses this gap by enabling the model to classify previously unseen activity classes without requiring direct supervision on those classes. This is particularly relevant in scenarios where human annotations are costly or unavailable, or when new activities emerge dynamically. While significant progress has been made for ZSAR in tasks such as image classification and object recognition, recognizing human activities in video—a more complex and temporally dynamic modality—remains a challenging and relatively underexplored problem. Despite numerous approaches for zero-shot learning in computer vision, traditional methods for ZSAR in action classification often depend on predefined semantic attributes of actions, either specified by domain experts or derived from image-based features. These attribute-based methods are frequently constrained by the quality and availability of gold-standard attribute annotations, especially for large-scale action vocabularies. Moreover, most existing methods focus on object-centric attributes, whereas activities, represented by action verbs, are inherently different in that they reflect temporal, human intent-driven, and socially embedded behaviors. These defining characteristics of action verbs suggest a need for attribute models that explicitly capture the functional, contextual, and linguistic properties of action verbs rather than focusing solely on the visual appearance of objects involved. In this paper, we explore large-scale ZSAR by focusing on the linguistic attributes of action verbs. We propose a novel method that leverages unstructured linguistic resources—specifically, dictionary definitions and distributed word representations—to induce semantic attributes of verbs related to their execution, intent, and typical context. These attributes are then used as a bridge between the visual features extracted from action videos and the textual descriptions of unseen actions, enabling zero-shot prediction. Notably, our model does not rely on manually annotated action attributes and, instead, learns to infer meaningful action attributes directly from language, overcoming a major limitation of existing ZSAR methods. Comprehensive experiments demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach, showing that the inferred action attributes provide accurate and robust predictive signals for zero-shot recognition of human activities. By focusing on the linguistic construction of action meaning, our framework not only improves performance in the zero-shot setting but also contributes to a more interpretable and generalizable understanding of human actions..

Constituency parsing is a fundamental task in natural language processing, aiming to uncover hierarchical syntactic structures in sentences by decomposing them into nested phrases. Transition-based parsing methods, which incrementally build parse trees by applying a sequence of transition actions, have gained popularity due to their computational efficiency and strong empirical performance. However, despite recent advances, several challenges remain when applying these methods to resource-poor or morphologically complex languages such as Chinese. This is particularly true when integrating part-of-speech (POS) tagging, a crucial precursor to parsing, into a unified framework. Traditional pipeline systems, where POS tagging precedes parsing, are prone to error propagation: small tagging errors can cascade and harm downstream parsing results. Moreover, learning accurate transition sequences in large search spaces is hindered by the competition among sequences of varying lengths, and the limited expressivity of local features makes it difficult to capture long-range structural and semantic dependencies. In this paper, we propose a transition-based constituent parser for Chinese that tightly integrates POS tagging and parsing in a shared model architecture, addressing these long-standing issues. To mitigate error propagation, we jointly estimate POS tags and syntactic structures, directly modeling the interaction between the two tasks and enabling mutual correction of errors. Second, we introduce a novel beam-search decoding strategy that aligns parser states across action sequences of different lengths, reducing biases caused by sequence size differences and improving the efficiency of exploration in the search space. Finally, we extend the feature set to include non-local features—such as those capturing larger syntactic patterns—and semi-supervised word cluster features, which provide additional linguistic cues in the absence of full syntactic labeling. These features enhance the model's ability to generalize across diverse syntactic constructions and improve robustness in the face of data sparsity. We evaluate our proposed techniques on the Chinese Tree Bank (CTB) 5.1 and CTB 6.0 editions, two widely used benchmarks for Chinese syntactic research. Experimental results demonstrate that the integration of POS tagging, search state alignment, and augmented feature representations lead to substantial performance improvements over existing state-of-the-art systems. Specifically, our parser achieves a constituency parsing accuracy of 86.3% (F1) on CTB 5.1 and 87.1% on CTB 6.0, outperforming all previous systems in the literature. These results highlight the effectiveness of our approach in improving parsing accuracy for Chinese, while offering a more principled and robust alternative to traditional parsing pipelines.

The annotation of search queries with linguistic structures, such as part-of-speech (POS) tagging, segmentation, and capitalization, plays a crucial role in modern information retrieval systems. Effective query annotation enables downstream tasks, such as query understanding, intent classification, and semantic search, by providing a deeper representation of the input. However, search queries pose a unique and significant challenge for natural language processing (NLP) tools due to their brevity, syntactic variability, and often idiosyncratic construction. Unlike conventional text, search queries are frequently phrased as isolated terms or keyword phrases, and may lack sentence structure, punctuation, or even capitalization patterns expected by standard NLP pipelines. As a result, traditional NLP techniques, optimized for well-formed text like news articles or social media posts, often fall short when applied directly to query data. To address the shortcomings of existing methods, and to improve the robustness of query annotation in real-world settings, this paper introduces a novel probabilistic approach for   joint annotation of search queries  . Our approach considers the interdependencies between different types of annotations, treating the annotation task not as a series of isolated decisions, but as a coherent and interrelated problem. This is particularly important in the context of search queries, where human intent often spans multiple linguistic dimensions simultaneously. The proposed method begins by leveraging unsupervised learning techniques to generate a robust baseline of independent annotations using queries along with pseudo-relevance feedback—information derived from the relevance of documents returned for those queries. This allows for the capture of useful signals even in the absence of manually annotated training data. Building on this initial annotation layer, we design a stacked classification framework that incorporates the interdependencies between annotation types, such as how capitalization and segmentation might inform part-of-speech tagging, and how POS tagging might, in turn, help identify the boundaries of individual query terms. By integrating these dependencies during the classification process, the system is able to achieve improvements in annotation accuracy, even when training data is scarce. The effectiveness of this approach is validated through experiments on a diverse set of queries extracted from real-world web search logs. Our results demonstrate that the proposed method significantly outperforms conventional techniques, making it particularly well-suited for handling both short keyword queries and more verbose, natural language-based searches. This work contributes to the growing body of research on query processing by offering a scalable and accurate annotation pipeline tailored to the unique properties of search queries.

Recent advancements in machine learning have significantly enhanced the performance of learning-to-rank (LTR) systems, which are essential for information retrieval and recommendation tasks.
