This method allows the model to progressively learn from the most informative training examples to the more challenging ones, enhancing the overall learning process and improving the model's robustness against noise. By integrating the dynamic transition matrix with curriculum learning, our approach not only better models the noise but also leverages an efficient training strategy that significantly improves the overall performance of the distant supervision pipeline. We conduct comprehensive experiments across a wide range of relation extraction scenarios to evaluate the effectiveness of our approach. Our results demonstrate that the proposed method consistently improves upon the performance of both traditional and state-of-the-art distant supervision models. Moreover, our experiments highlight the robustness and adaptability of the dynamic transition matrix across diverse extraction tasks and data configurations. These results indicate that our approach represents a significant step forward in managing label noise in distant supervision and has the potential to enable more reliable and scalable relation extraction systems in the future.

The task presented involves studying the readability of a text in the Bangla language, considering two key influencing factors: the target reader's background and text features. This objective is approached computationally, leveraging both human annotations and machine learning techniques to categorize and assess text difficulty. The study specifically examines how different features — categorized as "classic" and "non-classic" — influence reader perception, and how these perceptions vary among different reader groups. To efficiently address the research problem, a novel Bangla readability dataset has been developed, consisting of 135 documents annotated by 50 readers from two diverse backgrounds. This dataset forms the foundation for evaluating the relative contribution of the identified 20 text features to perceived readability. The methodology involves a preliminary correlation analysis to uncover relationships between these features and reader-determined difficulty levels. Based on these findings, support vector machine (SVM) and support vector regression (SVR) techniques are employed to model reading difficulties, tailored to the different reader groups, and using varying feature combinations to assess their predictive capabilities. The study finds that the perception of text difficulty is significantly influenced by the reader's background, underscoring the context-dependent nature of readability. Notably, this research represents one of the first systematic efforts to computationally explore and model text readability in Bangla, a language for which such studies remain limited. The outcomes have significant implications for developing adaptive content for diverse audiences, enhancing accessibility, curriculum design, and natural language processing applications in the Bangla language. By identifying the most influential text features and observer-level variability in difficulty perception, the work advances the understanding of readability at both linguistic and computational levels. Future directions may consider extending the dataset to include a broader range of reader demographics and exploring deep learning approaches to further refine readability models. Overall, the study contributes valuable insights into the interplay between text features and reader background, highlighting the importance of personalized models in text readability assessment. This research not only fills a critical gap in Bangla language resources but also encourages broader cross-linguistic studies on reading comprehension and text accessibility. Its methodological approach can serve as a blueprint for similar initiatives in other under-resourced languages. Ultimately, this work bridges the gap between theoretical linguistic analysis and practical computational modeling, offering a robust foundation for future readability research in multilingual contexts. The practical applications of such findings could extend to education technology, automated tutoring systems, and accessible information design, among others.

Recent advancements in natural language processing (NLP) have enabled sophisticated technologies to understand and extract structured information from unstructured text. Two key tasks in this domain are cross-document co-reference resolution (CCR) and named entity linking (NEL). CCR is concerned with computing equivalence classes over textual mentions that refer to the same entity across a collection of documents, enabling the holistic understanding of entities even as they appear under different expressions. In parallel, NEL disambiguates such mentions by mapping them to unique entities in a knowledge base (KB), or to a null entity if the mention does not appear to refer to any known KB entity. The coexistence of these two tasks suggests a natural interplay: co-referential mentions often share the same KB entity, and conversely, well-linked entities can guide the resolution of co-referential relationships. However, traditional approaches have largely treated these tasks independently, often missing the opportunities for mutual benefit that their joint processing could offer. In this paper, we propose C3EL, a novel unsupervised framework that jointly models both CCR and NEL, exploring the synergistic interplay between the two. C3EL recognizes that effective NEL can provide high-quality features to support the resolution of co-reference chains, as linking to a known entity provides context that disambiguates textual mentions. Likewise, by resolving co-reference clusters, CCR offers a broader context of discourse that can help disambiguate linked entities more effectively. This paper introduces an iterative algorithm that alternates between CCR and NEL steps, with each focusing on the most confidently resolved mentions. As the process continues, the system iteratively refines the co-reference chains and the entity links, leading to more accurate results in both tasks. To achieve this joint modeling, we design a framework that builds on the output of each task to inform the other. In particular, we augment the feature space for NEL by incorporating the co-referential relationships derived from CCR, enhancing the model's understanding of contextual similarity. Simultaneously, the entity links obtained from NEL are used to enrich the CCR model by providing distant knowledge features that represent how entities are connected within the knowledge base. This integration is key to capturing inter-document context and resolving ambiguity across a broader scope than what a single-task model could achieve. Experiments conducted on two distinct corpora—news-centric and web-centric—demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed joint framework.

Recent advancements in multi-task learning (MTL) in natural language processing (NLP) have demonstrated the potential of jointly training models on multiple related tasks to improve overall performance. By leveraging shared representations between tasks, these methods aim to enhance generalization and reduce the need for large amounts of task-specific data. Typically, this is achieved by linking intermediate layers of the neural network, where the shared layer captures common features and task-specific layers focus on individual characteristics. Despite the success of these approaches, one of the key challenges in conventional MTL architectures remains the lack of control over feature sharing. In standard architectures, feature sharing is either fully or partially enforced, often without considering whether the shared features are beneficial or harmful to neighboring tasks. This static and non-discriminative sharing can lead to the contamination of feature spaces, especially when tasks are not closely related or share conflicting patterns. For instance, a feature that is predictive in one task might be misleading in another, leading to interference and degradation of performance. This issue is particularly acute in text classification tasks, where the input data’s semantic and syntactic structure can vary widely across different domains and genres. To address these limitations, we propose a novel multi-task learning framework, the Leaky Multi-Task Network, designed to learn  what to share  between tasks dynamically. At the core of our architecture is the Leaky Unit, a building block that introduces memory and forgetting mechanisms to regulate the flow of information between tasks. The Leaky Unit modulates the influence of shared features by incorporating a parameterized gate that adapts during training, allowing the model to selectively retain useful features and discard irrelevant ones. By making the sharing process more flexible and adaptive, our approach mitigates the negative impact of interference and enhances the robustness of multi-task learning. Empirically, we evaluate our model on five diverse text classification datasets spanning different domains such as news, sentiment, and topic classification. The results show consistent improvements over existing MTL methods and highlight the effectiveness of the Leaky Unit in managing feature flows. Additionally, ablation studies provide insights into how task heterogeneity influences the learnability of the sharing mechanism. Overall, this work contributes a new perspective on how neural MTL models can learn to regulate feature sharing and raises important considerations for building more adaptive and resilient multi-task architectures in NLP tasks. This approach not only advances the state-of-the-art for text classification but also opens up new avenues for exploring dynamic sharing strategies in broader MTL settings.

Synchronous context-free grammars (SCFGs) have long been a foundational component in statistical machine translation (SMT) systems. These grammars are used to model alignments between source and target language sentences, enabling the simultaneous derivation of a source-language tree and a target-language tree in a way consistent with the grammar. However, one persistent hurdle in leveraging SCFGs for practical SMT systems is the decoding complexity. Classical algorithms for parsing with SCFGs require the grammar to be in Chomsky Normal Form (CNF), a restricted form in which every production rule is either binary (yielding two non-terminals) or unary (yielding one terminal). This requirement is rooted in the need to ensure cubic time complexity in the decoding process, typically achieved using pushdown automata-based methods such as the CKY-style parsing algorithm. The most well-known approach to achieving CNF for SCFGs is the synchronous binarization method introduced by Zhang et al. (2006). This method transforms arbitrary SCFG rules into CNF by introducing additional non-terminals as "bookkeeping" symbols to maintain the original structure. While this technique ensures that the grammar meets CNF, it incurs a significant drawback: the constant factor overhead associated with binary productions is high and leads to increased decoding times in practice. As a result, synchronous binarization, despite its utility in establishing cubic time complexity, often performs poorly in real-world applications due to these inflated computational costs. To mitigate this issue, DeNero et al. (2009) introduced Lexical Normal Form (LNF), a grammar formalism that is a superset of CNF and avoids the need for synchronization with additional markers. LNF maintains the cubic time guarantees of CNF under certain implicit assumptions about the structure of the grammar, particularly with regard to the maximum scope of dependencies between source and target non-terminals. However, these assumptions have not been rigorously explored or defined in the literature, leaving a gap in understanding the full extent of LNF's applicability. In this paper, we address this gap by making DeNero et al.’s implicit assumptions explicit. Furthermore, we generalize their findings by identifying a broader class of SCFGs—termed  scope-3  grammars—that can also be parsed in cubic time without the need for binarization. Notably, by pruning rules not in scope-3 from a grammar extracted using the GHKM method (Graehl et al., 2008), we demonstrate improved translation performance compared to synchronous binarization. Our contributions thus open the door to more efficient and effective decoding with SCFGs by reducing the dependence on binarization and expanding the grammatical space available for practical SMT systems.

Solving math word problems automatically has long been an attractive yet challenging area in natural language processing and artificial intelligence. Math word problems not only require understanding the language and context of the problem but also demand the ability to translate this understanding into a mathematical equation that can be solved to obtain a numerical answer. Traditionally, approaches to solving math word problems have relied heavily on handcrafted rules and feature engineering, which are labor-intensive, domain-specific, and often lack generalization. A more promising direction is the use of statistical learning methods, which aim to automatically learn patterns from annotated datasets. However, even these methods often require careful feature extraction and are limited by the complexity of the problem representations. Recent advances in deep learning have opened new possibilities for addressing the challenges in math word problem solving. Among these, sequence-to-sequence models, based on recurrent neural networks (RNNs), have shown great success in tasks that involve transforming natural language into structured outputs. In this paper, we investigate the use of a deep RNN-based model to directly translate math word problems into equation templates. Our approach moves away from the manual feature engineering typically required in statistical learning frameworks, allowing the model to learn complex relationships between the problem text and the corresponding equations from the data itself. In addition to the RNN model, we further enhance the translation process by designing a hybrid architecture that integrates a similarity-based retrieval component. This retrieval model leverages information from previously solved problems to provide additional context and support during translation, improving the overall robustness of the system. By combining the generative power of the RNN with the inductive capabilities of the retrieval model, our hybrid approach offers a more effective way to decode the underlying equations from the natural language description. Experiments conducted on a large and diverse dataset demonstrate that both the RNN model and the hybrid model significantly outperform state-of-the-art statistical learning methods in accuracy and problem-solving capability. These results highlight the potential of deep learning as a viable and efficient alternative for tackling the complexities of math word problems without reliance on manual feature crafting. Our work not only contributes to the advancement of AI in math education but also paves the way for developing more intelligent and adaptable systems for automated problem solving. The performance improvements achieved by the proposed models suggest that end-to-end deep learning is a promising direction for future research in math word problem solving.

Prevalence estimation is a crucial task in many fields, including public health, social science, and information retrieval, where the goal is to infer the relative frequency or distribution of unlabeled classes within a given group or population. A representative application would be determining the proportion of positive sentiment in a document collection when direct labeling is infeasible or too costly. Traditional methods for prevalence estimation often rely on aggregating and adjusting the outputs of discriminative classifiers, a strategy that has proven effective but tends to overlook a critical aspect: the uncertainty inherent in classifier predictions. In scientific inference, particularly when making high-stakes decisions or assessing the reliability of group-level findings, it is essential that uncertainty is quantified and reflected in the results. The limitations of current practices become especially evident when considering that classifier predictions are rarely perfect. Yet many standard approaches yield point estimates of prevalence without explicitly accounting for the variance or risk of error in the classifier itself. As a result, inferences about the population-level distribution of classes may lack the interpretability and robustness required for valid scientific or policy-relevant conclusions. To address this, we introduce a new paradigm for prevalence estimation grounded in generative probabilistic modeling. By explicitly modeling the uncertainties in both class distribution and classifier predictions, we provide a framework that is not only more statistically principled but also better aligned with the demands of real-world data analysis, where class distributions often shift unpredictably between training and testing environments. At the core of our approach is the demonstration that a discriminative classifier—such as a standard text classification model—can be re-interpreted as a generative model under a Bayesian framework. By estimating the implicit likelihood function that a classifier uses to assign probabilities to individual examples, we are able to derive a group-level prevalence distribution through Bayesian inference. This formulation enables fast and scalable computation of prevalence estimates and their associated confidence intervals. Moreover, the generative perspective allows us to naturally model and quantify the uncertainty introduced by both the data and the classifier itself, leading to more reliable inferences. In this paper, we propose two key contributions. First, we present a generative modeling approach to the problem of prevalence estimation that incorporates uncertainty in a principled way. Second, we evaluate the performance of this method in terms of its ability to produce accurate confidence intervals with proper coverage, and we show that it is robust to discrepancies in class priors between training and test distributions.

The interaction between gender and power dynamics has long been a topic of interest in sociology, organizational studies, and sociolinguistics. Gender is not merely an individual attribute; it is a socially constructed identity that influences how individuals interact, communicate, and exert influence within organizational settings. Language, as a primary medium for interaction, can reveal much about how individuals navigate and construct power relationships. Gendered communication patterns have been observed across diverse domains, with implications for how individuals assert authority, build social connections, and manage interactions. However, the intersection of gender and power in digital communication—specifically in the context of written managerial communication—remains underexplored in computational linguistics and NLP research. This study addresses this gap by investigating how gender and gender environment impact the manifestation of power in the context of email exchanges within professional settings. We focus on the Enron email corpus, a widely used dataset in email and language studies, and present a significant extension of it by annotating the gender of senders for 87% of all messages with high reliability. This annotated dataset enables the empirical investigation of how gender shapes communication strategies and the expression of power through language. Drawing from sociolinguistic literature, we test two specific hypotheses: (1) that women in managerial roles are more likely to employ face-saving communicative strategies, and (2) that women generally use language more explicitly to build and maintain social relationships. These hypotheses are rooted in broader sociolinguistic findings that women often adopt cooperative and supportive communication styles as a means of navigating power imbalances and fostering social cohesion. In addition to examining individual-level gender effects, we introduce the concept of "gender environment" to the computational analysis of written discourse. Defined as the gender composition of an email thread, gender environment allows us to explore how the overall context of a conversation modulates power-related language strategies. Our results indicate that certain manifestations of power are significantly influenced by the gender makeup of the interaction context, suggesting that power dynamics are not only a function of individual identity, but also of the social and communicative environment. Finally, we demonstrate the utility of gender information in the task of predicting the direction of power between pairs of email participants. Our findings highlight the importance of integrating gender into computational models of power and communication, and underscore the value of nuanced sociolinguistic insights in understanding digital workplace interactions. Through this work, we advance the computational study of gender and power in written communication and open new avenues for research in social dynamics and language use in organizational settings.

Parsing a sentence is a complex cognitive process that requires integration of linguistic knowledge with constraints of working memory and attention. Computational models designed to simulate this process must therefore account not only for syntactic structure and parsing accuracy, but also for the cognitive load and difficulty incurred during incremental comprehension. In this context, Hierarchical Hidden Markov Models (HHMMs) have emerged as particularly promising frameworks for cognitive modeling, as they combine an explicit representation of working memory with a parallel hypothesis space akin to psycholinguistic theories of incremental sentence processing. Moreover, HHMM parsers are computationally efficient and can approximate the bounded rationality of human sentence processing, making them well-suited for quantifying the cognitive difficulty of language comprehension. This paper focuses on the right-corner variant of the HHMM parser, a model that simulates the incremental construction of syntactic structures in a left-to-right manner, mirroring the incremental nature of human sentence processing. While previous work has demonstrated that HHMMs can achieve parsing accuracies comparable to those of more complex chart-based parsers, their potential as a cognitive model for quantifying processing difficulty remains under-investigated. This paper advances this line of research by exploring whether the right-corner HHMM parser is capable of generating complexity metrics that reflect the incremental difficulty a reader might experience when processing a sentence. We examine standard complexity metrics—such as surprisal—which have been widely used in psycholinguistics to measure processing difficulty, and reformulate these metrics within the HHMM framework. In addition, we propose a novel metric called  embedding difference , which is grounded in the hypothesis that the HHMM’s internal state representation mimics syntactic working memory. Embedding difference assesses the divergence between the current parser state and the predicted state, and we hypothesize that this divergence reflects the difficulty of maintaining syntactic structures in memory during parsing. By evaluating these metrics on a corpus annotated with reading time data, our results demonstrate that HHMM surprisal predicts empirical reading times more effectively than other baselines, such as those extracted from beam search or entropy-based parsing models. Furthermore, the embedding difference metric contributes uniquely and significantly to the predictive power of the model, suggesting that it captures an aspect of syntactic memory management critical to incremental comprehension. Our findings support the usefulness of right-corner HHMMs not only as efficient parsing models but also as robust simulation tools for measuring sentence processing complexity.

Privacy policies play a critical role in the digital economy, serving as the primary mechanism through which users are informed about how their personal data are collected, used, and shared by online platforms and organizations. These documents are not only a legal requirement under data protection regulations such as the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) and the California Consumer Privacy Act (CCPA), but they also function as a bridge between consumers and the companies that handle their sensitive information. Despite their importance, privacy policies are often criticized for being overly long, complex, and difficult for the average user to understand. A particularly salient issue lies in the prevalence of vague language within these documents. Vagueness, which is characterized by imprecise, ambiguous, or overly general expressions, can hinder users' ability to make informed decisions about their data and undermines the transparency that these policies aim to provide. The impact of vague language in privacy policies is twofold: from the user's perspective, it diminishes comprehension and trust, and from the regulator's perspective, it complicates the enforcement and accountability of data practices. Prior research has primarily focused on simplifying the structure and language of privacy policies, but few have directly addressed the automatic detection of vague words and sentences. This shortcoming is a significant barrier to improving policy transparency at scale. Automated tools that can identify vague language would not only support users in better understanding their rights but also enable regulators to assess compliance more effectively, and assist organizations in self-evaluating the clarity of their data disclosures. In this paper, we address the problem of detecting vague content within privacy policies from a computational perspective. To our knowledge, this is the first work to consider the automatic detection of vagueness in this context. We introduce a novel human-annotated dataset consisting of vague words and sentences in privacy policies, which we use to benchmark our proposed methods. We explore the effectiveness of different models for detecting vagueness at both the word and sentence level, including context-aware and context-agnostic approaches for word-level vagueness, and auxiliary-classifier generative adversarial networks (AC-GANs) for sentence-level vagueness. Our experiments provide empirical evidence of the feasibility of automatically detecting vague language in privacy policies, laying the groundwork for future research in policy transparency and user empowerment. Moreover, we conclude with practical recommendations for mitigating vagueness in privacy communications, informed by our findings.

The task of error correction in non-native language text has become increasingly important with the exponential growth of multilingual internet content and real-time language processing applications. Among the many errors commonly made by non-native English speakers, preposition misuse is particularly problematic due to the syntactic and semantic intricacies of prepositions in English. Automated correction of such errors is a challenging problem that requires more than superficial linguistic processing, as context and deeper syntactic understanding are often essential. A widely used approach to this task involves the use of discriminative classifiers, which are trained to distinguish between correct and incorrect preposition uses in given contexts. However, the effectiveness of such classifiers heavily depends on the quality and relevance of candidate corrections they are presented. In error correction tasks, the supply of candidate corrections typically assumes that all possible prepositions are potential candidates for correction. While this inclusive approach ensures completeness, it is also computationally expensive and inefficient, as not all prepositions are equally relevant in a given context. In fact, when analyzing real-world data, it becomes evident that a majority of preposition confusions are non-uniform and often follow specific patterns based on the non-native speaker's lexical or syntactic preferences. By identifying and modeling these patterns, we can significantly restrict the set of candidate corrections, improving both computational efficiency and classification performance. In this paper, we investigate the problem of generating context-sensitive confusion sets for preposition correction using an annotated corpus of non-native English texts. Our approach aims to identify the most likely preposition confusions for a given error and limit the candidate correction set accordingly. We propose and evaluate several methods for generating these confusion sets, which either rely solely on the presence of a given correction in the corpus or further incorporate the frequency of confusion for a specific preposition pair. Through empirical evaluation, we demonstrate that reducing the candidate set based on observed correction patterns significantly enhances both the precision and recall of the error correction system. Notably, we find that methods that account for the likelihood of confusion outperform those that do not, offering the most effective context-sensitive correction framework. Our results highlight the importance of leveraging corpus-derived patterns to refine candidate sets and improve the overall efficacy of preposition error correction in non-native text. This research contributes a practical framework for building more context-aware and linguistically informed error correction systems.

The task of Native Language Identification (NLI) involves determining the author's native language from text they have written in a non-native language. It has gained significance in various applications, such as forensic linguistics, content moderation, and cross-lingual systems. NLI has traditionally been approached as a classification problem, where the goal is to discriminate between different native language classes based on the linguistic patterns present in the target text. Most existing research in this area has relied on a feature set consisting of character and word n-grams, part-of-speech (PoS) n-grams, and function words. While these features have shown reasonable success, they are often limited in capturing complex, long-range lexical and syntactic patterns that may be critical for accurate identification. Recent research has highlighted the importance of higher-order collocations and syntactic structures in distinguishing native language influence. These patterns are not easily captured by simple n-gram models due to their variable lengths and compositional nature. Adaptor grammars—probabilistic grammatical frameworks that allow for modeling sequences at varying abstraction levels—offer a promising way to address these limitations. By integrating syntactic structure with lexical context, adaptor grammars can represent variable-length collocations of both PoS tags and words, enabling a more flexible and human-aligned modeling of language use. In this paper, we explore the utility of adaptor grammars for NLI. We adapt this framework to capture arbitrarily long, induced collocations from mixed textual elements (PoS tags and words), and evaluate them within both maxent and syntactic language model classification settings. To provide a suitable baseline for comparison, we introduce a simple yet effective baseline model derived from standard NLI features. Our empirical results indicate that collocations extracted in a supervised and learned fashion significantly improve classification performance when used in a maxent model, outperforming traditional features. However, the impact of the same collocations on syntactic language models is more nuanced, suggesting that further work is required to better integrate long-range collocations into these models. This study contributes to the ongoing exploration of structural and statistical features for NLI, with a focus on leveraging probabilistic grammar models to better model the syntactic and collocational richness of language. As such, it opens new directions for building more expressive and interpretable machine learning systems for language-based author profiling. We believe that our approach offers a principled way forward for capturing the subtle linguistic cues that distinguish native speakers from non-native speakers of a language.

Recent advancements in natural language processing (NLP) have focused heavily on semantic understanding, with tasks such as semantic role labeling (SRL) and word sense disambiguation (WSD) playing pivotal roles in achieving sentence-level semantic representation. SRL aims to identify predicate-argument structures in a sentence, enabling the extraction of key semantic relationships between verbs and their syntactic dependents. On the other hand, WSD seeks to determine the most appropriate meaning of a word based on contextual usage, a crucial step for disambiguating polysemous words that often underpin predicate-argument structures. While these tasks are essential, prior research has often treated them as separate problems, with systems developed independently and results processed in a pipeline fashion. This isolation, however, overlooks the rich and nuanced logical dependencies that exist between the two tasks, where decisions in one task can significantly influence the quality of the output in the other. For instance, an accurate identification of a word's sense can enhance the precision of argument role labeling in SRL by providing a clearer understanding of the verb’s semantics. Conversely, the context provided by the semantic roles in SRL can directly inform the disambiguation of a polysemous word, particularly when syntactic or lexical features alone are insufficient. Given the strong interdependencies, we argue that a combined, joint modeling approach is both natural and beneficial. This paper presents a method for jointly modeling WSD and SRL using Markov Logic, a probabilistic logic formalism that allows for the integration of first-order logical constraints with probabilistic graphical models. By doing so, we can capture complex and conditional relationships between the semantic roles of a predicate and the potential senses of its arguments in a unified and tractable framework. Our model is evaluated on the OntoNotes 3.0 corpus, a widely used benchmark annotated for both SRL and WSD. The results demonstrate that our joint Markov Logic approach not only satisfies the logical constraints between the two tasks but also significantly outperforms the pipeline counterparts in terms of overall accuracy for both WSD and SRL. This work highlights the importance of considering inter-task relationships in semantic modeling and opens new avenues for incorporating logical reasoning into joint learning frameworks. As such, it contributes to the growing body of research emphasizing the value of integrated and relational models in the field of NLP. Through this approach, we advance the goal of building more context-aware and semantically rich representations of natural language.

Recent advancements in natural language processing (NLP) have underscored the importance of coreference resolution as a fundamental component for comprehension in syntactic, semantic, and discourse modeling. At its core, coreference resolution involves identifying expressions in a text that refer to the same underlying entity or event, enabling systems to construct a coherent world model from discourse. However, the task remains challenging due to linguistic complexities, such as variation in mention expressions, ambiguities, and context-dependent resolutions. Among the various challenges in this domain, determining anaphoricity—that is, identifying whether a linguistic mention is anaphoric (i.e., refers back to prior discourse) or not—plays a critical role in improving system performance. A significant body of recent work has demonstrated that explicitly identifying and filtering non-anaphoric mentions before coreference resolution can enhance the accuracy and coherence of coreference chains. This preprocessing step helps reduce the noise introduced by mentions that do not contribute to discursive continuity, thereby simplifying clustering mechanisms and enabling more effective resolution of anaphoric relations. Despite these insights, existing approaches to anaphoricity determination often rely on traditional rule-based heuristics or shallow machine learning models that do not fully exploit the complex interdependencies between mentions in discourse. To address these limitations, this paper introduces a novel, graph-cut-based formulation for anaphoricity determination. Our method models the decision process as a graph optimization problem, where each mention is represented as a node and weighted edges capture linguistic and contextual features of their relationships. By applying graph-cut algorithms, we efficiently partition the discourse into anaphoric and non-anaphoric clusters in an end-to-end system. We evaluate the effectiveness of our approach by integrating it with a learning-based coreference resolution system and analyzing its impact on performance using the widely adopted ACE (Automated Content Extraction) data sets. Our experiments demonstrate the superiority of the graph-cut-based model over state-of-the-art alternatives in both precision and recall for anaphoricity determination, translating into improved overall coreference resolution accuracy. This work contributes to the broader goal of making coreference resolution more robust and context-aware by formalizing anaphoricity as an integrated graph optimization problem. The results highlight the value of leveraging discriminative, dependency-aware models for preprocessing tasks, which can lead to substantial gains in the downstream performance of coreference systems. By demonstrating the efficacy of a principled, graph-theoretic approach to anaphoricity determination, we open new avenues for research at the intersection of discourse modeling and machine learning in NLP.

Conversations form the backbone of online social systems, enabling the exchange of ideas, support, and collaboration. However, such interactions are often derailed by antisocial behavior—harassment, personal attacks, or incivility—that not only hampers individual participation but also degrades the overall health and sustainability of the platform. Current approaches to addressing undesirable behavior tend to focus on detecting such content   after   it has occurred—often relying on moderation systems that only intervene when the damage has already been done. This reactive approach is insufficient for environments where early disruption can irreversibly affect the tenor and viability of online discourse. The critical gap we aim to bridge is enabling   early prediction   of when a conversation is at risk of turning hostile, thereby allowing for timely interventions that could potentially avert such outcomes altogether. In this work, we introduce a novel task: the prediction of conversational failure   from the initiation phase   of an online interaction. Our goal is to identify early linguistic, pragmatic, and contextual signals that are indicative of a conversation "going awry," enabling proactive measures that can guide or redirect discourse before it spirals into undesirable territory. The challenge lies in the subtle, often ambiguous nature of early communication: while overtly hostile content is easier to detect, early warning signs often involve more nuanced aspects of language—such as conversational rhythm, politeness strategies, sarcastic undertones, or rhetorical devices—that are not easily captured by conventional toxic language detection models. To address this, we develop a framework for capturing pragmatic devices commonly employed in the initiation of conversations. These devices form the conversational "footing"—the linguistic strategies through which participants establish the tone, intent, and boundaries of the exchange. By analyzing these opening interactions, we uncover their predictive value in relation to future discourse trends, particularly in detecting early-stage signals of antisocial degradation. Importantly, our framework is designed to be agnostic to the domain of interaction, making it adaptable across a range of online platforms, from discussion forums to social media channels. We demonstrate the validity and feasibility of our task by applying this framework in a controlled setting. Our experiments reveal that early linguistic cues indeed carry meaningful predictive power for the subsequent trajectory of a conversation, even when such outcomes are not yet visible in the text itself. These findings not only highlight the value of analyzing the very beginning of conversations but also advocate for rethinking how we approach the early detection of harmful discourse on digital platforms.

Minimum error rate training (MERT) has long been a standard methodology in optimizing machine translation (MT) systems, particularly when the goal is to maximize performance on a given automatic evaluation metric such as BLEU. In this process, system parameters are iteratively adjusted to yield translations that are expected to achieve the lowest possible error rate on a specified tuning set. While MERT has proven to be an effective optimization strategy, its reliance on automatic evaluation metrics raises a significant concern: these metrics often do not align well with human judgments of translation quality. In practice, MT systems are often ultimately evaluated based on human assessments, which are more nuanced, context-sensitive, and reflective of real-world user preferences. This discrepancy between the objective used in training and the real-world evaluation criteria poses a challenge for system developers seeking to optimize for actual performance. Human-in-the-loop methods offer a promising alternative, but their practicality is often limited by the cost and effort of involving human evaluators at every stage of the training process, especially during iterative optimization like MERT. Incorporating human judgments at the tuning stage would not only be resource-intensive but could also be operationally infeasible, given that MERT requires many iterations of model evaluation and parameter adjustment. To address these limitations, we propose a novel approach that allows the integration of human judgments in a more scalable and reusable manner. We introduce RYPT, a human-informed evaluation method that leverages a pre-built and reusable database of human judgments, eliminating the need for real-time human input during the MERT process. In this paper, we examine the feasibility and practical advantages of integrating human judgments in MERT through RYPT. We first assess the diversity of the translation candidates produced during the search process and investigate how redundancy among these candidates can be exploited to make more accurate and reliable evaluations. Crucially, we demonstrate that RYPT not only effectively incorporates human intelligence but also outperforms BLEU as a predictor of actual translation quality. By laying the groundwork for a more human-centered approach to MERT, this work opens new avenues for improving MT system optimization in alignment with real-world evaluation standards. Our findings suggest that with careful design, it is possible—and beneficial—to bring human insight into the training loop without incurring prohibitive costs or complexity. Through this investigative study, we aim to stimulate further exploration into the potential of human-centered metrics in the training and development of MT systems, ultimately leading to more robust and user-aligned outputs.

Recent advancements in statistical machine translation (SMT) have increasingly focused on improving model accuracy through sophisticated feature engineering and model optimization techniques. Among these, discriminative training has emerged as a powerful method for improving translation quality by directly optimizing translation features with respect to a target objective, such as maximizing the likelihood of reference translations. Discriminative training approaches typically involve log-linear models, where features contribute with scalar weights that influence the overall score of a candidate translation hypothesis. These methods have demonstrated considerable success in small-scale feature-tuning scenarios, particularly when used for parameter re-estimation under a predefined feature space. However, the inherent complexity of SMT systems, characterized by vast search spaces and exponential model size, has made it challenging to scale discriminative training to large feature models with millions of parameters. The traditional paradigm for discriminative training in SMT is limited either by the number of features or the number of parameters used during optimization. This is primarily due to computational constraints and the lack of efficient training algorithms that can scale to the high-dimensional continuous feature spaces required in modern translation systems. Furthermore, as SMT systems grow in complexity—especially when integrating neural features or lexical constraints—model pruning becomes an essential component of efficient decoding. However, pruning impacts the full translation model by removing low-probability hypotheses, which can cause loss of distributional coverage and degradation in translation accuracy. One of the central challenges in constructing robust SMT systems, therefore, is maintaining high translation accuracy while ensuring computational feasibility through effective model optimization and pruning strategies. In this paper, we tackle the above limitations by proposing a novel approach to scale up discriminative training in log-linear SMT models. Specifically, we build upon the work of He and Deng (2012), extending their framework to train discriminatively with a massive number of features—including features with 150 million parameters—representing a significant leap in the scale of parameter space considered for discriminative training in the SMT literature. By leveraging distributed and batch-optimized learning algorithms, we demonstrate that such a large-scale model can be efficiently trained while maintaining computational stability. Moreover, we present a pragmatic application of discriminative training as a mechanism to redistribute probability mass lost due to pruning, compensating for distributional shifts and recovering translation performance. Through experiments on the widely adopted NIST MT06 benchmark, we demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach, delivering significant improvements over a strong baseline system.

The use of vulgar language is a multifaceted and culturally embedded phenomenon that plays a significant role in human communication. Despite its prevalence and potential impact on interaction, understanding why individuals choose to use vulgar expressions, and what specific purposes they serve beyond their overtly controversial nature, has remained an underexplored domain in computational linguistics and sociolinguistics. Vulgar words often transcend the boundaries of simple transgression—they are employed for various functions such as expressing aggression, demonstrating emotional intensity, establishing camaraderie, signaling group identity, or even conveying humor. This rich diversity of intentions behind their use has made vulgar language particularly challenging to interpret and model within computational pipelines, especially in domains such as sentiment analysis, hate speech detection, and social media monitoring, where such nuance is crucial. Prior work on vulgar language has predominantly focused on whether or not specific words appear, rather than the broader context in which they are deployed. A lack of annotated data that captures the functional diversity of vulgar expressions has hindered researchers from developing systematic quantitative analyses of their usage or modeling these nuances computationally. This is particularly problematic, as the same word can have starkly different implications depending on context—vulgar expressions may serve as aggressive insults in one context, while in another, they can reflect solidarity or shared experience. In response, we introduce a novel annotated dataset comprising 7,800 tweets drawn from users with known demographic traits. Each instance of a vulgar word is marked with one of six distinct functional categories, enabling a quantitative exploration of the pragmatic use of vulgarity in natural language. Our dataset is the first of its kind to comprehensively annotate the social and linguistic functions of vulgar expressions at scale, bridging the gap between sociolinguistic theory and supervised learning applications. Leveraging this resource, we present the first detailed empirical analysis of how vulgar language is employed across different contexts and social groups. We then develop and evaluate a classification model that predicts the functional category of each vulgar word based on its surrounding context, achieving 67.4 macro F1 score across six classes. Moreover, we demonstrate that modeling the intent behind the use of vulgar language enhances the performance of downstream tasks. Specifically, we show that utilizing our predicted categories leads to state-of-the-art performance in hate speech detection, underscoring the importance of capturing the nuanced motivations behind vulgar expressions in building more accurate and context-aware NLP systems.

Recent advancements in machine translation have significantly improved the fluency and accuracy of automatic systems, particularly through the adoption of statistical and later neural methods. Traditional phrase-based translation models have predominantly relied on discrete representations of linguistic units, such as phrases or words, to estimate translation probabilities based on maximum likelihood estimates. While such models have proven effective in many scenarios, they suffer from several limitations, especially in their ability to model context and generalize beyond the training data. The reliance on discrete units often necessitates a fixed vocabulary and restricts the model's ability to adapt to new or rare phrases. Moreover, conventional phrase-based systems typically operate over n-gram or phrase tables with pre-defined alignment rules, which limits their flexibility and scalability. A key challenge in the current landscape of phrase-based translation is the inadequate modeling of context. When training data is limited, these models tend to overfit to the most common phrases while failing to capture subtleties in meaning or syntactic variations. This limitation results in a degradation of performance, particularly when translating out-of-domain phrases or handling morphologically rich languages. Furthermore, as language is inherently compositional, many aspects of meaning and syntax cannot be directly captured by discrete representations. In response to these challenges, we propose the use of continuous space translation models as a novel approach to enhance the performance of translation systems. These models replace standard discrete representations with continuous vector representations of translation units. By constructing a shared continuous space for source and target languages, these models are capable of capturing the nuanced relationships between linguistic units and their contexts through their geometric properties. This methodology facilitates smoother probability estimation and improves the model's ability to generalize to unseen data. To scale this approach to a large set of translation units, we utilize a multi-layer neural network with a State Output and Unit Linkage (SOUL) architecture. This architecture enables the joint computation of translation unit representations and the estimation of the associated translation probabilities, allowing for efficient and effective learning. Our experiments demonstrate that continuous space translation models can be trained successfully and integrated with traditional n-gram translation systems to significantly enhance performance. We present empirical results on both small-scale and large-scale English-to-French translation tasks, confirming the robustness and effectiveness of our approach in improving translation accuracy while retaining scalability. These findings suggest a promising direction for future developments in the field of neural and continuous space models in machine translation.

Recent advancements in natural language processing (NLP) have enabled deep learning models to achieve significant success in a variety of tasks, particularly in relation extraction (RE), where the goal is to identify and classify semantic relationships between specific entities in text. Distantly supervised relation extraction (DS-RE) has emerged as a popular paradigm to alleviate the labor-intensive task of manual data annotation by automatically generating training data using knowledge bases (KBs). Specifically, if a sentence contains two entity mentions that appear as a known relation in a KB, it is labeled as a positive example for that relation; otherwise, it is considered negative. However, this automated label assignment often results in a large number of noisy or irrelevant instances, particularly false positives, due to the ambiguity and variability of language and the broad scope of relationships in free text. To address the challenges posed by noise in DS-RE, attention mechanisms have been widely used to improve the robustness of models by learning to focus on relevant contextual information. However, traditional 1-D vector attention mechanisms, which assign a scalar weight to each word or sentence in a flat, unstructured way, are often inadequate for capturing the complex, multi-faceted relationships required to distinguish valid from noisy instances in DS-RE. In particular, these models fail to capture the hierarchical and structural dependencies that exist at both the word and sentence levels in natural language. To overcome these limitations, this paper introduces a novel multi-level structured self-attention mechanism tailored for DS-RE within a multi-instance learning (MIL) framework. The proposed method employs a bidirectional recurrent neural network (RNN) to model the sequential information in each instance. At the word level, we introduce a structured self-attention mechanism that constructs a 2-D matrix, where each row represents a weighted distribution across different features or aspects of an instance related to the two entities of interest. This allows the model to dynamically focus on different aspects of the entity mentions and their surrounding contexts. At the instance level, we propose another structured attention mechanism, where the 2-D matrix captures the weight distribution across multiple instances, enabling the selection of the most relevant and valid sentences for relation classification. By combining these two levels of structured attention, the proposed framework captures richer and more discriminative representations, which are particularly effective in DS-RE settings with noisy data. Recent advancements in cross-lingual representation learning have primarily focused on leveraging parallel corpora or bilingual dictionaries to align word embeddings between languages. However, the scarcity of such resources—particularly for low-resource language pairs—has motivated the exploration of alternative modalities, such as images, as a shared external signal that can facilitate the induction of cross-lingual mappings. Images offer a natural medium for aligning different languages, as they are often annotated with multilingual descriptions that transcriptionally link text and visual features across language boundaries. In this paper, we explore the use of shared visual information to improve the alignment of text embeddings in different languages, without the need for direct textual alignment like bilingual dictionaries or even monolingual word vectors. We propose the use of Deep Partial Canonical Correlation Analysis (DPCCA), a novel neural architecture based on the classic statistical method of Partial Canonical Correlation Analysis (PCCA). In contrast to standard CCA and its deep variants, which aim to maximize the correlation between two views—typically text and text in source and target languages in cross-lingual settings—PCCA aims to maximize the correlation between the two textual embeddings  conditioned on  a third shared variable, which in our case is a visual representation derived from images. This conditioning allows the model to focus only on the textual correlation that is shared due to the common visual context, thereby leading to more interpretable and semantically coherent cross-lingual representations. Our approach leverages multilingual image datasets that contain textual descriptions of the same images in two languages. For example, a photo might be annotated with a French label in one source and with an English label in another. These bilingual visual annotations provide a weak form of supervision—shared context—through which alignments can be inferred. Our model is capable of learning non-linear projections of text embeddings in both languages such that their similarity is maximized given the shared visual information, even when no explicit lexical or syntactic alignment is available. To achieve this, we design a deep neural transformation of textual features and develop a novel stochastic iterative algorithm for optimizing the DPCCA objective. This allows the model to scale effectively to large datasets and to handle noisy or sparse visual-textual alignments. The performance of our models is evaluated on tasks such as multilingual word similarity and cross-lingual image description retrieval. Results show that our approach outperforms several existing methods, even though no visual signal is used during the inference phase.

The annotation and representation of discourse structure is a pivotal yet underexplored challenge in natural language processing (NLP), particularly for morphologically complex and structurally flexible languages like Chinese. Existing frameworks for discourse analysis, such as the Rhetorical Structure Theory (RST) and the Penn Discourse Treebank (PDTB), have primarily focused on English and introduced effective theoretical and methodological tools for modeling discourse relations. However, as these approaches are tailored to the syntactic and pragmatic properties of English, their direct application to Chinese discourse often encounters limitations, especially in terms of capturing hierarchical and relational dependencies adequately and meaningfully. This paper addresses the gap by proposing a novel structural framework for modeling Chinese discourse—a Connective-driven Dependency Tree (CDT) scheme that encodes discourse rhetorical relations and their hierarchical dependencies using explicitly annotated connective elements. The CDT structure, inspired by the principles of RST and architectural ideas in the PDTB, introduces an innovative encoding mechanism wherein elementary discourse units (EDUs) are treated as leaf nodes, while connectives—hallmarks of discourse relation and structure in Chinese—serve as internal nodes. This connective-driven representation enables the explicit modeling of discourse hierarchies and rhetorical relations, with connectives directly dictating the structure of the tree and the nature of the underlying discourse relations. Furthermore, the notion of discourse nuclei—central elements in RST—is re-examined through the lens of dependency theory, and is globally determined based on the role of connectives in establishing dependency and prominence within the discourse tree. By leveraging the CDT scheme, we carry out the first large-scale manual annotation of a Chinese discourse corpus, resulting in the construction of the Chinese Discourse Treebank (CDTB) with 500 annotated documents. This corpus not only complements existing discourse resources but also serves as a foundation for training and evaluating machine learning models for Chinese discourse parsing. Preliminary evaluation on the CDTB demonstrates that the CDT scheme is well-suited to the structural and rhetorical properties of Chinese discourse and that the annotated corpus is valuable for advancing research in Chinese computational linguistics. This initiative lays a foundational stone for building robust discourse processing tools and deepening our understanding of Chinese language structure from a discourse-centric perspective. In doing so, it contributes significantly to the broader vision of cross-linguistically adaptable NLP systems capable of delivering rich semantic interpretations by incorporating discourse-level knowledge. go to 400 words. Recent advancements in natural language processing (NLP) have led to the development of a wide range of word embedding techniques, designed to capture semantic and syntactic properties of words through vector representations. Evaluating these representations typically involves either extrinsic measures, which assess performance on downstream NLP tasks, or intrinsic evaluations, which provide more focused insights into individual properties of the vector spaces themselves. While extrinsic evaluations are useful for overall performance assessment, intrinsic evaluations help uncover the internal representational capabilities of word embedding models. Traditional intrinsic evaluations often rely on similarity-based measures, which compare individual word vectors to assess proximity between related concepts. Such point-based evaluations provide valuable insights but have limitations: they primarily evaluate global properties of embeddings and overlook the complex, structured subspaces that may be essential for capturing nuanced semantic relationships. For example, these evaluations may not reliably reflect a model's ability to encode relationships like animacy, topicality, polysemy, or syntactic roles, which are often indicative of better performance in downstream tasks. We propose a novel intrinsic evaluation methodology for word embedding representations that focuses on the evaluation of specific subspaces within the vector space. Our framework is grounded in four fundamental criteria derived from the characteristics of natural language, each of which presents challenges for NLP systems. These criteria encompass the human-like modeling of semantic hierarchies, syntactic variation, semantic ambiguity, and task-relevant generalization. We develop targeted tests to probe whether a given embedding model encodes sufficient subspaces to meet these linguistic criteria. This contrasts sharply with traditional intrinsic methods, which lack such targeted investigation at the subspace level. By viewing embeddings not just as isolated points but as structured subspaces, our approach offers a more granular and meaningful evaluation of the representational capabilities of various embedding models. We apply our methodology to a comparative analysis between a classical count-based vector model (e.g., TF-IDF) and contemporary neural network models (e.g., Word2Vec, GloVe, FastText). The results not only highlight the strengths and weaknesses of each model with respect to the fundamental linguistic criteria but also provide a more comprehensive and linguistically grounded evaluation of word embeddings. Our work thereby contributes a new perspective to intrinsic evaluation, offering a robust framework for understanding how well word representations capture the complexities of natural language. This approach not only enhances the interpretability of various embedding techniques but also supports more meaningful comparisons and informed model development.

The task of identifying entity mentions from unstructured text, particularly in the context of noisy web data, remains a central and challenging problem in natural language processing (NLP). With the exponential growth of textual content across the web, data sources are often heterogeneous, full of noise, and vary significantly in structure and formatting. This makes automated entity mention identification a difficult and error-prone process. While some entity types, such as dates, times, email addresses, and institutional codes (e.g., course numbers), often follow predictable formats, the sheer diversity and unconstrained nature of web documents render even these seemingly straightforward entities challenging to identify reliably. The problem becomes even more complex when the goal is to balance high precision and recall, given the limitations and variability of patterns that web data present. Regular expressions (REs) are a standard tool used for pattern matching and entity extraction due to their expressive power and efficiency. Despite their widespread use, REs are inherently brittle in dynamic and noisy environments. They can fail to capture variations in formatting, are frequently incomplete for real-world input, and are non-trivial to maintain, especially when new or less common patterns arise. Furthermore, attempts to create robust and comprehensive REs for complex or diverse entity types are often impractical, as it is nearly impossible to anticipate all possible variations. As a result, many modern NLP systems have shifted towards deep learning models that can learn complex patterns from large datasets. However, these models often require extensive labeled training data, which is expensive and time-consuming to obtain for every new entity type or domain. This paper presents a novel and practical approach that integrates the strengths of regular expressions, deep learning, and a minimal human-in-the-loop component into a unified framework for entity mention mining in web data. The method begins with the collection or creation of REs for a specific entity type. These REs are used to extract weakly labeled examples from a large document corpus. A neural network is then trained to predict these weak labels, leveraging the patterns captured by the REs while learning to generalize beyond them. To refine the model and improve accuracy, a small set of documents is labeled by a human expert, and the network is fine-tuned on this expert-verified data. The resulting system combines the scalability of REs, the generalization capability of neural models, and the precision of human supervision in an efficient and cost-effective workflow.

Statistical Machine Translation (SMT) has long been a central area of research in computational linguistics and natural language processing. The advent of phrase-based SMT has significantly improved the quality of translation outputs by modeling bilingual word sequences, enabling systems to capture more robust and natural language phenomena compared to earlier word-based approaches. A pivotal component of phrase-based SMT is the  decoding  process, which involves searching for the most likely target sentence given a source sentence. A fundamental decision in this process is the  direction  of search: whether the decoder constructs the target sentence from left to right, from right to left, or through some combination. Traditionally, most phrase-based SMT systems employ a  left-to-right  (L2R) decoding strategy, inspired by the well-known assumption that sentence production in many languages proceeds left-to-right. However, this assumption is not universally valid. Some languages and language pairs may benefit more from an opposite decoding direction, especially those where the structural properties, such as word order or syntactic alignment, differ significantly between the source and target languages. Recent research has increasingly shown that decoding direction can have a profound impact on translation performance, though the extent and nature of this impact remain relatively underexplored in the context of a large-scale and diverse evaluation framework. This paper addresses this gap by systematically investigating the impact of decoding direction in phrase-based SMT. We compare the traditional L2R strategy against a  right-to-left  (R2L) approach and evaluate the effectiveness of combining the strengths of both directions through a  bidirectional  decoding strategy. The goal is to determine whether language-specific biases in decoding directions can be mitigated by integrating both left-to-right and right-to-left search strategies. Our evaluation involves an extensive experimental analysis covering 272 different language pairs, representing a wide range of structural and typological diversity. We find that the optimal decoding direction is highly dependent on the language pair, with R2L often outperforming L2R for many configurations. More notably, the bidirectional decoding strategy consistently outperforms both unidirectional approaches across nearly all language pairs, suggesting that integrating alignment preferences from both directions leads to more accurate and stable translation performance. Our analysis demonstrates that such improvements are largely independent of specific language typological properties, highlighting the value of bidirectional approaches in building more robust and generalizable machine translation systems. These findings have important implications for the design of phrase-based SMT systems and open new avenues for exploring decoding strategies that abstract away language-specific constraints.

Recent advancements in natural language processing (NLP) have enabled significant improvements in the task of event extraction, which aims to identify structured information about real-world events from unstructured text. Despite these gains, many challenges remain, particularly in scenarios where event descriptions appear implicitly or are embedded within richer, more complex narratives. Traditional event extraction systems heavily rely on the presence of event keywords and clear event indicators to identify and classify roles such as agents, themes, and locations. However, in many real-world contexts—such as social media, financial reports, or historical documents—events are often described indirectly or appear in "secondary contexts," where the event itself is not the main topic of the sentence or paragraph. This makes the identification of event role fillers significantly more difficult, especially when event keywords are absent or ambiguous. To address this challenge, our research focuses on improving event extraction by learning to detect event role fillers in secondary contexts—situations where the presence of an event is implied or only partially described. We propose a multilayered event extraction architecture designed to progressively "zoom in" on relevant information, even when it is not explicitly tied to event lexical triggers. By layering different types of classifiers within a structured pipeline, our model can gradually isolate event-related information from the surrounding text. At the heart of this system is a document genre classifier that first identifies whether a text contains event narratives. This is followed by two sentence-level classifiers, each responsible for narrowing the scope of event-related content within the document. Finally, noun phrase classifiers extract the role fillers associated with the event, even in the absence of explicit event keywords. This layered approach not only enhances the ability to detect events in indirect or semantically complex texts, but it also allows the model to be robust in heterogeneous document settings where event descriptions are sparse or encased in surrounding context. Through comprehensive evaluation on the MUC-4 event extraction dataset, we demonstrate that our pipeline outperforms existing systems in identifying role fillers, particularly in secondary contexts where previous methods struggle. This work contributes to the broader goal of building more context-aware and nuanced event extraction systems capable of understanding events beyond their most obvious lexical markers. By extending the scope of event detection into secondary contexts, our architecture moves the field of event extraction closer to truly understanding events as they appear in the real world.

The process of early language acquisition is a remarkable feat of cognitive development in which infants must learn both the meanings and forms of words in their native language and understand how these forms can vary across different productions. This dual challenge involves acquiring a lexical inventory and simultaneously building a mental model of phonetic and phonological patterns that govern how words are uttered in real speech. For instance, the English word "the" can surface phonetically as [Di], [D@], or even [Ø] in certain contexts. Capturing this kind of articulatory flexibility is essential not only for recognizing and producing spoken words accurately but also for distinguishing words from one another. Despite the intertwined nature of these two learning tasks—building a lexicon and learning phonetic variation—most computational models of early language acquisition treat them separately. Lexical learning models often assume a fixed set of canonical word pronunciations, thereby ignoring the fact that each word in a child's lexicon is actually represented by a constellation of variable forms. On the other hand, phonetic and phonological models in computational linguistics usually focus on articulatory patterns without explicitly building a vocabulary. This compartmentalized view is at odds with behavioral and perceptual evidence suggesting that infants integrate information from both lexical development and phonetic perception as they listen to and learn language from their environment. In this paper, we present a unified Bayesian model that simultaneously learns a lexical inventory and a model of pronunciation variability. Our approach leverages the natural co-occurrence of phonetic forms in child-directed speech and models their relationship to lexical items through probabilistic clustering. The model is structured to learn both a language model over lexical items and a log-linear model of phonetic variation based on articulatory features. Notably, it does so without access to annotated word boundaries or a pre-defined lexicon, relying instead on a bootstrapping process to jointly infer these from transcribed surface forms. We evaluate our model on a realistic child-directed speech corpus that includes naturally occurring phonetic variation. We consider both cases where word boundaries are provided as gold-standard annotations and settings where they are automatically inferred. Our findings demonstrate that modeling phonetic variability not only aligns better with empirical observations of how children learn language but also leads to more accurate and robust lexical learning as compared to systems that ignore pronunciation diversity.
